#5088. XRP Briefly Drops to $0.89 as Crypto Liquidity Retreats

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

XRP has joined the wider cryptocurrency sell-off with a particularly sharp move, briefly touching about $0.89 as investors cut exposure to riskier assets. The level is notable because it takes the token back toward prices last seen in late 2024, but the more important story is what lies behind the drop: falling liquidity, negative momentum and a market in which even established cryptocurrencies are struggling to attract fresh buyers.

This is not a claim that XRP's network has stopped working or that a specific legal ruling triggered the move. The latest price reference comes from market reporting published on November 15, and prices can change significantly after that snapshot.

CoinDesk reported that XRP traded as low as roughly $0.89 amid the downturn. The token's decline for the quarter was around 36% at the reporting snapshot. Bitcoin and Ether were also under pressure, which points to a market-wide reduction in risk rather than a wholly isolated loss of confidence in the XRP Ledger.

Altcoins frequently move more aggressively than Bitcoin in both directions. Their order books can be thinner, the pool of marginal buyers smaller and speculative positioning more sensitive to sudden changes in sentiment. That combination can turn a difficult trading week into a dramatic percentage move, particularly when traders close leveraged positions into weak liquidity.

The same report cited approximately $19.13 million in net weekly withdrawals from US XRP exchange-traded funds, while noting that cumulative inflows since the products launched in November 2025 were still around $1.5 billion. Both figures can be true. A negative week signals near-term caution, but it does not erase a longer period in which investors built exposure through regulated market products.

What matters next is whether withdrawals persist and whether they are accompanied by genuinely weaker spot demand. ETF flows are only one distribution channel for XRP, so they should not be treated as a perfect measure of every holder's intentions. The wider Bitcoin ETF outflow trend covered by NewsBTC suggests the retreat is not confined to XRP products.

It is easy during a sell-off to treat a token's market price as a verdict on every development effort associated with it. In practice, those are separate issues. Developers can continue building features while market participants reduce their exposure, just as a strong price rally can occur without any corresponding improvement in network use.

For example, NewsBTC recently examined the XRP Ledger's work on quantum-resistant accounts, a longer-term technical initiative that should be assessed on its own timetable. Investors following XRP need to distinguish changes in network capabilities, adoption and liquidity from movements driven by broader risk appetite.

The obvious question is whether XRP can reclaim and maintain higher prices once trading conditions normalise. But watching a single support line will not settle the outlook. Rising spot volume on recoveries, steadier derivatives funding and improving ETF flows would each offer different evidence that demand is returning. Continued stablecoin contraction across crypto markets could work in the opposite direction.

The central takeaway is that XRP's fall is severe without necessarily being mysterious. A market that is reducing leverage and cash-like liquidity can punish liquid altcoins quickly. Until there is convincing evidence that that process has run its course, calling an exact bottom would be a guess rather than analysis.

#5087. XRP Exchange Balances Hit Yearly High, but Long-Term Holders Stay Put

Home » Trendsetter News » XRP Exchange Balances Hit Yearly High, but Long-Term Holders Stay Put

XRP exchange balances have reached a one-year high, while the share of tokens untouched for over a year nears its annual peak.

XRP held on exchanges has reached a one-year high even as the share of coins untouched for more than a year approaches its own annual peak, according to figures cited by wealth-focused commentator Kamilah Stevenson.

Her latest video examines that split following a roughly 10% price decline, arguing that investors’ financial circumstances can matter as much as their market convictions.

Stevenson cites CryptoQuant data showing approximately 11.8 billion XRP on exchanges, the highest balance in a year. That puts more tokens within easy reach of trading, although exchange deposits alone do not establish that holders intend to sell.

Meanwhile, Glassnode figures cited in the video put the share of XRP unmoved for more than a year at roughly 56%, up from 51% in January. Stevenson also says XRP exchange-traded funds still hold about 1.19 billion tokens, despite a small outflow ending a reported 13-week inflow streak.

“Both groups saw the same price,” she says. “They reacted to it in completely opposite ways.”

The contrast is striking, but the metrics have limits. Coins remaining stationary demonstrate inactivity, not necessarily fresh buying or confidence, and neither measure establishes where XRP’s price goes next.

Dr. Stevenson identifies three recurring sources of selling pressure: leverage, investing money needed for near-term expenses, and entering a volatile market without a plan.

She cites roughly $25.7 million in XRP liquidations on Binance during a recent sell-off as an example of positions being closed regardless of investors’ intentions.

Her broader bullish case rests partly on institutional activity involving Ripple and its RLUSD stablecoin.

The YouTube video names Standard Chartered, Cross River Bank and DriveWealth among firms involved in custody, banking or settlement developments.

Those developments should not be treated as equivalent to demand for XRP itself. Nor does institutional infrastructure guarantee that token prices will recover.

The most durable point is about liquidity: cash reserves and manageable exposure reduce the likelihood that an unexpected bill or margin call dictates a sale.

Exchange balances may signal potential selling pressure across the market; they cannot reveal which holders can afford to wait.

#5084. Stablecoin Supply Shrinkage Raises a Bigger Question About Crypto Liquidity

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Crypto investors spend plenty of time staring at Bitcoin charts, but one of the more revealing signals this month may be the amount of dollar-backed stablecoins circulating across the market. Recent data suggests that the combined supply of major stablecoins has contracted materially from its earlier peak. That matters because these tokens are often the cash-like instruments traders use to move money between exchanges, DeFi protocols and new positions.

A shrinking supply does not automatically cause a market crash, and it certainly does not mean every stablecoin holder has left crypto. It does, however, raise a practical question: is the industry's readily deployable dollar liquidity getting smaller just as prices are falling?

CoinDesk's November 15 market report described the combined stablecoin market retreating toward roughly $244 billion, compared with a peak near $270 billion in May 2026. It also cited Glassnode data indicating a decline of approximately $17 billion over a one-month period. These are market snapshots from particular datasets, not a count of dollars sitting in every crypto trading account.

The distinction is significant. Stablecoin supply changes when issuers create or redeem tokens, but balances also shift among blockchains, venues and use cases. An on-chain transfer from one exchange to another does not shrink total issuance. A redemption in which tokens are destroyed can do so. Comparing data providers therefore requires consistent definitions and time windows.

Stablecoins serve several functions at once. They can be a temporary refuge during volatile markets, a settlement instrument for trading and a payments rail for companies that want digital dollars without holding Bitcoin or Ether. When aggregate supply grows, traders often interpret that as potential purchasing power entering the ecosystem. When it contracts, one plausible reading is that capital is being withdrawn or used elsewhere.

But supply and demand are not a one-step equation. A dollar token sitting idle in a wallet may be less important to near-term prices than a smaller amount actively circulating through exchanges. Conversely, a market can recover even while headline supply remains flat if existing balances change hands more frequently. The connection is useful, not deterministic.

The business case for stablecoins does not disappear when trading demand weakens. NewsBTC's coverage of Bitso Business's reported payment volumes illustrates how companies use digital dollars for transfers and settlement rather than speculation. Likewise, USDC's rollout through Samsung Wallet on Solana shows the payments and consumer-access dimension.

That creates an interesting tension. Trading-led demand can ebb even as infrastructure for real-world payments develops. Analysts should therefore ask where supply is shrinking, what users are doing with the remaining balances and whether dollar liquidity on exchanges is tightening faster than demand in payments networks.

Net issuance and redemptions from major issuers are an obvious starting point. Exchange stablecoin balances, cross-chain transfers and DeFi borrowing rates can help provide context, provided their methodology is clear. More importantly, these series should be compared with spot buying and ETF flows rather than used in isolation.

A return to stablecoin growth would not guarantee a rally, but it could indicate that more cash-like capacity is entering the system. Until then, the contraction is another reminder that crypto prices are shaped by the availability of capital as much as by the promise of the underlying technology.

#5082. Tron, Tether and Chainalysis Form a New Crypto-Crime Task Force—Replacing One That Just Collapsed

Tron, Tether and Chainalysis Form a New Crypto-Crime Task Force—Replacing One That Just Collapsed

Tron, Tether, and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis have launched a joint effort to hunt down and disrupt criminal activity involving the USDT stablecoin, just weeks after a nearly identical alliance, with a different analytics partner, quietly fell apart.

Announced Wednesday, the Digital Crime Task Force aims to identify illicit activity involving Tether’s USDT on the Tron blockchain and surface it for law enforcement before criminals can move their funds.

The pitch is a shift from reactive to proactive: rather than waiting for a victim to report a crime or an investigator to flag tainted funds, the group says it will proactively trace criminal networks and coordinate asset freezes, drawing on Chainalysis’s intelligence and AI-powered investigative tools. It will also accept tips and freeze requests from police.

“Criminals are using AI to move faster than ever, and waiting for a victim to report a crime is no longer good enough,” said Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino, noting the company has frozen more than $7 billion tied to illicit activity while working with over 360 law enforcement agencies across 73 countries.

Tron founder Justin Sun framed it as protecting the millions who rely on USDT, which circulates on Tron to the tune of more than $94 billion.

The notable wrinkle is what this new alliance replaces. Tron and Tether previously ran a similar operation, the T3 Financial Crime Unit, formed in 2024 with rival analytics firm TRM Labs and later joined by Binance. Together, the group froze more than $450 million in tainted assets.

But Bloomberg reported earlier this month that T3 was quietly disbanded in late August, with people familiar citing slow response times and a lack of coordination among its members. Its collapse went public just days before the record $6.4 billion Binance hack.

Swapping TRM for Chainalysis is a pointed move, given the two are fierce competitors. Chainalysis has even sued the U.S. government over an ICE contract awarded to TRM without competitive bidding, underscoring the rivalry now running through crypto’s crime-fighting infrastructure.

The new task force says it will target a broad sweep of threats, from romance and investment scams to stolen funds, terrorist financing, North Korean cyber operations, cartel money laundering and child-exploitation material.

The group also framed the effort around a coming era of autonomous AI agents transacting onchain, which it warned will open fresh avenues for criminal exploitation.

The activity of investors who are trying to cash out or pull their holdings away from exchanges could be the key here. Growing payments volume most likely reflects growing fear among investors, as some of them move funds to exchanges in order to liquidate their coins.

Payments volume rises, but so does the bear market pressure, with a possibility of a further downturn that could make things worse than they already are.

#5078. Ether ETFs Approach an Unwanted Record After Seven Weeks of Outflows

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

US spot Ether exchange-traded funds are edging toward an uncomfortable milestone. The category has now recorded seven consecutive weeks of net withdrawals, placing it one additional negative week away from matching the longest losing streak identified in the current dataset. That is an especially awkward backdrop for Ethereum supporters who see exchange-traded products as a bridge between the network and traditional investment accounts.

The withdrawal trend does not tell us that institutions have abandoned Ethereum, nor does it measure how much activity is occurring on the blockchain. It does indicate that ETF demand has been persistently soft during a period of broader market stress.

The Block's review of SoSoValue figures put net withdrawals from US spot Ether ETFs at about $398.9 million for the week ending November 13. That marked a seventh consecutive weekly outflow, with cumulative withdrawals of roughly $2.42 billion since late September. Another negative week would tie the eight-week losing streaks the category has previously experienced.

A single week's figure can be influenced by a handful of large transactions, but seven weeks is long enough to warrant closer examination. NewsBTC's report on the November 9 Ether ETF outflow captured one daily episode; the accumulated weekly data reveals how the pressure has persisted beyond that session.

Owning an Ether ETF share and using Ethereum are fundamentally different activities. A fund investor primarily seeks financial exposure to ETH's price, subject to the product's particular structure and fees. A blockchain user might be paying transaction charges, supplying liquidity, issuing a token or building an application. The two can influence one another over time, but neither provides a complete picture of the other.

For this reason, it would be a mistake to use fund outflows as evidence that smart contracts are no longer being used. A better test of network health also considers transactions, fees, applications, security and adoption. Those indicators require interpretation too, particularly as activity shifts across Ethereum's scaling ecosystem.

The Ether figures arrived in a week when spot Bitcoin ETFs also lost more than $1 billion, and other crypto fund categories largely experienced withdrawals. That broad pattern suggests investors may be reducing digital-asset exposure generally rather than rotating decisively from ETH into BTC. It is a different story from one in which capital leaves one token product but pours into another.

There is still an important distinction between price losses and fund flows. ETH's falling market value can reduce ETF assets without any redemption, while net withdrawals reflect investor activity through the fund structure. Keeping those measures separate prevents the discussion from exaggerating the selling actually revealed by the data.

The network's DeFi ecosystem continues to evolve, including proposals over how protocols capture fees and share economic value. Aave's recent reserve-factor discussion is one example of the operational debates taking place independently of fund investor sentiment.

For the next trading week, investors will watch whether Ether funds can interrupt the run of negative flows and whether the change is broad or concentrated in one vehicle. A positive week would not erase the preceding losses, but it would be a measurable sign that some buyers are reconsidering. Until then, the ETF channel remains an obvious pressure point for Ethereum's market narrative.

#5076. Kava Lend Exploit Exposes a Dangerous Gap in DeFi Collateral Accounting

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

An exploit at Kava Lend has drained roughly 55 million KAVA tokens from the lending protocol, highlighting a class of DeFi vulnerability that can remain dormant until unusual market conditions make it dangerous. The incident did not involve an attacker magically creating unlimited tokens. Instead, on-chain analysis indicates that a tiny balance in a largely inactive stablecoin market caused the protocol to overstate the value of collateral, opening the door to repeated borrowing.

The attack and the sharp fall in KAVA's price unfolded on November 14. The protocol team has said the incident was contained within Kava Lend, but a full official post-mortem and recovery plan had not been published in the reporting reviewed for this article.

According to The Block's account of the incident, the attacker targeted a Kava Lend market for BUSD, a stablecoin whose issuer stopped minting new tokens in 2023. The market was barely active. By pushing its effective net supply extremely close to zero, the attacker triggered a calculation that exaggerated the accounting value of deposits by approximately 243,000 times.

This was not a huge cash deposit suddenly becoming a huge amount of real money. It was a software-accounting error: the lending system treated collateral as far more valuable than it actually was. Such errors are particularly dangerous in lending protocols because borrowing limits depend on accurate collateral valuations. If that relationship breaks, the system can approve loans that no legitimate market price would support.

The attacker reportedly executed 127 KAVA borrow transactions, drawing roughly 55.2 million tokens from the pool. At the price before the attack, those tokens were worth approximately $3.76 million. Around 49.2 million KAVA were then sent to BNB Chain through LayerZero, with sales producing about $2.09 million in BNB and USDT, according to the published on-chain analysis.

Those figures describe different things. The larger dollar value is an estimate based on the pre-attack token price, while the smaller amount describes proceeds realised after heavy selling into a falling market. The amount borrowed, value lost by lenders and value ultimately recoverable may differ. A definitive accounting should await the protocol's incident report.

Kava said the event was not an infinite-mint problem and was isolated to Kava Lend. It also reported precautionary steps affecting bridging, while some trading venues restricted KAVA transfers. Those actions may limit additional damage, but they do not automatically replenish tokens owed to depositors or explain how the accounting failure escaped detection.

The most useful follow-up is not a dramatic price prediction. It is a clear statement about who bore the loss, whether any market remains impaired, what code changes are proposed and whether those changes have undergone independent review. The availability of an audit label alone cannot substitute for understanding the exact edge case that failed.

Lending protocols routinely make complex decisions using collateral ratios, interest indexes, liquidity pools and oracle prices. As NewsBTC's coverage of Aave governance shows, even mature money markets require ongoing decisions about risk and economic design. Institutional interest in lending infrastructure makes those controls more consequential, not less.

The Kava case is a reminder that the most damaging exploit may come from an apparently forgotten market rather than a heavily traded one. For anyone depositing into a DeFi lender, exposure to every supported collateral market can matter, even if they never personally touch the asset that starts the chain reaction.

#5074. XRP Backer Counters SWIFT’s New Speed Report

Home » Ripple (XRP) » XRP Backer Counters SWIFT’s New Speed Report

The preference for nearly-immediate settlement time windows unites a roster of banks in SWIFT’s chain trial.

A Swift report highlighting faster cross-border payments drew a pointed response from Digital Asset Investor, who replied that he prefers 3-4 seconds and pointed to XRP.

The exchange underscores the ongoing contrast between improvements in traditional interbank messaging and the settlement times associated with blockchain-based rails.

Swift’s Spotlight on Speed report, released this week, shows that 50% of payments on its network now reach the recipient institution within 40 seconds, with 75% arriving within 10 minutes.

What will define the next generation of cross-border payments?The answer? More than just speed.Throughout @Sibos, conversations repeatedly focused on the customer experience. How do we make cross-border transactions more intuitive, more transparent and more predictable for… pic.twitter.com/yZoeZMDN4z

The cooperative noted that these figures put the industry ahead of the G20’s target for one-hour end-to-end processing by 2027 in the interbank leg of the journey.

The same report emphasizes that the “last mile”, the period after a payment reaches the receiving bank and before it is credited to the beneficiary’s account, still accounts for about 80% of the average end-to-end journey time.

Across 40 receiving markets analyzed, median last-mile processing sat near one hour in roughly one-third of cases, with wide variation between cross-border markets.

The conglomerate has called for greater use of one-leg-out models that connect international payments to domestic instant systems to reduce those final delays.

Digital Asset Investor’s reply to the Swift post was brief: “I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP.” The comment references the XRP Ledger’s typical ledger close time of roughly 3-5 seconds, which provides finality for on-ledger transfers.

I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP. https://t.co/tBqXtEsqeM

In Ripple’s On-Demand Liquidity (ODL) model, XRP is used as a bridge asset so that currency conversion and settlement can occur without pre-funded nostro accounts.

End-to-end ODL flows that include exchange conversions have been described in the 3-5 second range for the core ledger step, though real-world completion including compliance and local payouts is often measured in seconds to a few minutes depending on the corridor.

The two claims are not measuring identical segments of a payment. Swift’s 40-second figure tracks time to the recipient institution, while the longer last-mile delays occur after that point.

https://t.co/ZA3CcggMOf @swiftcommunity @XRP @realfrandeolza @Archie_XRPL

XRP’s cited 3-4 second window refers primarily to ledger settlement of the bridge asset itself.

Traditional systems still handle the bulk of global bank-to-bank volume and benefit from established compliance and messaging standards; blockchain rails emphasize reduced pre-funding and faster finality on the asset transfer.

Whether the shorter settlement window on XRP produces a meaningfully better end-user experience continues to depend on how the on- and off-ramps, local banking rails, and compliance steps are integrated in any given corridor.

#5073. 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit

'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after 33 years, and some of the loudest names in crypto and artificial intelligence think the company just made a spectacular mistake.

On Thursday, Nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation as president, CEO, and board member, and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO. The move followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China, as well as concerns over a reported relationship with an Nvidia employee.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia said in a board statement that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and its independent investigation remains underway. The allegations about foreign intelligence have not established that Huang knowingly provided information to a foreign government.

But even without any leaks, the scandal was enough for the board to decide to let him go.

The market did not welcome the transition. Nvidia shares fell 14% at Thursday’s opening bell; with more than $500 billion wiped from U.S. stocks in a single minute. The company that was once the most valuable in the world has now fallen to third on that list.

Nvidia was already under pressure before the scandal, and Huang’s departure raised a particular problem for a company built so closely around its founder: Who, exactly, can replace him?

Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, the Binance co-founder and one of crypto’s most influential executives, said “it's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.” Bitcoin entrepreneur and former Kraken executive Dan Held agreed, writing, “He shouldn't have resigned,” and argued that Huang’s personal problems should be weighed against the company he built.

It's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.

— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) November 12, 2026

U.S. intelligence officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset, but Nvidia says it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, and Singaporean authorities said they lacked sufficient evidence to establish that she committed a crime. As of today, no law enforcement agency has presented any hard evidence against Alice Huang.

Anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote. “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.”

Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.

— Anthony Pompliano 🌪 (@APompliano) November 12, 2026

Surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat.

For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked, alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. In other words, the crypto solution to a potential platform bottleneck is to stop trusting a single platform.

That concern is more than a slogan for a founder whose Venice AI business is built around private access to open models. Voorhees previously told Decrypt that the antidote to excessive control over AI was “open-source decentralization.”

Some developers saw a deeper threat in Huang’s departure: the loss of a powerful corporate champion of downloadable AI models, whose underlying parameters, or weights, can be run outside the companies that built them.

The worry is that an Nvidia without Huang could become less willing to confront firms that keep their most advanced models behind proprietary services.

Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate and hardware entrepreneur, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. He pointed to a “Pace the Frontier” campaign and argued that Huang responded by building the Open Secure AI Alliance, ending his post with, “And today, we lost him.”

OpenAI and Anthropic have spent millions lobbying the US Congress to ban open weights.

When they formed the "Pace the Frontier" group to push for strict limits on open models, Jensen stepped up right away.

He created the Open Secure Alliance to fight back.

Look at the list of… pic.twitter.com/OeasotcLO3

In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance, which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions.

The broader conspiracy claim needs, of course, much more evidence. The Pacing the Frontier initiative is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang.

OpenAI subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said explicitly that his company had never advocated such a ban.

Other posts on social media showed how much anxiety the debate had generated. A commenter replied to Song that they were now “counting on Huawei and Deepseek for the very survival of the OSS community.”

Huawei and Deepseek are two major Chinese companies, known for their open-source developments

I can't believe now I am counting on Huawei and Deepseek for the very survival of the OSS community. What a loss...

— Look4Newways (@sflk2026) November 12, 2026

The issue comes with a rather large business backdrop. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire the open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027.

That arrangement could put both the hardware used to build AI and the largest hub used to distribute open models under one company’s influence—arguably, the most powerful company on earth.

Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney was among the highest-profile tech executives to condemn the exit. “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” he wrote, praising Huang for keeping innovation moving even as Nvidia grew into an enormous company.

A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity. Jensen founded and ran one of the few companies to reach a massive scale while driving massive continued innovation and ubiquity, while others fell into the trap of ever-increasing extraction. https://t.co/AkS5XT9HF8

— Tim Sweeney (@TimSweeneyEpic) November 12, 2026

Perplexity AI co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas took a more personal approach. “Thank you Jensen Huang for 33 years of bold leadership,” he wrote. He also credited Huang’s generosity toward other founders, including himself, for helping shape the future of American AI.

Peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, argued that the decision felt rushed. “If that spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” he wrote on X. “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.”

If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal. Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.

— Peter Steinberger (@steipete) November 12, 2026

Financial commentator The Kobeissi Letter had urged the board to consult shareholders before any decision, arguing that there was no obvious replacement and citing research on the costs of ousting successful CEOs. After the announcement, the account called the resignation “the most costly mistake of the AI Revolution.”

Former DWS executive and corporate-governance critic Desiree Fixler invoked directors’ fiduciary duty, saying the board should protect shareholders instead of indulging what she called a media frenzy.

In general, most of the reactions were supportive, separating personal affairs from business. The corporate espionage angle has apparently not swayed tech enthusiasts.

This Jensen Huang thing is so ugly. Guy takes a company from zero to absolute pinnacle, through blood, sweat, and tears, a pure founder’s founder, great products, makes so many people rich beyond their imaginations, champions open free local AI, and then the incumbent modern…

— Neil Woodfine (@nwoodfine) November 12, 2026

Not everyone outside that chorus thought the security questions could be set aside. North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer had called for Huang’s exit, warning about the risk of blackmail and saying the internal investigation was insufficient. The concern from Washington has been largely uniform: the possibility of compromising pressure against the leader of a company central to U.S. AI infrastructure.

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has remained supportive of Huang: “He’s definitely suffering,” he told the press. “I think he’ll be in good shape.”

Speculation about Huang’s next job spread just as quickly as criticism of his last one. Responding to an X user asking him to hire Huang, Elon Musk replied, “That would be an honor.”

Nvidia says its board is searching for a permanent CEO from inside and outside the company, with Kress running the business in the meantime. Its next scheduled earnings report is November 17, the first major financial update investors will receive after Huang’s departure.

This week, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao shared a comparison of Bitcoin charts ahead of the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs and called it "an interesting analysis." Several users in the replies to his post blamed the drop in Bitcoin on selling by Binance.

Binance is the largest crypto exchange by trading volume, and a large share of futures liquidations takes place on the platform. On Nov. 13, crypto exchanges liquidated 187,389 traders for a total of $1.65 billion in 24 hours, and 88% of that amount came from long positions, according to CoinGlass. Still, the CVD on the Binance spot market has stayed positive since Oct. 31.

Coinbase is the custodian for most U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, including BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, and many U.S. institutional investors trade on the platform through Coinbase Prime.

Anthropic is set to start trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19, and the selling on Coinbase comes ahead of the listing. Fundstrat managing partner Tom Lee has called the recent drawdown in Bitcoin a temporary rotation of money into mega-IPOs, and in the 50 days before the Anthropic IPO, Bitcoin has lost around 18%.

The CVD on Coinbase fell most sharply between Nov. 10 and Nov. 14, and Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 during this period, according to CoinGlass data.

#5071. What’s keeping Bitcoin buyers away despite 2 leverage flushes in 5 days?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

On 29th October, the largest hack in crypto’s history took Bitcoin to a low near $76,200. A few days later, on 5th November, an AI-driven tech crash spilled into crypto. The Nasdaq 100 fell by 6.4%, while semiconductor stocks tumbled by 12%.

This chaos set off leveraged liquidations of roughly $1.1 billion and pushed Bitcoin’s price below $74,000.

Two different shocks, a historical Binance breach, and an AI token sell-off. Though they seem unrelated on the surface, this time they were actually the catalyst for the same event. What Bitcoin saw was a surge in speculative positioning, but what the king coin did not see was a buyer.

The market’s first take on the Binance hack was that crypto had passed a test. Bitcoin fell by about 6% from its 28th October close — a fraction of the 15% to 39% drawdowns after the controversies surrounding Celsius, FTX, BlockFi, and Bybit.

Matt Mena, Crypto Research Strategist at 21Shares, told AMBCrypto,

What we find most encouraging is how the market handled the worst of it. The largest hack in crypto’s history caused a far smaller drawdown than past crises; the protocols kept running, and none of the structural drivers broke.

Unfortunately, institutional resilience is not retail demand. The market simply treated a smaller slump as evidence of Bitcoin’s underlying strength. However, whether anyone wanted to buy Bitcoin [BTC] was a separate question, one the hack never answered.

Still, institutional strength hasn’t eased the feeling of dread felt by many retail investors. And, a major factor can explain why.

The most important signal is what happened after the liquidations: Nothing. Bitget Wallet’s analysts put it plainly that the leverage reset “has cleared some speculative excess, but is yet to address the underlying demand problem.”

Looking at the data, one can see why. Most importantly, the ETF flows changed drastically. There were $2.6 billion worth of inflows in September 2026, which turned into $290 million of net outflows in October. Currently, U.S ETF holders sit underwater below their cost basis of $82K.

How ETF holders behave below breakeven remains the key tell for November.

Also, stablecoin supply has not been moving outside the $305 billion zone, a sure sign that liquidity is sitting still.

Finally, one cannot forget the fallout caused by the Binance hack.

When the exchange reopened withdrawals, the queue moved fast. The exchange processed $4.65 billion against $1.01 billion of deposits in under ten hours; net outflows reached about $5.8 billion over 24 hours!

Each of these factors may not matter when seen separately, but when read together, they describe the same thing — capital leaving or sitting still. The leverage is gone, and the bid is not there to replace it.

For 21Shares, $73,000 is the 200-day moving average, and “the line that would reopen the bear-market debate.”

Bitget analysts told AMBCrypto that Bitcoin must hold the $73K–$74K range.

The 73,000-74,000 range is now the zone Bitcoin needs to hold. Stabilization would require more balanced derivatives positioning and sustained positive ETF flows. Reclaiming and holding $80,000 would signal stronger demand, while a decisive break below $73,000 could expose $68,000. If $68,000 also fails to hold, the selloff would suggest more than a temporary leverage flush.

When the same number pops up again and again, it stops being a coincidence and starts pointing to a pattern — that Bitcoin is either in a temporary flush or at the start of something deeper.

If buyers do return, Bitcoin can comfortably start holding $80,000, and stronger demand would emerge as a result. Getting back above $81,000 to $82,000 would finally put the largest holder cohorts back in profit.

Both reports are similarly aligned on what won’t fix Bitcoin’s buyer problem: Macro relief without demand. In fact, Bitget’s analysts asserted,

A durable Bitcoin recovery will depend on improving liquidity and Spot demand, not macro relief alone.

Matt Mena framed the same requirement as a four-part checklist.

We are watching four things into November: Bitcoin holding $76,000 to $78,000 and reclaiming $80,000 to $82,000, Binance completing withdrawals and proving its reserves, credit spreads, oil and long-end yields, and whether ETF flows return. If those turn, the setup for the final weeks of the year remains constructive.

Notice what’s on both lists: ETF flows, liquidity, Spot demand, and positioning. All of them are things buyers have to do.

There is naturally no doubt that macro factors can move Bitcoin’s price. If everything aligns, a rally can happen tomorrow. However, seasoned investors know that this will never be the same as rebuilding buyer interest.

Ultimately, a macro relief rally would leave Bitcoin’s demand problem exactly where it was.

The calendar offers a boost for Bitcoin regardless of which way the ball drops, as December’s Fed expectations hinge on U.S CPI and PPI readings. For the uninitiated, hotter readings will reinforce rate-hike expectations, and a softer core inflation will trigger a relief rally.

However, Bitget’s analysts draw a line between the two outcomes, noting,

This week’s inflation data adds another test. Hotter readings could reinforce December rate-hike expectations, while softer core inflation could trigger a relief rally. But a durable Bitcoin recovery will depend on improving liquidity and spot demand, not macro relief alone.

Basically, a relief rally can be classed as a macro event, not a demand event. The inflation print can only deliver the former, and the latter can only come about by real flows.

Here, it’s also worth being precise about what the 5th November AI crash tells us. 21Shares calls it,

A renewed wobble in artificial intelligence (AI) equities pulled the Nasdaq-100 down almost 4%.

That’s the mechanism in a nutshell. Even this time, crypto’s fall was the result of trading alongside a risk asset.

Still, if Bitcoin’s move below $74,000 was driven by the AI wipeout, then the absence of a bid is more telling. Eventually, we come back to the same problem of missing buyers.

Leverage has been reset twice in a week — Once by Binance’s $6.3 billion hack, once by an AI shocker. And the buyer bid has hardly appeared either time.

That’s what makes $73,000 a critical level to watch. If buyers return and hold this level, they could help Bitcoin reclaim $80,000. This would also imply that BTC’s demand problem is cyclical, not permanent.

However, a break below $73,000 will hint at — and a failure at $68,000 will confirm — that Bitcoin’s breakdown is structural. Bitcoin’s recovery hinges on a single level, and the lack of buyers has never been felt stronger.

Onchain data platform CoinGlass seeks to answer why XRP's price is down. Its analysis, generated from the past 24 hours of futures, spot and ETF data, points to three indicators that help explain the pressure on XRP.

XRP fell for 10 straight days from November 5 to November 14, 2026. Price lost momentum after losing the daily MA 200 at the close of October. The cryptocurrency lost another crucial support in early October, the daily MA 50, weakening bulls.

#5069. Why Binance’s ‘kill switch’ couldn’t stop hackers from draining $6.3B — Explained!

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

There is a certain irony in pulling the emergency brake, only to discover that the machinery you’re trying to stop is operating beyond your reach.

Binance encountered a rather expensive version of that problem on 29th October. Attackers compromised its wallet signing infrastructure and obtained authority to move cryptocurrency through mechanisms that did not depend on the exchange’s ordinary withdrawal process. Suspending withdrawals could interrupt that process. It could do considerably less about permissions already established on Ethereum.

By the time the attack was contained, approximately $6.3 billion had been stolen and Binance’s engineers had developed a specialised procedure to revoke malicious on-chain authority. The exchange could shut down affected services, but Ethereum would continue recognising the delegation until it was explicitly cleared.

Brian Cubellis, Chief Strategy Officer at Bitcoin custody platform Onramp, offered his two cents to AMBCrypto,

Pausing withdrawals turns off the exchange’s own software, but it does nothing about permissions the attacker has already written to the blockchain

The distinction is an uncomfortable one for an institution entrusted with billions in customer assets.

Binance subsequently coordinated freezes of stolen funds and began replenishing the affected holdings, reporting approximately 98% replenishment by 4th November. Its financial response was substantial.

However, it still is worth questioning what remained possible while its emergency controls were taking effect.

By the way, for those unaware, the attack began well before 29th October and nowhere near a blockchain.

According to Binance’s 3rd November incident report, an engineer downloaded a tampered installation package for an AI coding tool in June. The exchange detected the anomaly and replaced the device, but the attackers had already gathered intelligence about its employees and infrastructure. Well into September, another engineer was approached through a fictitious recruitment process involving interviews and a malicious coding assignment.

By 20th October, the attackers had used compromised employee systems and internal AI tooling to access additional machines. In doing so, they ultimately obtained credentials that opened the way to Binance’s wallet signing infrastructure.

It all paid off on the 29th. Between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, hot wallets transferred approximately 223.46 million XRP, 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker controlled addresses. Bitcoin and other assets followed. Chainalysis subsequently estimated the overall theft at approximately $6.4 billion.

What was the most consequential part of this intrusion though? The attackers gained access to Binance’s signing infrastructure, the very machinery responsible for authorizing transactions.

On Ethereum, the attackers exploited EIP-7702, a mechanism that allows an externally owned account to delegate execution to smart-contract code.

Ordinarily, that flexibility expands what a wallet can do. Here, according to Binance, the compromised signing infrastructure was used to grant malicious code execution rights over an Ethereum hot wallet. The exchange described 50 signed transactions involved in manipulating the account’s nonce and establishing the delegation.

The unsettling part comes next though. Those permissions remained valid on-chain even after Binance suspended withdrawals and shut down its hot-wallet services. The exchange could stop its own systems from processing transactions, but it could not simply switch off the authority the attackers had already established on Ethereum.

Then came another complication. Binance’s hot wallet used multi-party computation (MPC), which distributes the production of cryptographic signatures across multiple participants or components rather than relying on a single conventional private key. That architecture can reduce certain risks, but it also meant there was no single private key available to revoke the malicious delegation immediately.

Binance’s engineers had to DEVELOP a specialised revocation procedure while the incident was UNFOLDING. Of course, this took additional time, prolonging the effort to contain unauthorized asset movements.

At 23:56 UTC, the final reported unauthorized Ethereum transfer, involving 2,961.9 ETH, was confirmed on-chain. Binance said it had been broadcast earlier and remained pending before confirmation. At 00:10 UTC on 30th October, the exchange cleared the malicious EIP-7702 delegation with a new authorization to the zero address.

The distinction between broadcast and confirmation matters. So does the absence of an established total for funds transferred after withdrawals were suspended.

Binance acknowledged that suspension alone could not stop every unauthorized movement, but its disclosures do not establish a reconciled post-suspension loss figure.

There is a comforting simplicity to the idea of a kill switch. Something goes wrong, someone pulls the plug and the damage stops. Unfortunately, the blockchain has no particular obligation to respect an exchange’s internal emergency procedures.

Consider a hotel discovering that someone has obtained an unauthorized key card. Closing reception prevents new cards from being issued. The existing card still opens the door. Cancelling it, securing the valuables, and recovering what has already disappeared are separate jobs.

Now, this comparison has its limits, but it captures the dilemma facing exchanges whose wallet permissions outlive their own systems.

The problem surfaced in a public exchange between Haseeb Qureshi, Managing Partner at Dragonfly, and  Tudor Anastasiu. Tudor Anastasiu is a blockchain infrastructure and security engineer and the founder of Anastasiu Labs.

The disagreement exposes a distinction that is easy to overlook in the middle of a breach.

A defensive sweep can move assets to safety, provided the exchange can authorize and execute it before the attacker does. However, moving funds does not necessarily invalidate permissions already granted on-chain and it certainly cannot retrieve assets that have already disappeared.

So, that leaves a rather awkward question: If the signing infrastructure itself has been compromised, how does an exchange authorize an emergency transaction without trusting the very system it suspects?

Carlos Vendrell, Founder of Zealynx Security, sees the answer in testing the procedure under exactly those conditions.

The drill should start from a list of every approval and delegation each hot wallet has given, then revoke one of them for real while assuming the normal signing service is the compromised part, and time it

Binance’s experience does not establish that MPC inherently prevents rapid revocation. Nor does its disclosure prove that no emergency procedure existed before the breach.

However, it does establish that engineers developed a specialised procedure during the incident and doing so took additional time.

There was another complication here, one that made the situation look almost absurd. The compromised wallet was reportedly STILL receiving money.

In an analysis dated 4th November, Four Pillars reported that Binance’s deposit-consolidation system continued collecting funds into a compromised Ethereum wallet identified as Binance 14. This allowed the attacker to sweep newly arriving assets.

Nexus Mutual’s reconstruction offers a particularly striking sequence.

At approximately 21:44 UTC, it says the attacker swept 200 million USDT that another Binance-labelled wallet had deposited roughly 72 seconds earlier. Seventy-two seconds! Barely enough time to make a cup of coffee, yet apparently sufficient for a fresh transfer to reach a compromised address and disappear.

The researchers’ findings raise a problem distinct from EIP-7702. An exchange can work to revoke an attacker’s authority while other operational systems continue directing funds towards a dangerous destination. Interrupting those internal asset flows is another containment task and requires its own controls and confirmation.

According to Brian Cubellis, emergency preparedness must account for the loss of the usual signing infrastructure.

An exchange should prove, before it is attacked, that it can cancel any permission on its wallets and move exposed funds to safety even if its own signing system has been taken over

That is easier prescribed than engineered though.

An independent emergency signing path may accelerate recovery, but it also introduces powerful authority that must be secured. Build too much dependence into the ordinary system and the emergency route may fail alongside it. Concentrate too much authority in the alternative and the supposed safeguard becomes another attractive target.

Once stolen assets leave the exchange’s immediate control, containment becomes a race involving investigators, stablecoin issuers, blockchain networks and the attacker.

Chainalysis’s investigation also described an attempt to move approximately $500 million in stablecoins through a swapping address. Within roughly 20 minutes, the attackers reportedly converted around $325 million into assets less susceptible to issuer freezes, including Ether. The remaining $175 million was frozen.

There was a reason for the rush. Stablecoin issuers such as Tether and Circle can freeze certain tokens at designated addresses. Bitcoin and Ether, by contrast, have no equivalent central issuer with that power. Converting the stolen stablecoins into other assets could therefore put them beyond the reach of an issuer-imposed freeze.

This whole episode illustrates the limits of intervention once funds have escaped. Investigators may be able to follow the money on-chain, but knowing where it has gone does not necessarily give them the power to retrieve it.

Binance nevertheless managed to secure a substantial portion of the stolen assets. In its 3rd November report, the exchange said that approximately $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted through cooperation with issuers, law enforcement, and blockchain intelligence firms. By 4th November, it reported replenishing approximately 98% of the affected holdings through replacement purchases.

Of course, Binance had demonstrated considerable capacity to absorb the losses rather than pass them on to users. However, it tells us how much the exchange managed to secure or replace, not how effectively it prevented the attacker from continuing to move assets during the breach.

A year earlier, Bybit had encountered a different version of the problem with compromised transaction authority. In February 2025, attackers stole approximately $1.5 billion after compromising the environment associated with its Safe{Wallet} approval process.

According to Bybit’s forensic disclosure, malicious changes deceived signers into approving an unauthorized transaction. It also said that investigators found no indication that its own infrastructure had been compromised.

Both incidents exposed how much depends on the integrity of the authority behind a transaction. Multiple signatures offer limited protection when signers are misled about what they are approving. And as Binance discovered, shutting down a signing service does not necessarily invalidate authority already established on-chain.

An emergency kill switch sounds reassuring. Rather less reassuring is discovering, halfway through a breach, that the attacker has permissions your switch cannot revoke.

Binance’s experience raises an uncomfortable question for exchanges entrusted with billions in customer assets — Have they actually tested what happens when the systems responsible for protecting those assets become part of the attack?

An exchange should be able to demonstrate that it can revoke compromised permissions, move exposed assets to safety, and interrupt internal transfers without relying entirely on infrastructure it can no longer trust.

But what should customers make of an exchange’s public assurances when a breach is underway? AMBCrypto put that question to Vik Sharma, Founder and CEO of Cake Wallet,

A useful update names which approvals were revoked, which assets moved, and where, so customers can check it themselves

There are legitimate reasons to withhold sensitive operational details while an intrusion is underway. Once the immediate danger has passed, however, an exchange should be able to explain what its emergency controls actually stopped, when compromised authority was extinguished, and whether any assets remained exposed.

Binance deserves credit for publishing details of its response, coordinating substantial asset freezes, and committing its own resources to replenish affected holdings. Those measures helped absorb the financial damage. However, they also revealed why reimbursement and containment should never be confused.

A kill switch should buy defenders control, not merely time to figure out where control has gone.

#5068. AI helped hackers gain access at 10 unnamed organizations, researchers say

The November 12 investigation reports 25 operations against at least 19 organizations during August–September, with humans assigning targets and able to steer.

AI-assisted attacks accessed systems or retrieved data at 10 organizations, according to a November 12 investigation by Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42. The security research team tracked 25 operations against at least 19 organizations during August and September 2026, including semiconductor companies, defense and policy organizations, and civil-society groups.

Unit 42 said the attackers used a customized version of Cairn, an open-source framework for AI-driven penetration testing, paired with Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek models.

The reported outcomes went beyond reconnaissance. The researchers reported unauthorized access to a semiconductor company's production system and to more than one million member records at a US teachers' union.

Attackers also modified a live standards-ballot document and obtained nonpublic data at an industry standards organization, the researchers said.

Humans supplied targets and goals, sometimes adding intelligence gathered beforehand. The framework then planned, executed and recorded subsequent work.

Individual operations lasted from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, Unit 42 reported, with human steering still possible.

Activity: August–September 2026. Report: November 12, 2026. Unit 42 describes human-directed AI intrusions with continued steering possible.

Humans chose targets and could keep steering while agents repeated the intrusion work.

Campaign outcomes are Unit 42's findings. The diagram shows the design, not measured human-intervention frequency. Operations and organizations are different units; no success rate is inferred.

Conceptual workflow from Unit 42's description and Cairn's documentation. Arrows show task and information flow, not measured timing. Counts reproduce the report and use distinct units; no ratio or general success rate is calculated.

Campaign outcomes are Unit 42's findings. The diagram shows the design, not measured human-intervention frequency. Operations and organizations are different units; no success rate is inferred.

That arrangement let humans direct the campaign while agents sustained the intrusion work. Unit 42 assessed that a single operator or small team likely ran the activity and argued that autonomous orchestration expanded the number of simultaneous attempts they could sustain.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Unit 42 concluded that AI increased the scale and reach of the campaign, not its technical sophistication.

The November 12 investigation adds quantified outcomes to earlier reporting on AI-assisted attacks. CryptoSlate's November 5 coverage of CERT-In's CRAFTY FALCON advisory already named Cairn among AI-assisted offensive-security tools. The reports describe different observed activity; shared tooling does not establish a link between their operators.

Unit 42 assessed with moderate confidence that the activity it tracked represented China-nexus intelligence collection, based on language, tooling and target selection.

For defenders, the report's practical warning is that familiar gaps can support prolonged, coordinated intrusion attempts. Unit 42 says identity hygiene, reducing exposed attack surfaces and software patching remain effective.

Blockstream CEO Adam Back has commented on the rebound of Bitcoin after its overnight drop to a four-month low. On Sunday, Back posted a Bitfinex chart of Bitcoin on X with a one-word caption: "Bouncy."

Back created Hashcash, the proof-of-work scheme that Satoshi Nakamoto cited in the original Bitcoin whitepaper, and he was one of the first people Satoshi contacted about Bitcoin.

#5065. Illinois Crypto Tax Draws Unlikely Alliance of DOJ, Banks and DeFi

Illinois Crypto Tax Draws Unlikely Alliance of DOJ, Banks and DeFi

An unusually broad coalition, spanning the U.S. Justice Department, Wall Street’s biggest lobby, the national Chamber of Commerce and a who’s-who of crypto firms, has thrown its weight behind a legal challenge to Illinois’ first-of-its-kind tax on digital asset transactions.

The groups filed briefs this month in Illinois state court supporting a lawsuit from the Crypto Council for Innovation and the Blockchain Association, which are asking a judge to strike down the state’s Digital Asset Tax Act and permanently block its enforcement.

The tax imposes a 0.2% levy on the full value of a digital asset every time an Illinois customer trades, transfers, or stores it through a broker, even when there’s no sale, gain, or change in ownership.

Critics have called it among the most punitive crypto taxes in the country, in part because Illinois imposes no comparable tax on dollars, gold, stocks or any other asset, and no other state has anything like it.

On Nov. 6, the Justice Department filed a statement of interest arguing the tax undermines federal policy and U.S. leadership in digital assets, calling it vague and discriminatory for singling out crypto for treatment no other asset faces.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, which represents hundreds of broker-dealers, banks and asset managers, filed an amicus brief warning the tax reaches well beyond crypto-native platforms to the traditional banks, custodians and advisers increasingly offering digital asset products.

A separate brief filed Nov. 11 brought together crypto’s heavy hitters, led by the DeFi Education Fund, Andreessen Horowitz, Paradigm and Uniswap, and including Aave Labs, Chainlink Labs, Solana Policy Institute, Phantom, Jito Labs, Multicoin Capital and Stand With Crypto.

Their filing argues the law’s definitions are so vague they could stretch to software developers and decentralized protocols that hold no customer funds and have no way to identify users or know where a transaction occurred. The brief noted an estimated 2.64 million Illinoisans hold digital assets, the fifth-highest total of any state.

“This tax is unclear, discriminatory, unconstitutional, and harmful to the future of finance,” CCI CEO Ji Hun Kim and Blockchain Association executive Ashok Pinto said in a joint statement.

The challenge dates to August. As Decrypt reported, Illinois agreed in October to pause the tax until July 1, 2027, buying time for the court fight now underway.

#5063. AI models agreed with each other more than with reality in a new test

Science Prediction Universe found that pooling rankings improved average results, while shared scientific errors survived.

AI models agreed more closely with one another than with laboratory measurements in a new test of AI predictions. Pooling their rankings improved results on average, but several systems could still share the same mistake.

The Science Prediction Universe study, led by UniPat AI and submitted to arXiv on Nov. 11, tested 13 agent configurations spanning 12 models on 100 public tasks and 16 private tasks. Each configuration combined a model, reasoning setting and agent software. The study asked them to rank specified experiments across chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine.

Science Prediction Universe researchers reported that, on the public tasks, average agreement between scored configurations reached a Spearman rank correlation of 0.52, compared with 0.33 against measured outcomes. Agreement between agents exceeded their correlation with measurements on 81 of the 100 tasks. These averages use available scored predictions, with coverage varying by configuration.

Those figures describe how closely orderings match, rather than percentages of answers correct. Agents might rank reaction conditions by yield or materials by conductivity without having to predict numerical values. A perfect ordering without measurement ties scores 1; random rankings average 0.

The researchers found a benefit to pooling predictions. Averaging each experiment's position across configurations produced a consensus ranking that scored 0.08 points above the average submission, improving results on 73 of the 100 public tasks. The reported 95% confidence interval for the gain was 0.05 to 0.11.

On one oncology task, eleven configurations agreed at 0.9 but averaged just 0.27 against measurements. The benchmark’s best individual system also beat the consensus of its peers on matched tasks.

More broadly, tasks with greater agreement tended to have better predictions. The paper's agreement analysis therefore presents consensus as an informative but fallible signal. The authors explain that averaging can reduce errors that differ between systems while retaining common ones.

Pooling rankings improved average predictions in SPU. Comparing the public-task average with one oncology task shows why agreement still needs an experimental check.

Mean pairwise agreement was 0.52, while the mean score against measurements was 0.33, using available scored predictions.

Eleven configurations agreed strongly on one oncology task, but their rankings matched the measurements much less closely.

Agreement contains useful signal, but shared errors can survive a consensus.

Available scored predictions have unequal configuration coverage. The average covers 100 public tasks; the oncology view is one task with eleven configurations. Correlations are not percentages correct. Neither view measures human scientific ability.

Reported public-task agreement and measurement correlations share a -1 to 1 axis. Dot x = left + (correlation + 1) / 2 × axis width. Pooling paths are labelled schematic. Consensus gain is 0.081 score points (95% CI 0.054 to 0.110), higher on 73/100 public tasks.

Available scored predictions have unequal configuration coverage. The average covers 100 public tasks; the oncology view is one task with eleven configurations. Correlations are not percentages correct. Neither view measures human scientific ability.

The authors connect those shared errors to simple assumptions about how experimental outcomes should rise or fall. If several agents rely on the same mistaken relationship, collecting more of their opinions can preserve that error.

The configurations were scored on different task sets. Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 had scores on only 44 and 30 public tasks, respectively, largely because of safety refusals. Across the full benchmark, all 13 configurations shared just 28 scored tasks: 27 public and one private.

The public tasks also looked backward at published measurements and were selected after pilot evaluations. The private set contained only 16 tasks across four unpublished experimental series, limiting how broadly its findings can be applied.

There was useful predictive ability in that private set: twelve of the 13 configurations ranked the unpublished experiments significantly better than chance overall, according to UniPat's Nov. 12 results release. Of 208 official private runs, 159 were scored.

The study used no human prediction baseline. Its findings apply to ranking the experimental outcomes it tested, with lab measurements still needed to check the answers.

#5061. Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom: The AI Stock Winners and Losers After Jensen Huang’s Ousting

Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom: The AI Stock Winners and Losers After Jensen Huang’s Ousting

Wall Street is picking winners and losers from Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, and the market is treating the chipmaker's competitors considerably better than companies tied to its business.

Nvidia shares fell 4.59% to $165.75 Thursday afternoon, recovering from an opening price of $151.01 and an intraday low of $148.80.

The rebound softened an initial collapse of more than 14%, but the stock remained firmly in negative territory.

The selloff followed Huang's immediate resignation as CEO, president, and board member after reports of extramarital affairs and allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, although the company has not established that corporate secrets were compromised.

The stock was already in trouble before Huang stepped down. Nvidia had lost approximately $1.27 trillion in market capitalization between October 6 and November 6, raising questions about AI spending even before the leadership crisis intensified.

AMD climbed 5.79% to $584.89 after opening at $569.28, making it one of the clearest beneficiaries of Thursday's trading.

The company competes directly with Nvidia in AI accelerators, and uncertainty around Nvidia's leadership could make customers more interested in diversifying their chip suppliers.

Broadcom followed a similar trajectory, gaining 5.65% to $364.73 from an opening price of $356.80.

Unlike AMD, which competes through its own GPU products, Broadcom specializes in custom AI processors and networking technology, offering large customers a different way to reduce their dependence on Nvidia.

Google’s parent company Alphabet also advanced, rising 2.06% to $299.49 after opening at $293.77.

Those alternatives existed before Huang resigned, and Thursday's gains do not establish that Nvidia has lost customers. Investors may simply be pricing in better competitive opportunities if the leadership transition disrupts Nvidia's strategy or customer relationships.

Nvidia-backed CoreWeave suffered a much rougher session, falling 7.49% to $56.22 after opening at $50.91.

Its decline came just one day after the cloud provider surged 24.7% following quarterly revenue growth of 168%, so this may be just as much a correction after an explosive movement as it is a reaction to Huang’s ousting.

In any case, the relationship between the companies helps explain the anxiety among investors. Nvidia invested another $2 billion in CoreWeave in January and has an initial $6.3 billion agreement to purchase unused computing capacity through April 2032, making it an investor, supplier, and customer of the same company.

Any change in Nvidia's investment priorities could therefore affect CoreWeave beyond ordinary chip purchases, although neither company has announced changes to those agreements.

The pressure also reached the semiconductor supply chain. TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's advanced processors, fell 1.15% to $408.61 after opening at $394.62, while memory supplier Micron lost 2.70%, trading at $789.43 after opening at $769.31.

SK Hynix, another major supplier of high-bandwidth memory used in AI hardware, declined 3% to $137.98 from an opening price of $134.25.

These companies depend on broader chip demand, however, so their losses cannot be attributed entirely to Nvidia's leadership problems.

For investors, the immediate concern is less about whether AI chips will stop selling and more about how Nvidia manages its partnerships, financing commitments, and product roadmap without the executive who built much of that network.

Nvidia's board has said it expects operations and customer commitments to continue without interruption. The company is scheduled to report quarterly earnings on November 17, with Kress now leading the business through its first earnings announcement since Huang's departure.

Chandler Fang, founder of AI payments startup t54.ai, has said that the company's x402 Facilitator on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has processed more than 10 million AI agent transactions. Fang made the comments in an interview that the XRPL Foundation published on X on November 15, and the interviewer put the number of these payments at 11.7 million.

According to Fang, XRPL had almost no transactions made by AI agents three or four months before the interview, which was recorded at XRP Seoul 2026. "The entire volume got ramped up very quickly in the three months," he said.

The x402 Facilitator works as a bridge between AI agents and payments, and agents can use XRP or the RLUSD stablecoin to move money without a separate wallet setup for every agent. Fang said that more than 200 merchants are already on the network.

According to Fang, the most common use case is paying for AI compute. Instead of paying $20 to $200 a month for an AI subscription, an agent can pay around $1 or 50 cents for a single task. "Instead, they can purchase this single compute for about $1, or 50 cents, and it can be settled on the XRPL," Fang said.

Fang said that such payments have low value and high frequency, so the high throughput and low fees of XRPL give the network an advantage. He also expects agent payments to move into real-life purchases over the next few quarters. "We have the coffee shop right outside our booth, right? And we are trying to empower users to use XRP and agent payments to finish a real-life transaction," Fang said.

According to Fang, trust is the main issue for agent payments, and t54.ai's Trustline product focuses on risk management for the financial activity of AI agents. He compared the service with the chargeback feature of credit cards. "So there is no lawsuit. It is a similar experience for agents," Fang said.

t54.ai is also part of Mastercard's agentic payment program, where the startup is responsible for risk management. The x402 Facilitator processes transactions based on Mastercard Verifiable Intent, a protocol that verifies the behavior of AI agents.

Fang said that t54.ai, Ripple and Mastercard are in talks about a three-way collaboration, and the first results will be shown at an upcoming hackathon.

"The ten million transactions are just a starting point. I think next year you should expect a lot more transactions. Maybe even more transactions settled on XRPL will be done by AI agents than by humans," Fang said.
