#5059. Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks

Home » Interviews » Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks

An interview with Banxa’s Chief Product & Growth Officer on hidden scaling traps and the future of stablecoin payments.

Rapid growth is often seen as a sign of success in fintech. But as transaction volumes increase, weaknesses in payment infrastructure, fraud prevention and risk management can become harder to spot – and more costly to fix.

Shaun Heng, Chief Product & Growth Officer at Banxa, a global crypto payments infrastructure provider, knows these challenges firsthand. Before joining Banxa, Heng held product and growth leadership roles at MoonPay and CoinMarketCap, gaining experience across two major players in the digital asset space.

In this interview with DailyCoin, he discusses why rapid growth can expose hidden vulnerabilities in fintech, what it takes to build payment infrastructure that works at scale, and how stablecoins could reshape the future of global payments.

– When does rapid growth become a risk for fintech companies?

Our total transaction volume (TTV) grew 76% from January to August. Stablecoins increased by 117%. Great numbers. The first thing I asked was where they came from?

Growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it. That happens more often than people admit.

When volume doubles, every weakness doubles with it. That could mean fraud attempts, chargeback exposure, reconciliation breaks. Just to name a few. So you’re always looking at a great number next to problems that may not have appeared yet.

The second challenge is that fast growth is almost never evenly distributed. It could be one particular partner, region, digital asset, or payment method. That concentration is invisible on a topline chart, so we always look deeper to understand the drivers and future success.

And team culture is real. In a quarter everyone has worked so hard and exceeded targets, nobody wants to be the one asking hard questions.

The discipline I would push for is simple: break down the growth before you celebrate it. Where is it coming from? Which rails is it riding on? And what happens if one of those rails is withdrawn next week?

Growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it.

– What does a payment infrastructure provider need to deliver to make the crypto on-ramp experience seamless?

For a long time the industry shipped widgets, and a widget is a visible admission that someone else is handling this.

Banxa Native is headless by design. The partner owns the interface, the brand, the pricing presentation, the whole journey. We simply sit behind their stack. Users never

Returning users never verify twice, because existing KYC can be reused through token sharing. So, everything the user shouldn’t have to think about. That’s the definition of invisible.

In practice, it means the provider owns licensing, or a licensed local partner, in every market where money actually moves,  local payment methods, not just cards, because users pay the way their country pays.

Vietnam is the example I keep reaching for. We launched VietQR there in Q3, and it is already our top payment method in that region at roughly 42% of all transactions — driving a conversion rate close to eight times higher than cards. Same users, same product, same pricing. The only variable was letting people pay the way they already pay.

Then provider also need identity and KYC, including the ability to accept verification the partner has already done.  Settlement, in and out, with money arriving where it is supposed to on the day it is supposed to.

And it has to run in both directions, not just the buy flow. On-ramp, where a user pays with a local method and receives crypto. Off-ramp, where they sell and cashout to their own bank account.

A lot of products ship the first and treat off-ramp as a secondary problem, and that is precisely the moment a user discovers the money only moves one way.

For a European fintech, Banxa collects the local payment, exchanges and settles the fiat leg where the partner needs it. We carry the MiCA licence that passports across the EU — so they don’t have to build a crypto licensing and payments stack country by country.

One partner, one compliance review, one integration, both directions. That speed to market is usually why partners choose us.

– Banxa’s infrastructure supports stablecoin payments across B2B settlement, consumer payments, and cross-border transactions. What is the most overlooked challenge in making stablecoin payments work at scale?

Nobody has ever been excited about reconciliation, and it is the thing that decides whether you have a business.

A stablecoin transfer settles in seconds. That part is genuinely solved.

What is not solved is everything around it. The fiat leg still moves on banking hours and local scheme rules. You have a bank partner on one side, a chain on the other, and a treasury position sitting between them that has to be funded, hedged and accounted for.

Every transaction has to be matched across those systems, in the right currency, on the right day, with the right fee breakdown, in a form an auditor and a regulator will accept.

The second unglamorous thing is failure handling.

At scale, the interesting work is not the happy path. It is the payment that half-completes.

The most common example is card decline and for many reasons – bank limit, 3D Secure step that timed out etc. In most checkouts that ends the order and the buyer needs to start again, or more often leaves.

Then there are bank transfers that arrive three days late with a truncated reference. The refund that has to go back to a card when the crypto has already left.

Users judge you almost entirely on how those cases are handled, and those cases are where most providers quietly fall over.

We recently shipped Payment Method Switch, which lets the buyer change how they pay without losing the order. It separates the order from the payment, so a buyer can move from card to Google Pay without losing the order or redoing verification, and so they see the new method before confirming.

The third challenge is payment method coverage, which sounds like a commercial checklist and is actually an engineering and licensing dependency.

Supporting the way people pay in the US, Nigeria, Australia and Germany means four different integrations, four different fraud profiles and four different regulatory conversations. A switch only works if the alternative payment method is already connected and live for that buyer.

It matters because this is the layer the user is trusting without knowing it. When the plumbing is right, the experience feels effortless. When it is wrong, it does not feel like a backend issue. It feels like the product lied to them.

– Can KYC be more than compliance — can it actually become a growth advantage in crypto payments?

Yes, and I would go further. KYC is one of the highest-leverage product surfaces in payments. Most teams just never treat it as one.

Look at where users actually drop. It is rarely pricing. It is the verification step.

Someone has decided they want to transact, they have intent, and then they are asked to photograph a document on a screen that does not match the app they were just in. A meaningful share of them never come back.

That is not a compliance cost. That is a conversion problem.

So the advantage comes from three things.

First, verify once. If a partner has already verified a user to a standard we can rely on, that user should not be asked again. Banxa Native supports exactly this through token sharing, so returning users go straight to payment.

Second, verify proportionately. Not every transaction carries the same risk, so it shouldn’t carry the same friction.

Third, verify natively. No redirect, no third-party screen, no moment where the user wonders who they just handed their passport details to.

There is a trust argument too. In most of the world, people are more willing to move money with a platform that looks regulated, not less. Verification done well signals that this is a real financial product. Done badly, suggests the opposite.

My advice is to instrument it. Measure drop-off by step. Iterate. Most teams hand it to engineering once and never look again.

– Crypto payments come with a lot of risk, from payment disputes to fraud. Do you the industry underestimates the value of having someone else take on that risk?

Badly, yes. And the reason is that the cost of carrying it yourself does not show up as a line item until it is already a problem.

The fiat leg is reversible. The crypto leg is not. A card payment can be disputed months after the asset has left. That gap is where fraud lives.

So when a platform decides to run its own ramp, they’re usually pricing the integration work. What they are not pricing is the loss rate, the rules engine that has to keep up with it, the team watching it at three in the morning, the bank relationships that get withdrawn when your chargeback ratio crosses a threshold, and the capital you have to hold against all of it.

Those costs are lumpy and they arrive late.

The real value of transferring that risk is not just the losses avoided. It is focus.

With Banxa Native, the partner owns the experience end to end. We carry the regulated rails and the settlement behind it. They get to spend their engineering time on the things their users actually chose them for.

Risk you have not priced is still risk. Someone is carrying it.

– What’s one thing Web3 companies still see as “just compliance” that should really be treated as a product or growth issue?

Market access. Which licences you hold, and therefore which countries you can actually serve, is usually filed under legal. It is the single biggest determinant of your addressable market.

Teams spend enormous effort on acquisition and then discover the funnel is geographically capped. Users arrive, get to the payment step, and find out their country is not supported or their local payment method is not available.

From the user’s point of view, the product simply does not work. From the growth team’s point of view, the conversion rate is mysteriously bad in half the world. Nobody connects that back to a licensing decision made two years earlier.

The same is true of regulatory readiness ahead of a regime change. MiCA is the clearest recent example.

The companies that treated it as a legal deadline scrambled. The ones that treated it as a product decision kept serving European users without interruption while others paused service. Continuity of access is a growth outcome.

This is also why we think about our licence footprint as product surface area rather than paperwork. Banxa services users across North America, Europe, the UK, Latin America and Asia-Pacific, and is MiCA-authorised as a CASP in the Netherlands. For a partner building on Banxa, that footprint is not a compliance appendix in the contract. It is the list of countries where their product works.

My general rule: if a compliance decision changes who can use your product or how easily, it was never only a compliance decision.

– What development in crypto payments could have the biggest impact on the industry over the next few years?

Stablecoins becoming the default settlement layer for ordinary businesses that have no interest in crypto.

That is the shift. It isn’t necessarily about more people buying digital assets. It’s about companies moving money across borders faster and cheaper, with the stablecoin being an implementation detail they never discuss.

The future isn’t crypto payments. It’s better payments.

Stablecoin supply has actually contracted since May, from around $310 billion to roughly $286 billion. But payment volume went the other way. Allium reported it at $482 billion in the first nine months of this year, up 45% year on year.

Banks, card networks and large fintechs are integrating this into their products right now.

What makes it transformative is the disappearance, not the technology.

Consumers will keep using the apps and currencies they already trust. The rails underneath will change. Identity handled once, not repeatedly. Settlement in minutes instead of days. Fees people can actually see.

In many emerging markets, this will go further and faster than people in Washington or London expect, because the alternative is genuinely slow.

Digital dollars become the practical choice for savings and cross-border flows, not a theoretical one.

Most users will never know a stablecoin was involved. That’s the point.

The U.S. headline CPI (Consumer Price Index) was up 0.4% in October, compared to a 0.3% expectation. The metric’s brisk rise for the third straight month signalled that underlying inflation pressure was building up.

Inflation pressures came from high oil prices (due to the conflict with Iran) and import tariffs, alongside robust household and business spending.

On Tuesday, the 10th of November, Fed Governor Christopher Waller raised the prospect of an interest rate hike of 50bps.

Unlike the previous Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, there is no debate now about whether the Fed should pause or hike, but rather whether the December meeting will result in a 25 bps or 50 bps rate hike.

As a risk-on asset, Bitcoin and the rest of the crypto market are likely to suffer reduced capital inflows and lower demand. Retail pessimism was high, and there is debate around whether it is a good time to buy or still too risky.

The loss of the $80k level towards the end of October, alongside negative apparent demand, was a warning sign of further losses. Shark accumulation while the leading crypto’s price held above $75k was hopeful, but ultimately the sellers won the battle.

An improvement in risk-to-reward for buyers was highlighted, but it was too early to jump in. A short-term holder P&L flow to exchange divergence looked compelling, but has not resulted in any positive price reaction or recovering demand yet.

Meanwhile, institutional selling carried on. AMBCrypto reported that 14 companies have sold 108,247 BTC so far in 2026, worth around $8.08 billion. The biggest was MARA Holdings, which sold 40,581 BTC worth $3.03 billion as it worked to pivot to operating AI/HPC data centres.

Since the 5th of November, every BTC spot ETF trading day has seen outflows. Cumulatively, the figure has reached $1.484 billion in the previous six ETF trading days, at the time of writing.

The Bitcoin short-term holder supply has increased compared to the long-term holder supply. AMBCrypto reported that this pointed to increased price sensitivity towards short-term price swings.

During August’s explosive rally beyond $80k, there was an imbalance, also known as a fair value gap (FVG), on the weekly chart, from $65,391 to $76,670.

At the time of writing, the price was sinking into this FVG. Moreover, the midpoint of the FVG at $71,030 was breached. A weekly session close below this midpoint will confirm bearish strength.

As things stand, the strong downward move could also be part of a leverage purge.

Within just three months, the price has retraced into a key demand zone on the weekly chart. This timeframe’s bias remains bullish, and the pullback is still healthy. A session close below $64,133, the 78.6% Fibonacci retracement level of the swing move higher to $87,395, would be a sign that the bullish woes were about to extend.

The 6-month liquidation heatmap showed that clusters of liquidity built up around $74k and $68k have been taken out. The next major liquidity pocket to watch was $61.7k, with $64k-$65k also a region to watch.

Price is likely to be pulled lower to these areas in the coming days or weeks.

The realized price of different holder cohorts above showed that the short-term holders were mostly underwater. The 3-6 month cohort has its realized price at $65k, marking an important on-chain support level.

This level has a confluence with the liquidation heatmap, as well as the weekly imbalance. Hence, swing traders and investors have to be prepared for the possibility of a retest of this realized price level.

The adjusted MVRV metric employs both the 30-day and 365-day MVRV ratios to capture short-term capital inflows and momentum, as well as mark out the macro cost basis trend.

The aMVRV was above the baseline to signal a bull market phase crossover. Hence, the Bitcoin market regime has passed early bull territory and is in a bullish regime.

The deep price pullback in recent weeks was similar to the price pullback from $25,250 to $19,549 in March 2023. Back then, the market remained within a bullish phase despite the deep setback.

The bearish market pressure should not be taken lightly, data shows. At the same time, Bitcoin has a chance of recovery if it can hold above $64k-$65k.

This hold will likely look like a consolidation phase, followed by easing loss-selling and short-term holder panic. If these conditions are met, and others such as ETF capital inflows to signal sentiment recovery come true, investors can have more faith in a return to a bull market.

#5057. Lido’s lending plan could block loan repayments without stopping interest

The lending plan distinguishes a limited freeze from a broader pause that blocks repayments and lender withdrawals. Interest for the paused period can still be added once accounting resumes.

Under Lido Lend’s proposed emergency rules, borrowers could be blocked from paying down debt and lenders from withdrawing. When the pause ends, borrowers could owe more: the next successful interest update would count the time they spent locked out.

The distinction appears in Lido Lend’s November 9 consolidated proposal. The proposed lending protocol, built on a modified version of Morpho Blue, uses a controller contract to permit or reject market actions. It separates a limited market freeze from a broader controller pause. Only the second shuts down repayment, liquidation and lender settlement together. Lenders supply loan tokens that borrowers take out against pledged collateral.

The proposal reports that the core contracts are deployed on Ethereum mainnet, but the DAO would have to accept the protocol separately. Each market would then need its own motion or DAO vote. The forum discussion continued with a signer declaration on November 14; the thread did not announce a completed acceptance vote or creation of the first market.

A Guardian ban stops an account’s new borrowing and collateral maturation but does not itself stop repayment, liquidation, settlement or collateral withdrawal under the remaining rules. The expected first WETH/wstETH market would launch with one contributor-run Guardian and a 1-of-1 quorum, with independent Guardians intended later.

Under the market controller rules, a freeze stops new borrowing, new collateral from completing its activation delay, and collateral withdrawals from positions carrying debt. Repayment, liquidation, lender withdrawals and settlement remain available, subject to their ordinary checks.

The Risk Steward Committee could impose that freeze and tighten defined controller settings through its dashboard, but could not loosen them. The proposed Operational Committee would use bounded Easy Track motions, open to LDO-holder objections, for actions such as unfreezing.

Borrowers can pay down debt, a key consideration when comparing crypto loan terms. Lenders can withdraw available loan tokens or use eligible settlement, which reduces a lender’s claim and a borrower’s debt by the same amount in exchange for collateral valued by the protocol’s price feed.

Settlement is the mechanism behind the Fallback Exits CryptoSlate examined in October. Lenders can exit without available loan tokens, but settlement is subject to market rules and policy limits. Bad debt at the front of the borrower queue can block it.

An Exit Book, a system for posting withdrawal requests, has a separate pause that stops new withdrawal requests and fills in that book. Owners can still cancel requests or use underlying positions directly, but those routes cannot bypass a paused market controller.

A pause blocks those routes. The architecture specification says it stops actions subject to the controller, including repayment, lender withdrawals, liquidation, settlement and direct interest updates. Even a direct call to the core cannot bypass the pause. Vault-share transfers and core functions outside the controller’s scope remain available.

Blocking an interest-update call does not make the borrowing period free. The core accounting specification uses elapsed time to calculate interest, and the controller rules explicitly say a later successful accrual covers time since the last update. A borrower could therefore regain repayment access with a larger debt balance under the applicable interest-rate model.

Proposed controls differ in scope. A controller pause closes repayment and lender exits while elapsed-time interest still counts.

For the banned account, new borrowing and collateral maturation stop. Repayment, liquidation and lender exits remain subject to normal rules.

New borrowing, collateral maturation and debt-bearing collateral withdrawal stop. Repayment, liquidation and lender exits remain available under normal rules.

Repayment, liquidation and lender withdrawal or settlement are blocked, alongside other controller-checked actions. The interest clock is not stopped.

New requests and fills stop in the book. Cancellation and direct core or vault access remain subject to the underlying market’s controls.

A finite emergency power does not guarantee a finite interruption: a separate Reseal path can make an active pause indefinite.

Proposed Lido Lend design, not a live pause. Available routes remain subject to normal rules and other active controls. Interest depends on the IRM. Live market settings and permissions are not independently verified.

Source-bound permission and authority diagrams from the November 9 proposal and current specifications. Arrows identify affected action routes, not quantities or guaranteed execution. No numerical outcome chart is warranted.

Proposed Lido Lend design, not a live pause. Available routes remain subject to normal rules and other active controls. Interest depends on the IRM. Live market settings and permissions are not independently verified.

There is a protective reason to suspend more than new borrowing. The proposal warns that initial price feeds, or oracles, use issuer-published collateral rates, which may diverge from secondary-market prices. If collateral falls in the market without a corresponding rate change, liquidation may become uneconomic and settlement may deliver collateral worth less than the debt canceled. Pausing those transactions can contain that risk, while also interrupting borrowers trying to repay.

The proposed Lend Emergency Brakes Committee has a 3-of-6 signing threshold. Through CircuitBreaker, it could trigger one fixed-duration controller pause per registration while maintaining required liveness signals, called heartbeats. It could not select the duration, extend the pause or end it early.

The roles specification assigns duration configuration and pauser registration to a separate administrator within immutable bounds. The committee’s successful pause consumes its registration, so another use requires re-registration.

The repository’s mainnet profile selects a configuration with an initial pause of five minutes and a permitted range from one minute to 60 days. The first market’s actual setting has not been confirmed.

Automatic expiry also has an exception. The proposal says the protocol-wide Reseal Manager can make a pause indefinite when Dual Governance is outside its normal state. The published Reseal Manager and Dual Governance implementations require an active finite pause and an authorized Reseal Committee acting through the governance contract. That path can replace the finite pause with an indefinite one without a fresh ordinary DAO vote at that step.

These controls apply per Lido Lend market and do not themselves move user assets. Separate DAO-controlled proxy upgrades remain part of the protocol’s trust assumptions.

For the first WETH/wstETH market, watch for the configured pause duration and who can extend it indefinitely. Those decisions will determine how long borrowers could be stuck with an interest bill they cannot stop by repaying.

#5056. Binance Warns About AI Scams

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has warned of the rising risk of AI scams, including the use of deepfakes that impersonate Binance executives and staff.

The world's largest crypto exchange recently took to X to warn its users that improvements in artificial intelligence are making it harder to distinguish fake messages from real ones.

"AI deepfakes are making impersonation scams harder to spot," the crypto exchange said in a post.

The cryptocurrency exchange has assured its users that no one from Binance will ever reach out to them asking for money or offering unsolicited investment advice.

Binance says scammers are making realistic deepfake videos featuring executives and employees of the company.

Fraudsters are using these deepfakes, some of which are very realistic, to trick potential targets through fraudulent video calls.

That way, people who fall victim to the scam might think they are interacting with real Binance personnel.

Binance warned that scammers often try to reach potential targets through messaging apps such as WhatsApp or Telegram. They impersonate Binance employees by using their names, photos, and job titles to appear credible.

After making contact with a potential victim, the scammer may try to convince them to send crypto, take part in an exclusive investment opportunity, or take other financial actions.

Binance has called on crypto users to be cautious about any unexpected messages they receive, even if they seem to be from someone at the company they know.

A realistic appearance no longer guarantees a person's identity, given that AI can now easily mimic voices and facial expressions.

Users should double-check any suspicious messages through official Binance support channels before taking any action.

#5055. Who Is Colette Kress, Jensen Huang’s Successor as Nvidia CEO?

Who Is Colette Kress, Jensen Huang’s Successor as Nvidia CEO?

For the first time in 33 years, someone other than Jensen Huang is running Nvidia. And the person taking over is not an engineer, a chip designer, or a Silicon Valley founder.

Colette Kress, Nvidia's 59-year-old chief financial officer, was named interim CEO Thursday following Huang's abrupt resignation amid reports of extramarital affairs and allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.

Kress will remain CFO while the board searches for a permanent replacement, according to Nvidia's regulatory filing. She inherits a company worth trillions of dollars, a shaken investor base, and a management structure built around one man.

Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013, when it was primarily known for graphics cards used in video games. She arrived with nearly 25 years of financial experience across some of America's largest technology companies.

She spent eight years at Texas Instruments before joining Microsoft in 1997. During her 13-year tenure there, she became CFO of the Server and Tools division, overseeing financial strategy for Microsoft's enterprise computing business.

In 2010, she moved to Cisco as senior vice president and CFO of its Business Technology and Operations Finance organization, managing financial planning and business development across the networking giant's operations.

Kress holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University, according to her official biography.

Her move to Nvidia came with an unusual endorsement. Her two sons, then enthusiastic gamers, encouraged her to join the company responsible for the graphics chips powering their favorite games, according to Forbes.

Huang personally recruited her, explaining his vision for AI computing on a whiteboard during their discussions, Wired reported. At the time, Nvidia was the smallest company Kress had worked for.

When Kress joined Nvidia, its annual revenue stood at approximately $4.13 billion. By fiscal 2026, that figure had reached $215.9 billion, an increase of more than 50 times.

Huang drove Nvidia's technological strategy, but Kress oversaw the finances supporting its expansion from gaming hardware into data centers and AI infrastructure.

Her tenure included Nvidia's $6.9 billion acquisition of networking specialist Mellanox and an increasingly aggressive strategy of investing in companies that purchase its computing hardware.

Those relationships now include CoreWeave, in which Nvidia invested another $2 billion in January. CoreWeave's rapid growth reflects enormous demand for Nvidia-powered computing, alongside the financial costs of building that infrastructure.

Kress also became Nvidia's principal financial voice to Wall Street, regularly explaining margins, chip demand and revenue forecasts during earnings calls.

Forbes ranked her among America's richest self-made women in 2026, with almost $750 million in Nvidia shares as of Wednesday's close.

Kress takes charge as Nvidia faces questions about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending. Nvidia had already lost approximately $1.27 trillion in market value from its October peak before the board publicly announced its investigation on Huang’s love affairs.

She must also navigate Washington's restrictions on advanced chip exports to China and scrutiny surrounding Nvidia's commercial relationships. The board has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or U.S. national security were compromised in the allegations involving Huang.

Her financial expertise cannot entirely replace Huang's technical background or his personal relationships with developers, customers, and governments. Maintaining Nvidia's engineering leadership will require close coordination with the executives responsible for its chips and software.

Kress has promised to build on Huang's legacy, saying that “Nvidia's strength has always come from its people.”

Her first major public test arrives Tuesday, November 17, when Nvidia reports its third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings. The company has scheduled its results for approximately 1:20 p.m. Pacific, followed by an investor call at 2 p.m.

A dashboard shared by trader Flood estimates an unrealized loss of about $9 billion, but applies August purchase costs to November holdings.

Trader Flood, who posts as @ThinkingUSD, called Ethereum a “contender for the worst asset of all time” on Nov. 13, sharing a dashboard that put BitMine’s unrealized loss at about $9 billion.

The image marked the Ethereum treasury company 43% underwater. Its holdings match BitMine’s November disclosure, while its average-cost field is dated August. Applying that older average to the later balance approximately reproduces the dashboard’s displayed cost, leaving its loss figure dependent on that assumption.

Flood cited money lost to hacks, development time spent on inadequate tools and retail losses from betting on Ethereum’s price. He supplied no figures for those categories or comparative data establishing an all-time ranking. His criticism targeted Ethereum, with the BitMine dashboard providing a specific example of treasury exposure.

The image Flood shared listed 6,070,092 ETH, a $3,380 average cost, a $20.52 billion total cost basis and an $11.69 billion market value. Its displayed unrealized loss was $8,829,920,029.

The average-cost field is labeled as the filed average for Aug. 31, 2026. BitMine’s annual accounts reported 5,901,837 ETH at that date, with a cost basis of about $19.95 billion and a fair value of about $14.56 billion. Dividing the cost by the quantity gives approximately $3,380 per ETH.

Those accounts were filed on Nov. 10, but the holdings and cost figures describe the August balance.

BitMine’s Nov. 9 release reported a larger holding of 6,070,092 ETH as of Nov. 8 at 2 p.m. ET. Multiplying that quantity by the rounded August average produces roughly the $20.52 billion cost basis displayed on Flood’s dashboard.

That calculation extrapolates across two reporting dates. It reproduces the rounded total without confirming the dashboard’s underlying methodology or establishing what the expanded ETH holding actually cost. The November release supplies no updated aggregate cost basis.

The dashboard’s $8.83 billion loss estimate is therefore an unrealized mark against an assumed cost. It provides no evidence that BitMine sold those holdings and realized the loss in cash.

#5050. The Fed could rescue bond markets and still make life harder for Bitcoin

Lorie Logan wants emergency support for Treasury markets while favoring further rate hikes, leaving Bitcoin exposed to tighter monetary policy.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan proposed stronger tools to keep Treasury markets functioning during a crisis while leaving room for higher interest rates. Her November 13 remarks separate two potential influences on Bitcoin: relief from disrupted funding and pressure from further monetary tightening.

In the speech, Logan said the Treasury market was functioning very well and presented personal recommendations, rather than announcing an intervention or an adopted Federal Open Market Committee program. She said intervention should be reserved for extreme failures in intermediation; high or rapidly rising yields alone would not justify it.

Her rate outlook points toward further tightening. In November 10 remarks, Logan described current monetary policy as accommodative and called for at least two further quarter-point increases to make it modestly restrictive. She made the pace conditional on developments. The FOMC's October 28 decision had maintained the target range at 3.75% to 4%; her preferred path is distinct from that committee decision.

Her preferred starting point is lending against Treasury securities. The Fed could supply funding at a rate consistent with its monetary-policy target, supporting financial stability while maintaining the interest-rate stance it considers necessary.

Logan also proposed developing central clearing for the Fed's repo lending. Reducing the balance-sheet costs intermediaries incur when passing funding onward could help that money reach the broader market more efficiently during stress.

Purchases would serve a different need. When lending cannot resolve dysfunction, buying securities could free space on intermediaries' balance sheets so they can keep trading. But purchases are harder to separate from monetary policy because they can push down term premiums and stimulate the economy.

Logan suggested holding market-function purchases in a separate account and committing to sell the securities as soon as possible. She argued that purchases expected to unwind quickly should have much less effect on term premiums than holdings kept for years. That would limit the unwanted stimulus, rather than guarantee its elimination.

If lending is insufficient, purchases could free balance sheets. Holding them separately and selling promptly aims to limit stimulus.

Funding relief could support risk-taking while further tightening could still weigh on Bitcoin.

Personal proposals, not adopted policy or a current intervention. Logan wants further tightening. The Bitcoin connection is conditional analysis; the historical IMF study does not forecast a response. Prompt resale aims to reduce, not eliminate, stimulus.

For Bitcoin, the implication is conditional. Restoring disrupted Treasury funding could improve the environment for risk-taking. Yet further monetary tightening could still weigh on crypto risk appetite, even if the financial system were functioning more smoothly.

An August 2023 IMF working paper supplies historical evidence for that second channel. It finds that US monetary tightening reduces a common crypto price factor through risk-taking, resembling the transmission to equities. That aggregate finding is not a forecast of Bitcoin's response to Logan's proposals.

#5048. Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Bitcoin custody has always involved some degree of risk, but wallet manufacturers like Trezor—which build physical devices designed to keep a user’s private keys secure offline—are preparing for a post-quantum world where new challenges arise.

That’s because SHRINCS, the community’s leading candidate for a post-quantum signature scheme, allows users to make transactions using stateful signatures that require rigid state tracking to prevent funds from being stolen, according to Trezor CTO Tomáš Sušánka.

Proposed late last year by Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick and cryptographer Mikhail Kudinov, SHRINCS centers on a composite hash-based approach: users can make transactions using either stateful signatures or stateless signatures.

Stateless signatures are quite large—potentially affecting fees, signature speed, and other efficiency metrics—but are safe to reuse, while smaller, more efficient stateful signatures come with serious security risks when reused beyond a particular signing budget.

The stateful component of SHRINCS is made up of a tree of one-time signatures, and if these keys are accidentally used more than once, enough cryptographic information is revealed for someone else to forge that user’s signature and effectively steal funds.

If Bitcoin successfully adopts SHRINCS, maintaining a meticulous count of the wallet’s state will become a critical responsibility for wallet developers—with lots of potential edge-case security risks.

“You’re giving them an option to mess up,” Sušánka said during a recent episode of MARA Foundation TV, in reference to state tracking. “It’s our job to make it in a secure way, right? It shouldn't be the user’s job.”

To mitigate this risk, Trezor is weighing options for how to support secure UX in a post-quantum world. For instance, Sušánka said the company is considering making the heavier, slower stateless signatures the default setting for all users, tucking the riskier stateful option behind an advanced settings wall.

While Sušánka recognizes that SHRINCS may be the conservative cryptographic choice because it relies on the same cryptographic assumptions as SHA-256, he is “kind of torn on the topic because maintaining the state is a burden.”

“For example, you can have two Trezors with the same recovery seed. How do you share the state between those two? You really don’t,” he added.

“That being said, as it is with everything, this is about trade-offs,” Sušánka continued. “The [stateful] signatures are 10 times smaller ... That makes a big difference. So, I just don't want to throw it off the table completely.”

Sušánka went on to share that while many are focused on Bitcoin’s migration path to post-quantum addresses and signatures, hardware wallet devices will also need to be physically updated for full quantum protection. Most signing devices use quantum-vulnerable cryptography for hardware-specific security functions, like firmware and device authentication.

If users want to ensure their devices are secure in a post-quantum world, they will need to use “quantum-ready” devices—that is, devices that use post-quantum cryptography for device and firmware authentication as well.

In anticipation of these needs, the company is already shipping products like Trezor Safe 7 that support post-quantum cryptography for wallet authentication processes. Of course, transactions made on these devices will only be quantum-secure once Bitcoin itself upgrades to post-quantum security.

That said, Sušánka warned developers not to wait too long to give users migration options, as he believes the migration of potentially millions of users will take time.

“People should be ready to make compromises,” Sušánka said. “If we’re all going to be very strict on what can and cannot be done, we’re not going to get anywhere.”

André Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

#5044. Britain to spend £4 billion on grid bottlenecks. Can Bitcoin use the wasted wind?

Flexible mines could use curtailed Scottish wind, but most recent constraint spending paid for replacement power elsewhere. A proposed demand service would start in 2028.

Britain’s grid operator forecasts about £4 billion in costs from transmission bottlenecks in 2027, putting a practical question to Bitcoin mining’s flexible-power pitch: can miners cut costs by using Scottish wind that cannot reach other consumers?

The National Energy System Operator (NESO) published the forecast on Nov. 12. Its latest cost breakdown shows why the answer depends on where a mine connects and which expense it actually avoids.

Thermal constraints arise when transmission lines cannot safely carry all the available electricity. NESO can then pay generators to reduce output while securing replacement supply elsewhere.

The forecast concerns thermal constraints, rather than all electricity balancing costs. It is sensitive to gas prices and network availability. NESO estimates costs would be 16% lower without network outages, although those outages also enable reinforcement intended to ease future bottlenecks.

In its Nov. 9 outturn explanation, NESO reported total balancing costs of about £3 billion for 2025/26, including roughly £2 billion for thermal constraints. A little under £500 million was paid to wind farms to turn down.

Around 75% of thermal constraint costs paid for replacement energy, predominantly from gas units.

Scotland nevertheless presents a potential use case. NESO says 28% of wind in the northern area above a transmission boundary known as B6 was curtailed in 2025/26, compared with 13% across Great Britain.

A flexible mine could reduce wind turn-down costs by consuming otherwise curtailed electricity at a connection and time that helps manage the relevant bottleneck. But adding northern demand does not itself deliver more power south. While the boundary remains binding and southern demand is unchanged, replacement supply remains necessary there.

That limits the savings claim: reduced wind turn-down does not establish an equivalent reduction in gas generation, consumer bills or emissions.

That measures demand turned down, while absorbing surplus Scottish wind would require demand to turn up at the right location and time.

Its March 5 proposed Demand for Constraints design focused on Scottish boundaries. It contemplated registration and dispatch through the Balancing Mechanism, NESO’s system for directing electricity supply and demand in real time, with routes for both new connections and existing assets creating additional flexible demand. The March design proposed service deliveries from 2028, after the year covered by the forecast. It did not establish a Bitcoin-specific approval or payment entitlement.

For a mine, a usable connection, service qualification and enough operating hours to cover costs would all matter. For consumers, the relevant comparison is the expense actually avoided after accounting for the costs the project adds.

NESO’s test is overall system cost. The roughly £4 billion forecast identifies the scale of a grid problem; it does not price a mining solution.

#5041. Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy made $19.53 billion in profit last quarter. Yet MSCI, one of the world’s biggest providers of stock indexes, has decided Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin company no longer belongs in some of its major investment benchmarks.

MSCI’s November review lists “STRATEGY A”—the company’s MSTR shares—for deletion from the MSCI USA Index after trading closes November 30. That also removes the stock from broader indexes that include U.S. companies, such as the MSCI World and MSCI All Country World indexes.

That sounds technical, but the distinction matters: MSCI is not removing Strategy from the Nasdaq stock exchange, shutting down its business, or making it sell Bitcoin. It is taking MSTR out of stock lists that investment funds use to decide which companies to own.

Consider an ETF designed to copy the MSCI USA Index. When MSTR disappears from the list, the fund generally has to sell its shares, regardless of whether the fund manager likes Saylor’s strategy.

This is why it’s bad news for Strategy. It means less indirect exposition to investments.

MSCI adopted new rules in October for so-called non-operating companies. The idea is to keep investment vehicles—businesses that mainly hold financial assets—out of indexes meant to track operating companies. Its screening process considers a company’s operating assets and other financial measures.

MSCI’s deletion list does not spell out exactly which tests Strategy failed. The company, however, argues that raising capital, managing its Bitcoin treasury and issuing financial products amount to a genuine operating business.

In an August letter to MSCI, Strategy called the proposal “discriminatory, arbitrary, and misguided.” It argued that MSCI should be a “mirror of the market, not an arbiter of it.”

Strategy also maintains a software business, but Bitcoin now dominates its finances. The disagreement is whether its Bitcoin activity counts as running a company or mainly managing an investment portfolio.

Strategy’s latest quarterly earnings show $19.53 billion in net income. But that does not mean its software customers paid the company anything close to that amount.

Nearly all of its $20.91 billion in reported operating income came from a rise in the accounting value of its Bitcoin. Under rules adopted in 2025, changes in Bitcoin’s market price appear in Strategy’s earnings even when it has not sold the coins. A decline in Bitcoin can produce the opposite result.

Its software division, meanwhile, recorded $125.4 million in quarterly revenue, down 3% from a year earlier. Its $477.2 million in revenue for all of 2025 was slightly below the $486.3 million reported in 2019, before Strategy began buying Bitcoin.

The immediate risk is selling pressure on MSTR, not on Bitcoin itself. Strategy estimated that funds linked to MSCI indexes hold roughly 13 million of its shares, or 3.1% of its outstanding common stock. Not all of that necessarily translates into sudden sales, and Strategy says the amount is manageable.

But Strategy has repeatedly raised money by selling shares and other securities, then used those proceeds to buy Bitcoin. If its stock falls, selling the same number of new shares brings in less cash.

So the company would have to issue more shares to raise the same amount—or buy fewer Bitcoin.

That is why a stock-index decision could eventually matter to the crypto market. The exclusion does not force a Bitcoin sale, and it does not guarantee fewer purchases. It could, however, weaken a key source of funding for one of Bitcoin’s biggest corporate buyers.

#5038. Robots now run AI-written code without an AI calling the shots, succeeding 92% of the time

Robots completed 221 of 240 trials using Claude-written programs for tasks such as uncapping bottles. Human help was available during development, not execution.

Robot programs developed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 coding agent completed 221 of 240 physical evaluation trials, ACE-CaP-0 researchers reported in a study posted November 12. The result shows that task-specific skills can persist in code and run without the coding agent choosing each action.

The researchers behind ACE-CaP-0, a method for developing robot control programs, reported a 92.1% success rate across eight tasks. Each program was frozen before 30 separate evaluation trials, with no further updates. Human guidance and demonstrations were available during development.

The experiment separates program development from repeated execution. The agent's work produced a program that could be used repeatedly. During evaluation, that program still used perception and control systems to respond to observations, while its decision rules stayed fixed. Neither a human nor the coding agent remained in the execution loop.

ACE-CaP-0 separates assisted program development from repeated execution with live perception and control.

Human assistance is available during development; the frozen task program runs without a human or coding agent in the execution loop.

Authors' preprint account. Development permits human assistance; demonstration-collection resets are excluded from the ten-reset budget. Repeated execution on tested tasks does not establish reuse under new conditions.

Source-bound qualitative process diagram from sections 2 to 4. Arrows show code revision and runtime sensing relationships, not timing, trial quantities or comparative efficiency.

Authors' preprint account. Development permits human assistance; demonstration-collection resets are excluded from the ten-reset budget. Repeated execution on tested tasks does not establish reuse under new conditions.

Author-reported successful trials out of 30 for each frozen program. These were physical evaluation trials, separate from development; Table 1, November 12 preprint.

The physical setup used two Agilex PIPERX arms and three cameras. Tasks included inserting a charger, uncapping a bottle and packing shoes. Charger insertion succeeded in all 30 trials; bread packing, the weakest result, succeeded in 25. Mean physical execution times across tasks ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

During development, the coding agent wrote, ran, inspected and revised its code using physical feedback. It could ask for textual advice or demonstrations in which a person physically guided the robot arms. Those demonstrations supplied video, arm trajectories and key joint poses.

Development allowed at most ten human-assisted scene resets per task. Resets used to collect demonstrations were excluded, and the budget counted scene resets rather than all robot executions or demonstrations.

The agent could also use simulated experiments when they helped resolve a development question. In a charger-insertion comparison, on-demand simulation produced a program with 100% evaluation success, versus 86.7% for development without simulation. The comparison used one development run per condition.

That comparison also illustrates a cost trade-off. Development took 2.6 hours with on-demand simulation versus 3.7 hours without it, while output-token usage increased from 730,000 to 1,090,000. The time and token figures leave total development costs unresolved; the researchers call for accounting that includes demonstration effort.

Repeating evaluation trials measures how the resulting program performs. Establishing how consistently the development process produces an equally capable program requires separate development runs across tasks.

ACE-CaP-0 leaves behind task-specific programs that can execute repeatedly with fresh observations and fixed decision rules. The study provides evidence for that form of skill reuse after human-assisted development. Testing those routines under new conditions is the next step toward establishing how broadly they can be reused.

#5035. North Korea Stole $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls, DOJ Says

North Korea Stole $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls, DOJ Says

North Korean hackers have stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months using a social-engineering scheme built on secretly recorded footage and AI deepfakes, the U.S. Justice Department said Thursday, as it announced the seizure of the infrastructure behind the operation.

The scheme, which the FBI calls “FaceStealer,” turns video conference calls into a trap. According to the DOJ, hackers lure targets into meetings using accounts stolen from previous victims, then play prerecorded webcam footage of trusted contacts to simulate their presence and win the target’s confidence.

The group also generates deepfake videos of well-known figures in the crypto and related industries, using AI to make the ruse more convincing.

Once a target is at ease, the attackers manufacture a fake technical glitch, such as claiming the person can’t be heard, and offer a link to “fix” it, which instead installs malware.

From there, the hackers can drain crypto wallets or exploit the victim’s access to other systems, sometimes waiting months or more than a year before striking. The FBI said it seized over 900 webcam recordings of FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant.

The DOJ tied the operation to North Korean groups known variously as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff and APT38, among others, and warned the hackers have increasingly targeted open-source software developers in an apparent bid to enable supply-chain attacks.

The announcement came paired with an update on the record-breaking Binance hack. The department said it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen from the exchange on Oct. 29, part of over $2.7 billion frozen so far.

The FBI attributed that theft to the North Korean group TraderTraitor, and the regime has been laundering the proceeds at speed, spinning up a new wallet roughly every 25 seconds. North Korea has denied involvement, calling the FBI’s finding a political provocation.

The actions underscore how central crypto theft has become to Pyongyang’s finances. The U.S. recently sanctioned 11 people over a North Korean IT-worker scheme that moved millions in crypto, and researchers have cataloged the many ways the regime’s hackers break into crypto firms.

Officials said efforts to trace and recover the stolen Binance funds are ongoing.

#5034. Bitcoin now looks cheap by one measure after $1 billion in ETF outflows

Bitcoin’s valuation signal looks cheaper, but five completed ETF sessions lost $1 billion. A durable recovery still needs buyers.

Bitcoin's latest on-chain valuation alert has arrived after five consecutive sessions of net redemptions from US spot exchange-traded funds, highlighting a lower valuation before the demand evidence confirms that buyers are absorbing supply.

CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost reported on Nov. 15 that Bitcoin's market-value-to-realized-value ratio, or MVRV, had fallen below 1.2. The ratio compares Bitcoin's market value with the value of coins at their last-moved prices. He called it the third trigger of his valuation preset during the 2026 bear market. Yet five completed ETF sessions through Nov. 13 recorded combined net outflows of $1 billion, according to Farside Investors.

The alert identifies a gap between lower valuation and returning demand. A lower aggregate valuation does not show whether new buying can absorb coins being moved at a loss.

CryptoSlate’s Bitcoin page showed $65,461 in a snapshot captured at 10:44 UTC on Nov. 15. The page said its price had refreshed about five minutes earlier.

MVRV divides market capitalization by realized capitalization, which values coins at the prices when they last moved. It compares today's aggregate market value with an on-chain cost proxy.

Darkfost identified earlier alerts in February, when Bitcoin had crossed $60,000, and June to July, when it reached $57,000. He also said the preset is adjusted over time to reflect MVRV's long-term decline.

That adjustment matters to the historical comparison. The post does not supply a threshold-change history or reproducible backtest showing what followed each signal. Three alerts within a bear market do not establish three durable bottoms.

CryptoQuant's methodology guide discusses MVRV below 1 as a possible-bottom region. That is distinct from Darkfost's adjusted sub-1.2 alert.

Unlike the specific holder-cost cluster examined in CryptoSlate's Nov. 14 coverage, MVRV covers Bitcoin's aggregate valuation. Both use last-movement information, which records historical positioning rather than current buying.

A separate CryptoQuant note from XWIN Japan, available on Nov. 15, cited a spent output profit ratio, or SOPR, near 0.98. The note did not identify the variant or exact observation time, limiting comparisons with other SOPR readings.

SOPR compares the aggregate dollar value of spent outputs when they move with their value when created. Below 1 means the measured outputs moved at an aggregate loss. It does not establish that every transfer was an exchange sale.

Adjusted SOPR excludes outputs younger than one hour, while long- and short-term-holder versions separate older and newer coins around a 155-day boundary. Those series need to remain distinct when assessing whether loss realization is easing.

Demand offers a separate test. Farside Investors recorded $185 million in net outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs on Nov. 13. That capped five consecutive sessions of net withdrawals from Nov. 9 through Nov. 13.

These are dated fund flows, not Sunday transactions, and ETFs represent only one channel of Bitcoin demand. Still, continuing redemptions leave that channel withdrawing capital rather than supplying the recurring inflows that would strengthen a recovery case.

Nvidia's scheduled Nov. 17 results provide a near-term risk test. The company plans to release results around 1:20 p.m. Pacific and hold its call at 2 p.m. Pacific.

Nvidia’s results could affect appetite for risk assets, including Bitcoin. The test afterward is whether spot buying and ETF inflows return alongside improving spent-output profitability.

#5028. How $10,000 in stablecoins would have gained €420 without earning interest

A fixed dollar-token balance would have gained 4.9% in euros from September 1 to November 13 before costs. A stronger euro can reverse that effect.

A dollar stablecoin can keep its peg while the euro spending value of a European saver’s balance moves sharply. At a perfect $1 peg, an unchanged holding would have gained about 4.9% in euros between September 1 and November 13, 2026, using European Central Bank reference rates and excluding costs.

The ECB’s household stablecoin analysis puts that currency exposure in context. Its experimental 2025 survey evidence identifies ownership of dollar tokens among euro area consumers. The subsequent exchange-rate comparison illustrates a separate point: stability against the dollar does not promise stability against the currency used to pay the rent.

The bulletin draws on Consumer Expectations Survey modules from August and November 2025 across the 11 largest euro area countries. In August, 5% of consumers reported stablecoin ownership by themselves or household members, while 13% reported crypto ownership.

Among respondents with crypto holdings, 17% reported USDT, 12% USDC and 10% the euro-denominated EURC. Those percentages measure how common ownership was among crypto-holding respondents. They reveal no token’s share of invested capital. Respondents could select several assets, and the crypto-holder subsample comprised 1,286 people.

The ownership observations date to 2025. The ECB flags small samples, questionnaire sensitivity and possible misreporting. It also says the survey does not directly report how assets were used, so the figures cannot establish payment adoption or tell us what households earned.

The two-date illustration takes September 1 as its chosen baseline. Different holding periods can produce different currency returns. The ECB’s dollar reference-rate history shows $1.1590 per euro on September 1 and $1.1052 on November 13, the latest working-day observation available for this comparison.

With fewer dollars needed to buy one euro, the same dollar balance translated into more euros. For 10,000 unchanged tokens worth exactly $1 each, the illustrative value rose from €8,628 to €9,048, a gain of about €420 before costs. Dividing 1.1590 by 1.1052 and subtracting one gives a 4.9% increase.

That entire illustrated gain comes from currency movement. Token quantity and dollar price are held constant, with no interest earned. Actual households’ returns would depend on their holdings, timing and costs. The ECB also publishes its rates for information and discourages transactional use, so retail conversion quotes can differ from these translation values.

The euro value rises 4.87% in this chosen interval through currency translation alone, before costs.

More generally, gross euro value equals token quantity multiplied by the token’s dollar price, divided by dollars per euro. Income can change the quantity or value of a position; a depeg changes the dollar price; exchange rates change its euro translation. Conversion costs reduce what is available to spend. A stronger euro can reverse the currency effect even if the dollar peg remains intact.

A separate stablecoin-yield study by DefiLlama Research, published November 12, examined a November 9 snapshot of 98 stablecoin pools with at least $50 million supplied, no token incentives over the preceding 30 days and a recorded 30-day base annual percentage yield (APY).

It reported a median base APY of 4.1%. Forty-eight pools exceeded the study’s 4.2% three-month Treasury benchmark, dated November 5; that selected group’s median was 5.4%.

These are annualized yield measures based on a trailing 30-day window. They cannot be compared as realized returns with the September-to-November currency gain. They do show why a quoted income rate gives only part of the euro holder’s picture. DefiLlama links higher premiums to additional credit, trading, liquidity or underlying-asset risks, alongside the risks of using smart contracts.

Bare token ownership is different again. Circle’s European Economic Area (EEA) USDC white paper says USDC itself generates no interest for holders and gives them no entitlement to reserve income. Earning a DeFi yield requires a separate position with its own terms and risks.

Redemption also needs a currency and an access route. Circle describes USDC as redeemable one-for-one for dollars. Although Circle Mint is institutional, eligible EEA retail holders have a separate route through Circle France under its MiCA redemption policy, subject to identity and transaction checks and an EEA bank account able to receive USD. Third-party bank conversion or incoming-payment fees may apply.

A holder saving for euro expenses therefore carries a currency exposure alongside peg and investment risks. Someone setting aside tokens for a dollar expense or offsetting a dollar liability may have a different net exposure. The relevant question is what the balance will buy in the currency the holder actually needs.

#5026. Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Josh Hawley wants Congress to hit the brakes on new data centers, just as lawmakers are moving forward with legislation intended to make building the infrastructure behind America's AI boom easier.

The Missouri senator called for a nationwide moratorium Wednesday, listing it among five priorities for Senate Republicans during the six weeks before Democrats take control of the chamber.

“Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks?” Hawley wrote on X. His answer included a moratorium on data centers, alongside defunding Planned Parenthood, suspending the gas tax and other Republican priorities.

A spokesperson told Politico that Hawley wants a federal pause until Congress passes a “bill of rights giving taxpayers guarantees of no rate increases.” Hawley has not presented detailed legislation specifying which projects would stop or how long the freeze would last.

Data centers are the warehouses packed with powerful computers that train and operate services such as ChatGPT. Building more AI systems means installing more servers, which requires additional electricity, cooling equipment and often upgrades to local power grids.

Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks? Here you go:DEFUND Planned ParenthoodMORATORIUM on data centersSUSPEND the gas tax FUND rural hospitals SAVE AMERICA ACT

— Josh Hawley (@HawleyMO) November 11, 2026

The scale helps explain the concern. U.S. data centers consumed an estimated 183 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, according to figures cited by Pew, and that could climb to 426 by 2030. In other words, their annual electricity demand could more than double in six years.

On Monday, the Senate voted 73-25 to advance debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a proposal backed by lawmakers from both parties and President Donald Trump's administration.

The bill would speed federal reviews for energy projects and transmission lines, helping bring new power supplies online. It would also require data center operators to pay the additional grid costs their projects create, rather than shifting those expenses onto ordinary electricity customers.

In practical terms, Congress is considering how to keep construction moving without making households subsidize it. Hawley is asking lawmakers to stop new construction until consumer protections are in place.

His position is not entirely new. In February, Hawley introduced the GRID Act with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, seeking to make new data centers obtain electricity from their own sources rather than relying on existing grid supplies.

He now joins independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in publicly supporting a national pause. Their moratorium proposal goes further, calling for rules addressing AI's effects on workers and public safety as well as the environment.

The politics have shifted quickly. In the November 3 elections, voters backed restrictions on data center development across the country, including local bans and measures requiring public approval before construction.

A Pew Research Center analysis published Wednesday found 60% of Americans uncomfortable with a new data center in their area, including 54% of Republicans and 68% of Democrats. Another survey found 58% disliked political leaders who support building data centers near them.

Opponents worry about rising bills, water consumption and noise. Cities have already imposed restrictions, while OpenAI recently promised to cover electricity and grid costs at future campuses it owns and operates.

Industry supporters see a bigger economic risk. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned last month that a construction moratorium could trigger a recession because so much investment now depends on AI infrastructure.

A federal construction freeze could delay the additional computing capacity that AI companies expect to bring online, along with the power infrastructure built to support it. Existing data centers would not necessarily shut down, but the scope of Hawley's proposed moratorium remains undefined.

Hawley's call does not freeze a single project, and he has not said whether he would support the Sanders bill. For now, the Senate is debating legislation to speed infrastructure approvals, not legislation to ban new data centers.

#5024. Tether wants its gold token to rival ETFs

New institutional trading and borrowing routes put Tether Gold closer to traditional finance, but access and cash-out terms still matter.

Anchorage Digital’s support for Tether Gold gives eligible institutional clients routes to sell or borrow against XAUT as Paolo Ardoino promotes it as a gold-ETF challenger. The competitive test is how readily those routes deliver funds at the size and price a holder needs.

In Tether’s November 12 announcement, its CEO said he believes XAUT is on track to become “the first true competitor to the gold ETF market.” A day earlier, Anchorage announced custody, principal-desk trading and collateral support for the gold-backed token. Like gold-trust shareholders, token holders still depend on counterparties to turn that exposure into funds.

Tether said KPMG U.S. audited issuer TG Commodities S.A. de C.V.’s financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, issuing an unqualified opinion. The announced audit concerns that entity and year, rather than all current Tether reserves or today’s trading and financing terms.

For eligible clients, desk-sale proceeds come from the trading counterparty. Anchorage advertises USD or USDT borrowing against bank-custodied XAUT through arrangements with other clients. Borrowing preserves gold exposure but creates debt; the announcement does not establish bank-funded lending. It also specifies neither a universal sale settlement currency nor a fiat-withdrawal timetable.

Anchorage says it holds XAUT at Anchorage Digital Bank in the US or Anchorage Digital Singapore. The group’s footer names Anchorage Hold LLC as digital-asset trading provider, Anchorage Digital NY LLC for New York agency trading and A1 Ltd. as a principal-trading business. It does not identify one universal trade-contract entity.

Access is institutional, with limited high-net-worth availability and further requirements for certain trading. Custodied tokens lack Anchorage guarantees and FDIC or SIPC protection. Custody therefore provides neither an insured gold deposit nor assured liquidity.

Anchorage’s notice says US persons cannot purchase or redeem XAUT with TG Commodities. The issuer’s terms contain a qualification: US counterparties qualifying as eligible contract participants, a regulatory category, may be accepted at Tether Gold’s sole discretion. Direct purchases and redemptions also require verified issuer-customer status.

Platform eligibility, issuer eligibility and issuer acceptance are separate gates. Neither institutional access at Anchorage nor eligible-contract-participant status alone establishes the issuer’s acceptance. Anchorage’s notice addresses issuer transactions, rather than a blanket ban on permitted secondary trading or custody.

Even an eligible, verified issuer customer does not have an unconditional cash buyback. The terms describe whole-bar redemption for delivery in Switzerland. Instead of taking delivery, a customer can request that Tether Gold attempt a sale to a gold dealer or broker. Only a successful sale produces fiat proceeds, less fees; Tether Gold has no obligation to repurchase the tokens or bullion. That route also needs a buyer.

The iShares Gold Trust product page describes IAU shares trading on NYSE Arca through brokerage accounts. For an ordinary share sale, a market buyer supplies the money through the brokerage transaction. The trust is not paying the retail holder cash for redeeming a share.

Its currently linked prospectus, dated December 22, 2022, reserves creation and redemption of baskets to authorized participants, with gold exchanged for shares. Retail sale access and direct redemption access are different rights in this structure as well.

Borrowing without selling is also available within conventional brokerage arrangements, subject to approval. Fidelity’s margin FAQ lists ETFs held for at least 30 days as eligible collateral, with special security and account requirements, and says checkwriting, bank cards and bill payments can create or increase margin debt. That general policy establishes neither IAU-specific approval nor a particular borrowing limit.

Both structures need a counterparty. Switch between selling and borrowing to follow the funds.

The trading counterparty or market buyer supplies sale proceeds. The desk or broker provides the route.

Another bank client supplies XAUT financing; a brokerage lender may supply approved margin credit. Both create debt.

A sale needs a buyer; a loan needs a lender. Custody alone guarantees neither.

Anchorage notice excludes US direct issuer transactions; issuer terms allow discretionarily accepted US ECPs after verification. Neither custody nor ECP status establishes issuer acceptance. IAU trust redemption is AP-only for gold. Fidelity policy does not establish IAU-specific credit. Sale currencies, fiat withdrawal timing and loan terms remain client-specific.

Qualitative cash-direction diagram from the reported service mechanisms. Arrows show direction, not volume, speed or guaranteed availability. The borrowing panel compares client financing with a general brokerage margin route.

Anchorage notice excludes US direct issuer transactions; issuer terms allow discretionarily accepted US ECPs after verification. Neither custody nor ECP status establishes issuer acceptance. IAU trust redemption is AP-only for gold. Fidelity policy does not establish IAU-specific credit. Sale currencies, fiat withdrawal timing and loan terms remain client-specific.

CryptoSlate’s July analysis of XAUT lending already examined the comparison with brokerage margin and restricted gold-trust redemption. Anchorage’s offering extends the institutional service set; collateral utility alone does not make tokenized gold unique.

The measurable comparison remains uneven. iShares reported 9,023,902 IAU shares traded on November 13 and a 0.01% 30-day median bid/ask spread as of that date. Anchorage calls XAUT its most active tokenized-gold product, but its announcement supplies no comparable depth series, quoted spreads or executed lending totals.

Ardoino’s ETF challenge ultimately turns on usable access: a client who qualifies, a counterparty willing to transact and terms that deliver the funds required. Custody and collateral support create routes. Their availability at the needed size and price is the next test.

#5020. Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC), chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, has asked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, widening a congressional inquiry that has moved from Huang's private life to U.S. controls on chip exports to China. "The American people deserve answers," Scott wrote in a tweet announcing the requests on Thursday evening.

In a letter dated November 12, Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily at a public hearing on December 3 over public reports that "raise significant national security concerns." The committee has jurisdiction over export controls, "including their application to NVIDIA's exports of advanced semiconductors," he wrote. If Huang does not appear, the committee "is prepared to use all tools at our disposal, including subpoenas."

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology.

I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

The American people deserve… pic.twitter.com/Xu1kiNzkhW

— Senator Tim Scott (@SenatorTimScott) November 13, 2026

Scott asked Lutnick to testify on December 10, noting Commerce's "central role in issuing and enforcing export control regulations." A Lutnick spokesperson told NBC News that he had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily," while the White House said President Donald Trump "maintains complete confidence" in Lutnick.

Separately on Thursday, the Republican chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, China and Intelligence committees, Reps. Brian Mast (R-FL), John Moolenaar (R-MI) and Rick Crawford (R-AR), wrote to Huang, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department's under secretary for industry and security.

Huang was asked to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1 and Teter on December 2, with each given until 8 p.m. on Friday to agree or face a subpoena. Kessler, whose bureau administers export controls, was invited to a hearing on December 3.

"As reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and MegaSpeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three chairs said in a statement. They called on Congress to add four chip security bills to the annual defense authorization bill.

It is their second request. A letter dated November 4 had asked Huang to brief the committees on November 18. Mast told reporters on Thursday that Huang had agreed to brief lawmakers, NBC News reported.

At the center of the inquiries is Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. U.S. officials suspected the company of helping Chinese firms get around restrictions on advanced AI chips, The New York Times reported in October. Its sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the Times.

Megaspeed told the Times it had hired outside counsel to conduct an internal investigation. Nvidia has said it complies with U.S. export laws, according to NBC News.

The Times reported that U.S. officials had concluded that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, was a Chinese intelligence asset. China has rejected that as a smear, and Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion on whether she was a spy, according to BBC News.

Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife and resigned on Thursday. Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

Moolenaar told reporters that Huang had "been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls," Roll Call reported. On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), the Banking Committee's ranking member, and Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) asked Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to preserve records on Nvidia chip exports to China.

China's foreign ministry warned on Friday that tighter U.S. export controls on semiconductors would threaten the stability of global supply chains, Al Jazeera reported.

Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% at $166.19 on Thursday and were up 2.7% at $170.63 in premarket trading early on Friday, according to Yahoo! Finance. The company has lost almost $500 billion in market value since the close on Friday, November 6. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first under interim CEO Colette Kress.
