#4970. CFTC’s Selig accuses states of trying to ‘lock up’ prediction market founders

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Chair Michael Selig defends federal oversight of prediction markets as states pursue enforcement and the CFTC presses its authority in court.

Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig is turning up the heat on his criticisms of states' handling of lawsuits brought against prediction market platforms and their executives.

Speaking at the Cantor Convergence conference, Selig called the state suits "really egregious" and defended the platforms operating under what he has long called the CFTC's "exclusive jurisdiction."

"We're seeing states bring criminal charges, essentially trying to lock up founders and CEOs of these companies that are offering lawful products under a federal regime," he said.

The comments come amid a stretch of battles between the CFTC and roughly a dozen states and cities over whether event contracts offered on prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket constitute illegal gambling. Selig argued that the disagreements should be hashed out in court without threatening executives with time in prison.

"Somebody says it's gambling, somebody says it's a derivative," he said. "That's not something that should be at the risk of going to jail."

And instead of fighting on a case-by-case basis in multiple states, Selig wants to see the issue raised to the Supreme Court in a bid to solidify the CFTC's authority.

"I don't understand whether we're going to have every major CEO of an exchange locked up in a jail cell in Utah, or if we can just go to the Supreme Court and hash this thing out on the merits," he said.

On Thursday, the Justice Department and CFTC sued Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin to block his action against Kalshi.

Louisiana also filed a lawsuit Thursday targeting companies including Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood and Coinbase.

"I am concerned that some of the states are getting very aggressive," Selig said. "We’ll continue to defend our jurisdiction."

#4967. House Oversight Chair calls for possible ban on government officials’ prediction market bets over insider trading concerns

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Friday, the committee released its findings of an investigation it launched in May on insider trading risks in prediction markets among government officials.

The Republican chair of the House Oversight Committee is calling for new limits on government officials' use of prediction markets, including the possibility of an outright ban, amid growing concerns that public officials could use insider information to profit from bets on the platforms.

On Friday, the committee released findings from an investigation it launched in May into insider trading risks in prediction markets among government officials, military personnel, and those with security clearances. The committee sifted through 1,700 pages of documents and also received five bipartisan staff briefings from prediction market companies, said Chair James Comer, R-Ky.

Concerns in Washington have intensified over the past year, particularly after an active-duty U.S. Army soldier who used confidential information to place bets on Polymarket ahead of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro's capture. Thereafter, others in government have also been found using inside information to make money on bets on prediction markets, including the White House's former teleprompter operator. Political candidates have also faced allegations of insider trading on the platforms.

"Congress must consider additional reforms to prevent public corruption and restore the American people's trust in government," Comer said on Friday.

Those reforms should be legislation that restricts which bets federal employees, lawmakers and congressional staff can place on prediction markets — or an outright ban, the committee said.

"Whether it's an outright prohibition on trading on prediction markets or restrictions on some subset of contracts like government-related contracts, applying these restrictions to officials in all branches of government would strengthen ethical expectations that government personnel should not personally and financially benefit from access to non-public information associated with their work as government servants…" according to the memo.

Congress should also have a role in encouraging prediction market companies and federal agencies to share necessary information to enforce restrictions, the committee said.

Both major prediction market companies — Kalshi and Polymarket — have said they have taken steps to tighten controls to prevent government officials from using inside information. Lawmakers have also begun addressing the issue themselves. In April, the Senate voted to pass a resolution to ban members from trading on prediction markets.

#4966. Fed Chair Warsh Wants Answers on AI Inflation—and Bitcoin May Feel the Impact

Fed Chair Warsh Wants Answers on AI Inflation—and Bitcoin May Feel the Impact

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will convene a public forum Monday to examine whether artificial intelligence will bring down inflation, drive prices higher, or replace American workers.

The November 16 conference in San Francisco will bring together technology executives, economists, and employers to examine how AI is reshaping the economy.

The findings could influence how the Fed approaches interest rates, a major factor in Bitcoin's price movements as investors weigh whether to put money into risky assets or safer alternatives.

Warsh has argued that AI could help companies produce more goods and services at lower costs, easing inflation without requiring the Fed to keep borrowing expensive.

But some of his colleagues see a different problem: The AI boom is already making things more expensive, while the promised productivity benefits remain largely theoretical.

Building data centers requires enormous quantities of electricity, computer chips, construction materials, and skilled workers. When technology companies compete for those limited resources, prices rise.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned in September that AI investment was adding inflationary pressure and delaying the central bank's return to its 2% inflation target.

If AI eventually allows businesses to produce more without raising costs, inflation could cool, giving policymakers room to lower interest rates.

Lower rates generally make risky assets like Bitcoin or tech stocks more attractive because government bonds and savings accounts offer smaller returns, encouraging investors to seek higher gains elsewhere.

But if AI spending keeps inflation elevated, the Fed could maintain high interest rates or raise them further. That would make borrowing more expensive, strengthen the appeal of interest-bearing assets, and potentially drain money from speculative investments, including cryptocurrencies.

Bitcoin is already feeling that pressure. The cryptocurrency dropped below $69,000 Friday as stronger-than-expected inflation figures fueled concerns about another Fed rate hike.

AI also has a more direct connection to the Bitcoin industry than most may think of.

Both AI data centers and Bitcoin mining operations need access to large amounts of electricity. As AI companies compete for power and infrastructure, miners face pressure to secure affordable energy or consider more profitable alternatives.

Some are already abandoning Bitcoin mining altogether. Hyperscale Data shut down mining operations at its Michigan facility in September to accommodate an AI customer under a deal potentially worth more than $1.2 billion. The same has happened with other big names like Coreweave and other former Ethereum miners from its proof-of-work era.

Meanwhile, AI's potential impact on employment adds another complication.

Fed Governor Michael Barr warned Thursday of possible “serious short-term disruptions” as businesses increasingly replace human tasks with AI systems.

Widespread job losses could weaken consumer spending, slow economic growth, and eventually increase pressure on the Fed to cut rates. But a deteriorating economy could also push investors away from Bitcoin as they look to reduce risk.

Warsh himself acknowledged in August that AI represents “a new variable” for monetary policy.

The question now is whether AI's economic benefits will arrive quickly enough to outweigh the costs of building it.

Monday's conference will not determine the Fed's next interest-rate decision, scheduled for December 9. But it could offer clues about how policymakers view a technology boom that is increasingly influencing both Wall Street and the crypto market.

#4960. Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million

Dormant Bitcoin Wallets Wake Up After 16 Years, Moving $6.9 Million

Two Bitcoin addresses that had been dormant since 2010 suddenly moved $6.9 million worth of BTC on Friday, bringing two early mining rewards back into circulation after more than 16 years.

Blockchain tracking service Whale Alert flagged the first transfer at 4:08 a.m. UTC on November 13, when 50 BTC worth approximately $3.44 million moved from an address that had not spent its original mining reward since September 2010.

Just over two minutes later, another 50 BTC moved from a separate wallet with an equally long history.

Both transfers involved Bitcoin originally generated through mining, rather than coins purchased on an exchange. Their combined value today was approximately $6,885,068.

The coins came from two blocks mined on September 8 and September 19, 2010, respectively. Back then, Bitcoin traded for roughly six cents, meaning each 50 BTC reward was worth about three bucks.

At Friday's transaction prices of around $68,800 per Bitcoin, their combined value had increased approximately 1,147,511 times, equivalent to a 114,751,033% increase.

That percentage measures the appreciation in Bitcoin's market price (what’s known as unrealized gains), not money the holder has actually made by selling (which would be known as realized gains). In fact, it’s unknown whether this was a peer-to-peer transaction, an OTC sell, or simply a wallet switch for security reasons.

The $3 valuation is also an estimate. Bitcoin barely had a functioning market in September 2010, with historical prices showing a trading range of around five to seven cents. The Mt. Gox exchange had only opened that July, with its first recorded trade taking place at $0.04951 per coin.

The transfers are part of a broader trend of ancient Bitcoin wallets waking up in 2026. According to Galaxy Research data highlighted in August, Bitcoin that had remained untouched for at least a decade was moving at a pace rarely seen in previous years. In one 10-day stretch alone, six wallets dating back to 2011, 2012, and 2014 transferred a combined 553.59 BTC, worth more than $40 million at the time.

Some of those movements have been linked to security concerns, wallet upgrades, or transfers to professional custodians rather than outright selling. Friday's activity adds another 100 BTC to the growing list of early Bitcoin holdings changing hands—or at least changing addresses—after more than a decade of silence.

The blockchain provides a detailed record of where the money moved, but it doesn't reveal who controls the receiving wallets.

The first transaction split the 50 BTC into two new addresses, sending nearly 49.99 BTC to one and approximately 0.01 BTC to another, minus a tiny network fee.

The second transaction followed a similar pattern, transferring nearly 49 BTC to one address and approximately 1 BTC to another.

Both transactions cost just 1,110 satoshis each in network fees, equivalent to approximately $0.75. A satoshi is Bitcoin's smallest unit, worth one hundred-millionth of a BTC.

As of an on-chain check at approximately 14:00 UTC Friday, the 100 BTC had not moved again from their new destinations following the consolidation, and no sale has been identified.

#4957. Meta tests prediction market app using ‘cred’ points instead of cash: WSJ

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Meta’s employee trial advances its prediction market push as Kalshi and Polymarket battle state gambling lawsuits.

Meta has started internal testing of a prediction market app with its employees that would let users compete on guessing the outcome of events without putting real money on the line, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday.

The app, now going by the name Takes, lets users bet "cred" points, according to the report, which cited people familiar with the matter. Similar to other mainstream prediction markets that use money, correct predictions on Takes earn cred while wrong ones lose points.

The testing phase follows June reports that CEO Mark Zuckerberg directed employees to build a standalone prediction market app that would use points, though Meta had not ruled out eventually allowing real-money betting. At the time, the app was going by the name Arena.

The Journal's report does not say whether real-money contracts remain a possibility. Meta declined to comment or give a timetable for a public release.

It comes as real-money platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket are facing lawsuits from states that accuse them of offering illegal gambling. The platforms maintain that their event contracts are legal and fall under the jurisdiction of the federal government.

Speaking at the Cantor Convergence conference on Friday, Commodity and Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig criticized states for pursuing criminal charges against prediction market executives, adding that the disputes should be raised to the Supreme Court.

"Somebody says it's gambling, somebody says it’s a derivative," Selig said. "That's not something that should be at the risk of going to jail."

#4956. Trump nominates Hester Peirce successor among SEC, CFTC picks

The White House also named a former CFTC commissioner and two CLARITY Act veterans as nominees to fill vacancies at the SEC and CFTC.

US President Donald Trump has nominated Steven Levine to replace former Securities and Exchange Commission Commissioner Hester Peirce, one of the agency’s most prominent crypto advocates, as part of four nominations to fill vacancies at the SEC and Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The White House’s latest announcement on Thursday named two nominees each for the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, agencies whose decisions help shape US cryptocurrency regulation, among other functions. All four nominations require Senate confirmation.

The nominations would replenish several commissioner roles. The SEC currently has only two of its five commissioner seats filled, while CFTC Chairman Michael Selig is the sole member of his agency’s five-seat commission.

The nominations come weeks before Democrats are set to take control of the Senate in January, giving a narrow window for Republicans to confirm Trump’s picks.

Related: House Finance panel chair says regulator actions on crypto ‘fall short’ of CLARITY bill

Levine, a Republican, was nominated for an SEC term ending June 5, 2030, replacing Peirce, who left the agency in October. Peirce was a leading advocate for clearer crypto rules at the SEC, helping shape its approach to digital assets as the former head of its Crypto Task Force, while Levine’s views on crypto regulation are less publicly established.

Trump also nominated Democrat Kristin Johnson, a former CFTC commissioner, for the SEC seat held by Caroline Crenshaw, whose term has also expired. Johnson’s proposed term ends June 5, 2029. Johnson has advocated for stronger customer protections and conflict-of-interest rules for crypto firms in her time at the CFTC.

For the CFTC, Trump nominated Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland, both of whom worked on the Clarity Act. CFTC Chairman Mike Selig called them “two strong bipartisan picks” for CFTC commissioners and said he looked forward to working with them upon their confirmation.

The nominees would typically appear before the Senate Banking Committee for the SEC positions and the Senate Agriculture Committee for the CFTC roles. Following committee consideration, their nominations would go to the full Senate, where confirmation requires a majority vote.

#4954. JPMorgan’s Bitcoin and Crypto-Linked Holdings Approach $1 Billion

JPMorgan’s Bitcoin and Crypto-Linked Holdings Approach $1 Billion

JPMorgan Chase, whose CEO has spent years deriding crypto, is now sitting on close to $1 billion worth of crypto-linked stocks and funds, a regulatory filing shows, after the bank deepened those positions in the third quarter.

Adding up the disclosures in JPMorgan’s quarterly 13F, the form large institutional managers must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission to report their holdings, the bank held roughly $981 million across spot Bitcoin ETFs, Michael Saylor’s Strategy, and crypto exchange Coinbase as of Sept. 30.

Counting its stakes in Robinhood and Bitcoin miners, the total likely tips past $1 billion.

The largest piece is BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, or IBIT, where JPMorgan reported 11,408,930 shares worth about $540 million, a 9.6% increase in shares from the prior quarter, when the holding was valued at roughly $356 million. It held smaller positions in Grayscale’s and Bitwise’s Bitcoin ETFs, bringing its total spot Bitcoin ETF exposure to around $549 million.

The bank also leaned further into Strategy, the Bitcoin treasury company, raising its stake 36% to 848,932 shares, up from 624,387 at the end of June. That position was valued at about $131.3 million, up from $57.9 million a quarter earlier, reflecting both the added shares and a rise in Strategy’s stock over the period.

A roughly $301 million stake in Coinbase rounds out the core holdings, alongside positions in Robinhood and miners including Core Scientific and Hut 8. JPMorgan also disclosed sizable options tied to both IBIT and Strategy.

The company’s 13F is a snapshot as of Sept. 30 and doesn’t capture moves since, nor does it necessarily reflect directional bets. Banks often hold such positions to hedge or to facilitate client trades rather than to wager on price, so the near-$1 billion figure is better read as the scale of JPMorgan’s crypto-market activity than as a conviction call.

That nuance matters given CEO Jamie Dimon, who has called Bitcoin worthless and likened crypto to a fraud, even as the bank he runs steadily builds out digital-asset services.

Those services have expanded quickly. JPMorgan recently issued its first price forecast for Bitcoin, rolled out a deposit token called JPM Coin tied to bank dollars on Ethereum, and explored tokenized stocks alongside BlackRock and the DTCC.

The disclosure also lands during a rough stretch for Bitcoin funds. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have bled more than $1.4 billion over a recent five-day span as investors cut risk, a reminder that the institutional appetite captured in JPMorgan’s September snapshot has cooled since.

Bitcoin, which traded near $155 per Strategy share levels at quarter-end, has since slid well off its highs, today trading below $69,000.

#4953. Bitcoin Price Falls 14% in a Week to $65,000 as Weekend Selling Breaks Friday’s Low

Bitcoin price crashed about 13% over the past week and traded near $65,600 on Saturday.

Bitcoin price crashed about 14% over the past week and was trading near $65,200 on Saturday morning after sliding to about $65,000, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data. The move broke below Friday’s low of about $67,555 and marked the weakest level since mid-August, as weekend trading extended a selloff that has followed a stronger dollar and a fully priced December Federal Reserve rate hike.

A week ago, on Nov. 7, bitcoin was trading near $75,750. The decline steepened after Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, a shake-up that caused AI stocks to sell off which could potentially be responsible for sending bitcoin below $72,000. It slipped toward $71,000 by Thursday evening, then crashed to about $67,555 around midnight Eastern on Friday, its lowest level since August, before recovering toward $69,800 in the morning.

A brief pop above $70,000 after the producer-price report faded, and the bitcoin price spent Friday afternoon pinned below $70,000, near $68,900.

Selling resumed Friday evening and carried into the mid-$66,000s. Bitcoin briefly steadied overnight near $67,000, then sold off again after 8 a.m. ET Saturday, reaching that $65,500 low in the 10 a.m. hour and taking out Friday’s trough.

The Labor Department said Friday that the Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% in October, short of the 0.4% increase economists had expected. On an unadjusted basis, the index was up 6.5% from a year earlier, the largest 12-month rise since November 2022. The slightly cooler monthly figure lifted bitcoin above $70,000 for only minutes.

Bond traders were unconvinced. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed as high as 5.17% on Friday, a four-week high, and closed at 5.15%. The U.S. dollar index held at a 19-month high, its strongest level since April 2025. Boston Fed President Susan Collins said Friday that “soon, some additional tightening of Fed monetary policy may be appropriate,” and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said policymakers will, “in all likelihood, raise interest rates.” Higher rates raise the cost of holding an asset that pays no interest, and a stronger dollar has weighed on the bitcoin price for much of November. Traders fully priced a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting, CME FedWatch data show.

Chip stocks offered no cushion. The iShares Semiconductor ETF fell more than 3% on Friday, and Advanced Micro Devices dropped more than 8%. The Nasdaq 100 closed down 1.22%. U.S. stock and bond markets are closed Saturday, but those levels still frame the weekend session. Nvidia is due to report third-quarter results on Tuesday under interim CEO Colette Kress, the first earnings release since Huang stepped down.

Demand from spot bitcoin ETFs has not filled the gap. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) bled $2 billion over nine straight days of outflows through Wednesday, and the funds posted a sixth straight day of net outflows on Thursday. Weekend trading is typically thinner, leaving the bitcoin price more exposed to sharp swings in either direction.

Miners got some relief overnight. Bitcoin’s mining difficulty dropped 9.13% at 12:02 a.m. ET Saturday at block 975,744, falling from about 148.36 trillion to 134.82 trillion, the largest cut since June. Difficulty adjusts automatically every 2,016 blocks to keep average block times near 10 minutes.

The next tests for the bitcoin price arrive quickly. Traders will watch whether Saturday’s slide holds below Friday’s $67,555 low, and whether Nvidia’s report on Tuesday extends the chip-stock weakness that has followed bitcoin lower all week. With a December rate hike fully priced and the dollar at a 19-month high, any further jump in yields when markets reopen could keep pressure on.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $65,100.

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 as crypto sentiment hit its lowest level in more than four months, with analysts warning of institutional outflows, thinning liquidity and elevated leverage.

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday, extending its recent decline as investor sentiment deteriorated amid institutional outflows, tightening liquidity and broader macroeconomic pressures.

Bitcoin (BTC) is trading at $68,607.23 at the time of writing, down 9.2% in the last week, according to CoinGecko.

The drop coincided with a sharp decline in market sentiment. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index fell to 20 on Friday, its lowest reading in more than four months, putting it in “extreme fear.” The index last reached that level on July 8.

Bitcoin’s seven-day price chart. Source: CoinGecko

Vikram Subburaj, CEO of crypto exchange Giottus, attributed Bitcoin’s weakness to institutional outflows, tightening crypto liquidity and expectations of a December Federal Reserve interest rate hike. “Investors should avoid chasing short-term dips or using excessive leverage,” he said.

In a Friday report, 10x Research highlighted Bitcoin’s divergence from US equities. Between Nov. 5 and Nov. 12, Bitcoin declined 5.9% while the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.4%, suggesting the cryptocurrency was responding more to rising Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar than to technology stocks.

The research firm said Bitcoin was increasingly trading alongside gold, which fell 5.5% over the same period, as the US 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5%.

Meanwhile, institutional trading platform Talos also warned that thin liquidity and elevated leverage could amplify market volatility. Its weekly report showed Bitcoin order-book depth across major exchanges fell to $72 million on Nov. 9, roughly 33% below normal levels.

“Liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction,” said Tanay Ved, senior research associate at Talos. “A rebuild in order-book depth and a turn in capital flows would provide a firmer foundation for recovery.”

The selloff follows sustained withdrawals from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs). BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded more than $2 billion in net outflows across nine consecutive trading sessions through Wednesday, while broader funds shed nearly $1.44 billion over five sessions.

Preliminary Farside Investors data showed another $47.7 million in net outflows on Thursday, although figures for BlackRock and Fidelity were still pending.

#4948. Microsoft 365 outage hits Outlook email and Teams calendars worldwide

Microsoft began a wider patch rollout Friday as the outage disrupted government email and Microsoft 365 connectors in ChatGPT and Claude.

A global Microsoft 365 outage continued into Friday, disrupting Outlook email and some Teams features.

Microsoft said in a 7:25 am UTC update that a patch had improved stability on some servers and that it was working to deploy the fix more widely. The update, republished by the University of Pennsylvania, gave no timetable for restoration.

The outage began Thursday, leaving some users unable to access their Exchange Online mailboxes. Microsoft said a process that handles secure connection became overloaded, causing affected servers to stop processing requests.

The company said it attempted to restore services by restarting infrastructure, redirecting network traffic and expanding server capacity. Microsoft said there was no indication of a security breach.

The outage also affected features in Microsoft Copilot and Defender for Office 365. In Teams, users had trouble scheduling meetings and sending invitations. Microsoft said most Teams calls and chats continued to work.

Businesses and government agencies worldwide use Microsoft 365 for email and scheduling. Microsoft reported more than 450 million paid commercial seats for the suite in an October filing. Exchange Online hosts the mailboxes and calendars those organizations use, and outside apps, including AI assistants, rely on the same service to retrieve that data when users connect their work accounts.

OpenAI reported errors in ChatGPT’s Microsoft 365 connector. Anthropic said the outage caused most email, calendar and search requests through Claude’s Microsoft 365 connector to fail.

The US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit said its clerk’s office could neither send nor receive email for much of Thursday. Japan’s Finance Ministry said it was unable to receive email on Friday and Singapore’s Government Technology Agency told CNA that government email was among systems affected.

#4945. China’s $3.2 Billion AI Pipeline Still Calls for Nvidia Chips Washington Restricts

China’s $3.2 Billion AI Pipeline Still Calls for Nvidia Chips Washington Restricts

Chinese developers are planning and building billions of dollars worth of AI data centers around Nvidia processors restricted by Washington, according to a Reuters investigation published Friday.

After examining more than 150 procurement notices, investment plans and corporate records, the news agency identified projects worth over 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion). Many specify Nvidia's H100, H200, or H800 chips, which provide the computing power used to train and run advanced AI models.

But $3.2 billion is the total value of the projects, including buildings, electricity and other infrastructure. The documents do not establish that all the processors were obtained, or that any export laws were broken.

One proposed computing center in Fujian province is valued at 6.2 billion yuan ($873 million). Its official investment listing specifies H100 servers but is still seeking financing partners.

In Shaanxi, a state-owned engineering group won a contract linked to a 3 billion yuan center naming H100 and H200 chips. A 2.26 billion yuan project in Jilin proposes combining Nvidia hardware with Chinese processors.

Inner Mongolia has another proposed development specifying 625 H200 servers. Meanwhile, authorities in Wuxi reported that an H800 computing cluster began operating in March 2025. Operating facilities and proposed investments are not evidence of the same level of chip access.

Nvidia's processors can carry out thousands of calculations at once, making them valuable for AI training. Its widely used software also makes switching to rival systems more complicated and potentially expensive.

The United States began restricting advanced AI chip sales to China in 2022, citing national security concerns. In January 2026, the Commerce Department moved H200 export applications to case-by-case review, although sales still require licenses. H100 shipments remain more tightly restricted.

That leaves Chinese developers with a dilemma: design facilities around familiar Nvidia equipment they may struggle to acquire, or invest in alternative processors that can require software changes and additional engineering.

An IDC report cited by Reuters estimated Nvidia accounted for 34% of China's AI accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026, compared with 28% for Huawei. Those figures cover the broader chip market, not confirmed shipments of restricted models.

Chinese AI developer Z.AI has already released an image-generation model trained entirely on Huawei chips, demonstrating that competitive systems need not depend on American hardware.

Still, the new project records show how deeply Nvidia remains embedded in Chinese AI infrastructure plans. They also add pressure on U.S. officials facing congressional scrutiny over how advanced chip export rules are enforced.

#4942. Louisiana AG calls CFTC chair an ‘obsequious standard bearer’ for prediction markets following agency lawsuit

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The CFTC sued Louisiana on Friday, a day after a state judge ordered Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, Robinhood and dozens of affiliated entities to stop offering event contracts in the state.

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill accused Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Michael Selig of making "flatly false statements" on Saturday, a day after the agency sued the state to block a court order shutting prediction markets out of Louisiana.

"Flatly false statements by the 'obsequious standard bearer' for Kalshi and prediction markets. Gambling has been regulated by states for 250 years," Murrill wrote on X at 12:05 p.m. ET.

Murrill was replying to a Friday evening post in which Selig said event contracts "have traded openly in Louisiana for years, in compliance with the CEA and [CFTC] regulations." He called the state's "eleventh-hour 'emergency' lawsuit" against the industry "naked lawfare and a cynical political stunt."

"Under the Court’s logic, contracts such as interest rate swaps and weather derivatives, both of which are commonly traded financial instruments that the Louisiana economy is highly dependent on, are illegal gambling products," a Kalshi spokesperson told The Block. "Nothing could better illustrate why Congress gave the CFTC exclusive jurisdiction over our national financial markets."

"Prediction markets are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission under a federal framework, not a patchwork of state rules," a Polymarket spokesperson told The Block.

The CFTC and the United States filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana on Friday, naming the state, Murrill, the Louisiana Gaming Control Board and the state police's gaming enforcement division as defendants. The agency is asking the court to declare that state gambling laws are preempted for CFTC-regulated markets and to bar Louisiana from enforcing or extending the state court's order.

"The Commission's lawsuit seeks to maintain the status quo while the federal courts decide this issue in an orderly manner," Selig said in a statement. The agency said Louisiana is the 12th state it has sued to defend its claimed exclusive jurisdiction over derivatives markets.

On Thursday, the CFTC and the Justice Department also sued Arkansas to block its enforcement action against Kalshi. Selig told a conference audience on Friday that states were "essentially trying to lock up founders and CEOs" of prediction market companies, The Block reported.

Judge Jeffrey Johnson of the 21st Judicial District Court in Tangipahoa Parish signed the ex parte temporary restraining order Thursday afternoon, according to a copy Murrill posted on X. Murrill sued the companies earlier that day, making Louisiana the 11th state to sue one or more prediction markets.

The order names 31 entities tied to Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood, Crypto.com, Coinbase, Gemini, Interactive Brokers' ForecastEx, Novig, Underdog, IG Group and ProphetX. It bars them from offering event contracts on sports, elections, awards and other events to people in Louisiana without a state license, and requires them to geofence the state.

The order expires after 10 days unless the court extends it. A hearing on the state's motion for a preliminary injunction is set for 9 a.m. local time on Nov. 30.

Kalshi has cut off access for Louisiana users. A message in its app, seen in a screenshot reviewed by The Block, tells them, "Your government says you can't use Kalshi anymore," and says the state acted "without a hearing, notice, or due process." The screen includes a link reading "Protect your freedom to trade" and a button to "Join the movement."

The Block has reached out to Polymarket and Murrill's office for comment.

Updated at 4:45 p.m. ET with a statement from Kalshi and at 5:20 p.m. ET with a statement from Polymarket.

#4938. Kava Lend loses roughly $3.8 million to hack, sending KAVA token down nearly 40%

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Onchain data shows an attacker borrowed out nearly all of Kava Lend's KAVA, worth about $3.76 million before the attack, then bridged most of it to BNB Chain and sold it for roughly $2.1 million.

An attacker drained about 55.2 million KAVA tokens from Kava Lend, the native lending protocol of Layer 1 blockchain Kava (KAVA), late Friday after inflating the value of deposits in a dormant stablecoin market and borrowing against them, according to onchain data reviewed by The Block.

The tokens were worth roughly $3.76 million at the $0.068 price KAVA traded at before the attack. Kava Lend's module account, where the protocol's pooled deposits sit, went from holding 55.33 million KAVA to 0.19 KAVA in a little over an hour and a half.

"We are tracking unexpected behavior originating from a dApp within the Kava ecosystem," Kava wrote on X at 6:28 a.m. ET on Saturday in its first public acknowledgment of the incident, more than seven hours after the attack started.

In a follow-up post about half an hour later, Kava said it was aware of "the bridging and sale of KAVA tokens on BSC." "To clarify: This is not an infinite mint," the team wrote. "The event is isolated and contained within Kava Lend."

Kava hasn't put an official number on the losses or published a post-mortem report of the attack.

The exploit ran through Kava Lend's market for BUSD, the Binance-branded stablecoin that issuer Paxos stopped minting in 2023. The market was all but empty ahead of the attack, onchain data shows.

Kava Lend works out what depositors have earned by dividing the interest borrowers pay by the market's net supply, per Kava's public source code. The code skips the division if that supply figure is exactly zero; however, it doesn't check for figures that are minute, but still above zero.

At 11:01 p.m. ET on Friday, the attacker used a small BUSD loan to bring the market's net supply down to two hundred-millionths of a dollar. Over the next three minutes, Kava Lend multiplied the value of every BUSD deposit roughly 243,000-fold. That included BUSD the attacker had deposited ahead of time, which the protocol now counted as roughly 1.25 billion BUSD in collateral.

The attacker then borrowed KAVA against their deposit 127 times, using a second account to clear each loan and get around Kava Lend's cap on KAVA borrowing. The attacker appears to have prepared for at least a week, running repeated deposit and borrow cycles in the BUSD market from Nov. 8.

Beginning at 4:59 a.m. ET on Saturday, the attacker bridged about 49.2 million KAVA to an address on BNB Chain through Kava's LayerZero bridge. Most of it was sold within the hour for 3,006.5 BNB and 231,557 USDT, worth about $2.09 million combined, and the BNB has since been moved out. Another roughly 4.58 million KAVA went to five unlabeled addresses on Kava.

KAVA was trading near $0.042 at time of publication, down about 39% over the past 24 hours, according to The Block's Kava Price page. Partner exchanges paused deposits and withdrawals "as a standard precautionary measure," Kava said.

At 9:05 a.m. ET, Kava said it had paused the Axelar bridge "out of an abundance of caution," though the drained KAVA left the network through LayerZero. "We will share a complete incident report as soon as it is ready," the team wrote.

The Kava incident follows several lending protocol exploits this year where an attacker borrowed against collateral worth far less than the protocol believed. Cronos halted its network in August after an exploit of lending protocol Tectonic estimated at $75 million, and Hedera's Bonzo Lend was hit for roughly $9 million in July.

BMW didn’t take long to sell through inventory, with 2026 iX models essentially sold out in the US.

The iX landing page now redirects you to the new BMW X5 instead. According to online auto research firm CarsDirect, about 10 new iX models remain nationwide.

BMW’s Neue Klasse vehicles, starting with the new 2027 iX3, mark a step change from its previous EVs.

At the center is the Neue Klasse platform, which introduces BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive, new batteries, and an 800-volt electrical architecture.

BMW said the new Gen6 eDrive system delivers 30% higher charging speeds and driving range than its previous system, with some models seeing an even greater increase.

The 2027 iX3 50 xDrive, BMW’s first Neue Klasse vehicle, starts at $61,500 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 434 miles. In comparison, the 2026 iX xDrive 60 had an EPA range of up to 364 miles.

While the iX3 is a smaller, compact electric SUV compared to the iX, BMW is preparing to launch the iX5 as a more direct replacement.

The gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now on sale, starting at $72,100, but BMW is expected to launch the electric iX5 in early 2027.

Using a 144 kWh battery, BMW said the electric SUV will offer up to an estimated 435 miles of range on a single charge.

The iX5 is powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, delivering a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW says it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 will be an upgrade from the iX, adopting BMW’s Neue Klasse design. The setup includes a 17.9″ navigation touchscreen and the new BMW Panoramic Vision that spans the windshield. You can also opt to add the optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

The new drive platform is a huge improvement. Personally I'm glad to see it in the new i3 since I don't think everyone needs a 3-ton SUV.

Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, the iX5 is slightly longer and taller than the outgoing iX, with more of a traditional SUV design.

BMW is expected to open orders for the new iX5 60 xDrive this month, starting at $79,800, with a full launch in early 2027. It will be BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US.

Production is set to begin at BMW’s Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina by the end of the year, with the first deliveries expected in early 2027.

#4935. Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets? House Oversight Says Maybe

Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets? House Oversight Says Maybe

The chairman of the House Oversight Committee is raising the prospect of barring government officials from trading on prediction markets, citing concerns that insiders are using nonpublic information to profit on platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket.

In a staff memorandum released Friday, the committee detailed an investigation into insider trading by government officials, military personnel and people holding security clearances who have placed bets using information not available to the public.

The probe gathered nearly 1,700 pages of documents and included five bipartisan staff briefings from prediction market platforms about how they detect and report suspicious activity.

Chairman James Comer framed the issue around public trust. “Americans are rightly concerned about public corruption,” he said, arguing Congress “has a duty to ensure our laws adequately prevent insider trading” and prohibit officials “from profiting from nonpublic information.”

He said lawmakers must weigh “additional reforms to prevent public corruption and restore the American people’s trust in government.”

The memo’s central recommendation is that Congress consider new restrictions on federal personnel, ranging from an outright ban on trading prediction markets to narrower limits on specific contracts, such as those tied to government decisions.

Applying such rules across all branches, the committee argued, would reinforce that government employees shouldn’t financially benefit from access to nonpublic information, and would remove even the appearance of it.

The memo stressed that existing insider trading laws already apply to prediction markets. It cited the Commodity Exchange Act, as amended by the STOCK Act, which bars federal employees, members of Congress and others from trading commodity futures, options, or swaps on nonpublic information drawn from their positions.

The committee credited the platforms themselves for policing their markets, noting that most reported insider trading incidents were first detected and flagged to regulators by the platforms. It singled out Polymarket, which recently hired a former law enforcement expert and rolled out surveillance software called “PolyGraph” built with analytics firm Chainalysis, and Kalshi for strengthening their detection protocols.

The scrutiny follows a string of cases involving alleged insider trading by public officials and government employees.

A U.S. soldier was charged in April over alleged Polymarket trades tied to a military operation that resulted in the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Then, in August, the CFTC fined a former White House teleprompter operator for betting on presidential speeches.

The push also lands amid broader pressure on the sector, with the CFTC moving to assert authority over prediction markets in its fight against several states, while Sen. Elizabeth Warren sets her sights on the industry as the incoming Senate Banking chair.

#4933. Traders claim $6 million profit by spotting BitGo’s public pull request and frontrunning memecoin listing

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

A pseudonymous trader claims to have anticipated a memecoin's Robinhood listing, which sent its price soaring, by tracking code changes in BitGo's public repository and Wintermute smart contracts.

A pseudonymous trader said their group profited more than $6 million by buying two Robinhood Chain memecoins ahead of their Robinhood listings after spotting a public BitGo code change and analyzing Wintermute's onchain activity.

The trader, who posts on X as @3i, described their "edge" in an article published on Saturday that has drawn more than 300,000 views. The Block confirmed several of the public records the trader cites and found wallet activity that matches parts of the timeline, though could not verify the profit figures.

Robinhood launched Robinhood Chain, a Layer 2 network built on Arbitrum's tech stack, on July 1. BitGo announced wallet and custody support for the network the same day, while Robinhood has named algorithmic trading firm Wintermute as one of its largest crypto market makers in an SEC filing.

According to 3i, the pair began tracking Wintermute's wallets on Robinhood Chain and BitGo's activity on GitHub after it noticed that Wintermute had been moving tokens to Robinhood about an hour before earlier memecoin listings were announced.

Indeed, a BitGo developer had opened a pull request, or a proposed code change, in the company's public BitGoJS repository on July 27. Included in the code: "Add hoodeth:cashcat (Cash Cat) token to hoodethTokens.ts on the Robinhood Chain." The change was merged the next day.

While Cash Cat was launched on July 1, Robinhood didn't list the token until Aug. 6, ten days after the July 27 pull request was made.

BitGo released a new version of its code on July 29, which included the Cash Cat code change alongside a separate change that added support for 99 Robinhood Chain stock tokens. "The implications of this were huge, as it confirmed my hunch that Robinhood was the one behind this request," 3i wrote. "Why else would cashcat be in there next to their native stock tokens?"

Though 3i said the pair had been buying up the memecoin in the days after the pull request, eventually accumulating 1.5% of the token's overall supply, they had been waiting for a stronger signal to buy even more: Wintermute whitelisting the token, or transferring the token to Robinhood.

The trader claims that on Aug. 3 at 1:48 p.m. ET, their monitoring bot caught Wintermute approving the trading pool. "That was the alert we’d been waiting for," 3i wrote. "The desk had selected a venue to trade the exact coin we were holding."

The pair began buying slowly to avoid drawing attention to their wallets, 3i wrote. But about half an hour later, at 2:19 p.m. ET, a wallet the pair suspected belonged to a Robinhood insider placed an $11,000 limit order for the memecoin. Knowing that other traders were watching the same wallet, the pair abandoned the slow approach and bought more than $1 million worth of Cash Cat at once, bringing their holdings to around 4% of the token's supply, according to 3i.

Per onchain data reviewed by The Block, a wallet made its first Cash Cat purchase at 1:54 p.m. ET on Aug. 3, six minutes after the Wintermute alert 3i describes. After three small buys, the wallet bought about 12 million tokens in two swaps at 2:20 p.m. ET, one minute after the suspected insider's order, before moving the tokens to other wallets. In total, it picked up about 15 million tokens, or 1.5% of the supply.

Onchain analytics firm Bubblemaps flagged the wallet the next morning, noting that it had spent $1.1 million on the memecoin as part of $2.7 million in purchases by a cluster of fresh wallets. While 3i's article claims ownership of the wallets in question, The Block could not independently confirm who controls them.

The Block also identified a Wintermute-labeled contract on Robinhood Chain that keeps a public list of tokens it is approved to trade, which may be one of the three contracts 3i describes that carry that list. However, Cash Cat was not added to that list until around 6:31 a.m. ET on Aug. 5, nearly two days after the signal 3i claims to have caught, but still about 27 hours ahead of Robinhood's listing announcement.

Robinhood announced that Cash Cat was available to trade at 9:31 a.m. ET on Aug. 6, three days after the pair's largest purchase. 3i wrote that while they napped through the token's initial price spike following the listing, the pair still made more than $4 million between them by selling into the frenzy.

3i also claims the pair managed to get ahead of Robinhood employees who were themselves trading the listing. Another pseudonymous trader, clickless, published a separate account on the day of the listing describing a wallet they believed belonged to an insider, which placed a Cash Cat limit order before the announcement and ultimately lost money.

3i said the pair later repeated the trade with PONS, the token of a memecoin launchpad on Robinhood Chain. The trader said they began buying on Aug. 28 and that they and "friends" made $2 million, though the article does not explain how they identified the token.

What looked like a Sept. 2 listing of PONS, however, appeared to have been "some kind of honeypot for Robinhood to catch the insiders," 3i wrote. The trader added that most of the advantage described in the article has since faded.

On Sept. 15, the Department of Justice charged two former Robinhood engineers with commodities fraud and wire fraud for allegedly trading perpetual futures on Hyperliquid ahead of Robinhood listing announcements. Robinhood said at the time that it had investigated the matter and reported it to law enforcement.

The Block has reached out to Robinhood, Wintermute, BitGo and @3i for comment.

Binance co-founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao denied the exchange is selling Bitcoin as price losses led $2 billion in crypto positions to be liquidated over a 24-hour period this weekend.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) fell to its lowest level since July over the weekend as a selloff across major cryptocurrencies triggered roughly $2 billion in liquidations.

#4927. Yamaha unveils new NMAX E, bringing electric power to its popular motorbike lineup

Yamaha is expanding its electric two-wheeler lineup with a much more capable machine, unveiling the new NMAX E as an electric version of its popular NMAX sport scooter.

The 2027 Yamaha NMAX E is being positioned as a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter, putting it firmly above the low-speed urban electric scooters that have made up much of Yamaha’s electric lineup thus far.

At its heart is Yamaha’s new compact eAxle drive unit, which sends power to the rear wheel through a belt drive. The electric motor produces 6.7 kW (9 hp) of nominal power and peaks at 7.5 kW (10 hp), along with 33.3 Nm (24.6 lb-ft) of torque.

Yamaha hasn’t published a top speed in the specifications, but the NMAX E’s A1 classification puts it in the same general category as 125cc combustion scooters rather than urban mopeds.

Power comes from a centrally mounted 3.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, which Yamaha says provides up to 104 km (65 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 testing cycle. The L-shaped battery is mounted low and centrally in the chassis to help maintain a low center of gravity.

Unlike many electric scooters that rely on removable batteries, the NMAX E uses a fixed pack. Yamaha has compensated for that with an onboard 800W charger, allowing riders to plug the scooter directly into a household outlet or an AC Type 2 public charging station. A full 0-100% charge takes around 5.5 hours.

Riders can choose between three riding modes. Sport (S) mode offers the quickest acceleration, Touring (T) provides smoother power delivery for everyday riding and carrying a passenger, and Eco (E) reduces acceleration and top speed while maximizing range. Regenerative braking is also included.

The rest of the scooter is fairly well equipped, including traction control, ABS, 245mm front and rear disc brakes, 13-inch wheels, a 33mm fork, dual rear shocks, and even a reverse mode to make low-speed maneuvering easier.

Nice, the Nmax has always been the premium scoot we try to get when traveling in southeast asia. Always felt like it would've been even better electrified. No removable battery seems a bit of a miss. That might constrain a big chunk of demand.

A five-inch TFT display includes smartphone connectivity through Yamaha’s Motor On app, providing turn-by-turn navigation as well as battery status, ride information, maintenance reminders, and other connected features. There’s also keyless ignition, USB-C charging, LED lighting, and illuminated underseat storage large enough for a full-face helmet, depending on its size.

Perhaps most importantly, the NMAX E looks like a proper Yamaha scooter rather than an electric experiment. Its dual headlights and distinctive side panels closely follow the styling language of Yamaha’s existing MAX family.

That could prove important as established motorcycle manufacturers increasingly attempt to bring electric models into their existing lineups rather than treating them as separate curiosities.

Pricing and exact market availability haven’t yet been announced, but Yamaha is positioning the NMAX E as a 2027 model for the European market.

#4926. DOJ moves to seize $1.2B from Binance hack, disrupts FaceStealer scam

Authorities froze over $2.7 billion in Binance hack proceeds, while the separate FaceStealer scam stole over $400 million in 18 months.

The US Department of Justice said Thursday it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance.

The authorization covers part of the more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets that US authorities and private-sector partners have frozen since the Oct. 29 hack. Investigators are still working to recover additional funds, the department said in its announcement.

The FBI attributed the Binance hack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group in a cyber alert. Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denied North Korea’s involvement.

Binance said it had covered the affected assets with its own funds and that a new proof-of-reserves snapshot showed at least one-to-one backing for customer assets, according to its Thursday post on X.

In November 2025, the DOJ announced a separate enforcement action targeting about $15 million in cryptocurrency linked to North Korean hackers known as APT38.

Related: Crypto hack losses equal 57 cents per $1 earned onchain: Ark’s Valente

In a separate case, US authorities seized cloud infrastructure used in FaceStealer, a North Korean social engineering campaign that stole more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months, the DOJ said.

The hackers used secretly recorded footage of previous victims and AI-generated deepfakes of prominent crypto figures to gain targets’ trust on video calls. They used bogus technical fixes to trick targets into installing malware, the DOJ said.

The campaign targeted people working in crypto and Web3. The hackers also increasingly targeted open-source software developers and maintainers in attempts to gain access to their devices and software repository accounts.

The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant. The bureau also published guidance on how to protect against the scheme and what to do after a compromise in a public advisory.

Redacted stills from webcam videos recorded by FaceStealer hackers. Source: FBI

The DOJ said the hackers behind FaceStealer are known publicly by several names, including Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, APT38, BlueNoroff and Stardust Chollima.

#4925. Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to the Financial Times, putting a former Nvidia executive in contention for one of technology's biggest jobs.

Haas is one of several people under consideration, people familiar with the matter told the FT. There is no guarantee he will receive an offer or accept one. The FT said he maintains strong ties to Huang and some Nvidia directors.

Nvidia's board told Reuters it was still selecting an executive search firm and had not formally engaged any candidate. “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature,” it said.

Huang resigned Thursday after 33 years leading the company he co-founded, following reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a business executive suspected by U.S. officials of having Chinese intelligence ties. The company said it had no reason to believe its secrets were compromised.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones has become board chair. Analysts have also floated Nvidia data-center executive Ian Buck and AMD chief Lisa Su as possible successors, though those names are not confirmed appointments or offers.

An internal Nvidia suggestion-box post has attracted more than 1,600 comments, many supportive of Huang's reinstatement, according to Wired. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one anonymous employee wrote.

Other staff members have demanded transparency around his departure. The campaign shows Huang still has supporters inside Nvidia; it does not mean the board has opened talks to reinstate him.

Haas, 64, is a Silicon Valley-based semiconductor executive whose career spans engineering, product development and sales. He earned an electrical engineering degree from Clarkson University and worked at chip companies Tensilica and Scintera Networks before joining Nvidia in 2006.

He spent seven years at Nvidia as vice president and general manager of its computing products business, then moved to Arm in 2013. At Arm, he rose from strategic alliances to chief commercial officer in 2015 and head of its intellectual-property products group in 2017, before becoming CEO in February 2022.

That appointment came as Nvidia's proposed $40 billion takeover of Arm collapsed under pressure from regulators. Haas was suddenly running a business his former employer had tried, unsuccessfully, to buy.

He steered Arm back onto the Nasdaq in September 2023 at an initial valuation of about $54.5 billion, one of the year's largest stock-market debuts. The IPO also gave Japanese owner SoftBank a way to sell shares while retaining control.

Unlike Nvidia, which primarily sells graphics processors and related computing systems, Arm licenses chip designs and computing architecture to companies including Apple, Amazon and Qualcomm, earning fees and royalties when customers use its technology. Arm-based designs are now increasingly found in cloud servers as well as phones.

Arm reported $1.44 billion in revenue for the quarter ended September 30, up 27% from a year earlier. Royalties from data-center chips doubled, while Arm said initial commercial deliveries of its new CPU remain on track for early 2027.

Haas also sits on SoftBank's board and, since April, has served as CEO of SoftBank Group International, helping oversee its semiconductor and AI interests. A move to Nvidia would require untangling those ties, particularly because the companies are partners whose interests increasingly overlap in data-center hardware.

For Nvidia, the next leader would inherit not just its lead in AI chips, but delicate relationships with governments and customers as Washington debates tighter export restrictions on China. Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on November 17, with Kress at the helm and its permanent CEO search still underway.

#4923. Not Ready For a Facelift? No Problem: Welcome to The Era of “In-Between” Treatments.

No surgery, minimal downtime, a firmer, more lifted look—what’s not to love?

THE RISE OF BUZZY noninvasive in-office treatments is no coincidence. These days, people want to look sculpted, lifted, and more refreshed without having to make the somewhat uneasy decision to go under the knife. And as more and more patients seek meaningful results without committing to surgery, there’s a growing interest in treatments that bridge the gap between injectables and a facelift, aptly dubbed the “in-between” treatments.

These interventions will still give you meaningful lifting, volumizing, sculpting, and tightening results without as much downtime (sometimes, none at all) or diminishing returns on your investment. Think of them as the individualized, targeted treatments you can utilize before considering a face or neck lift. The trick is having a solid understanding of what specific technologies can—and cannot—accomplish. If you’re not pairing the right treatment with the right concern, you’re shelling out good money to “correct something it fundamentally cannot address,” explains Connie Yang, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City.

Filler, for instance, is effective for restoring strategic areas of volume loss on the face, but it can’t truly lift tissue or remove excess skin. “If you add more filler in an attempt to recreate a sharper jawline or lift the lower face, you’re just going to end up making the face look heavier and puffier, rather than more lifted and sculpted,” says Dr. Yang.

Meet the experts: Connie Yang, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist in New York City. Jennifer Levine, MD, is a double board-certified facial plastic surgeon in New York City.

In a similar vein to filler, energy-based skin devices such as radio frequency (think: Morpheus 8 or Xerf) or ultrasound devices such as Ultherapy that target the deeper, structural layers of the face can only do so much up to a certain point. “These treatments can give meaningful improvement in the right patient, but there’s a limit to how much contraction you can achieve non-surgically,” says Dr. Yang. If someone has significant jowling, excess skin, or deeper tissue descent, repeated treatment with these types of devices will end up giving someone only progressively smaller improvements over time.

To give you the LD on all of your options, we spoke with experts about what each treatment can realistically accomplish, what patients can expect over time results-wise, and when you should skip straight to surgery.

As a rule of thumb, most (not all) aesthetic professionals will generally advise you to exhaust all options before spending a pretty penny on a facelift. In the end, it’s an individual decision. Either way, in-office treatments can help to keep your skin radiant and build collagen to help you to get an even better result for when it is time for a facelift. Think about throwing a crumpled up sheet over your mattress in the morning: If you don’t iron it first, the wrinkles will still be there when you go to make the bed.

There's no one-size-fits-all approach because not all facial aging is the same. For patients that are truly getting closer to being surgical candidates, “focusing on improving skin quality and some degree of skin tightening can be your best bet, while at the same time managing expectations of the limitations of devices and their expected outcomes,” says Dr. Yang.

Double board-certified facial plastic surgeon Jennifer Levine, MD, who uses a combination of injectable treatments and non-surgical devices in addition to surgery in her practice, recommends treatment protocols depending on which components of aging are most responsible for the patient’s concerns.

The following treatment categories are considered the in-betweeners that you may want to consider before going under the knife.

“This is an important option for select patients with earlier skin laxity who want gradual tightening and a degree of lifting,” says Dr. Levine. Ultrasound imaging allows providers to actually visualize tissue layers and guide energy placement.

It’s FDA-cleared for use to lift the brows and help with lax tissue beneath the chin and neck—the places where aging skin can be most obvious. “I consider it an in-between treatment because it can address laxity through targeted tissue remodeling while the patient’s expectations remain appropriate for a nonsurgical result,” says Dr. Yang, but “[they do] not replicate the degree of lifting you can achieve surgically.”

These work best when texture, dermal remodeling, and modest tightening are the goals. Dr. Levine says that for these treatments, energy settings and treatment depth play a huge role and must be chosen carefully based on anatomy. RF microneedling is provider-dependent, especially because at the wrong setting, facial fat loss, unintended scarring, and nerve injury can occur.

“I consider this particularly valuable when fine lines, uneven pigmentation, and textural changes contribute substantially to an aged appearance,” explains Dr. Levine. Improving the skin’s surface can make a meaningful aesthetic difference, especially for someone who is beginning to develop skin laxity. She points out that “improvement in skin quality is a different endpoint from repositioning descended facial tissue.”

Ellacor is the best example of a true in-between option, says Dr. Yang, “because it actually removes microscopic cores of skin without surgery, allowing the skin to contract as it heals.” Instead of just heating the skin to stimulate collagen, it uses tiny hollow needles to physically remove microscopic columns of excess skin, scarlessly. As the skin heals, it contracts and remodels, which can help to improve wrinkles and laxity.

Patient selection for this treatment is especially important because there is some downtime involved and a risk of pigment change. That said, it’s useful for those with mild to moderate laxity and early jowling, who don’t quite have enough excess skin or tissue to warrant a facelift yet.

Brand Names: Sculptra, Radiesse, Juvederm, Restylane

When true volume deficiency contributes to someone’s overall concern, Dr. Levine says that conservative volume restoration with the use of hyaluronic acid fillers or biostimulatory injectables that boost skin’s own collagen production can help to improve contours and balance the face.

Let’s just get this out of the way right off the bat—age alone isn’t the biggest determining factor in whether or not someone would benefit from a facelift. Genetics, lifestyle choices, and how someone cares for their body and skin have a huge impact. “I have patients in their 40s with very little laxity who are excellent candidates for non-invasive treatments and younger patients whose anatomy or degree of tissue descent make certain treatments less effective,” explains Yang.

And while there’s no single telltale sign to know when it’s time for a facelift, one of the main factors is whether the patient has “skin laxity alone or true tissue descent that requires surgical repositioning,” says Dr. Yang. With skin laxity, the skin can appear creepy or loose with decreased elasticity and can be pinched more easily. “Tissue descent is a deeper structural change; if you manually reposition the deeper tissue upward and it significantly restores the contours of the cheek or jawline, that tells me that the concern isn’t just loose skin and that a facelift would be the solution,” explains Dr. Yang.

Even if someone is a candidate for a non-invasive treatment, if they're ultimately looking for a dramatic lift or significant change in their facial contours, then surgery may be the answer. Dr. Yang says that she is more inclined to recommend surgery after a patient has gone through multiple rounds of injectables or tightening treatments and they continue to chase the same concern with diminishing improvement or returns. “At that point, continuing to add filler or repeatedly treating with devices can become costly without addressing the underlying structural issue,” she says.

Before diving face first into a surgery, Dr. Yang encourages her own patients to really explore all of their options and think deeply about their long-term goals. If you know that a facelift is in your future, it may shape what is recommended to you by a provider. “I don’t want you spending years of over-treating or investing in procedures that may only give you marginal improvement.” Instead, she says, the focus should be on maintaining skin quality and aging well until you’re ready. Conversely, if you’re unsure whether surgery will ever be an option for you, finding the right provider to work with can help you to maximize non-surgical options available in order to get the most meaningful results possible.

Overall, the goal should be to maximize what you have and age well, while recognizing when you’ve reached the limitations of non-surgical treatments. “If surgery may eventually be the right choice, you want to arrive there with healthy, well-maintained skin,” she says. Amen to that.

#4922. Maximo milestone: friendly robot has completed 300,000 tasks

After completing the first half of Amazon’s Bellefield complex last summer, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)

If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast, that’s because it is. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now, with 300,000 tasks under its belt, the robot is proving to be both fast and durable.

“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.

Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.

(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.

The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one, which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course – but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb.

So Primoris’ Renewables is the name of a business, Maximo is the name of a solar robotics company incubated by The AES Corporation. Maximo makes a robot (also called Maximo I think) using NVDIVIA hardware and software, and also AWS cloud software, and Bellefield is a solar field owned by Amazon. Or so I gather so far.

The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages, making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site.

#4921. OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet to Let AI Agents Shop—Without Crypto

OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet to Let AI Agents Shop—Without Crypto

ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s dots complete purchases with tokenized card details, after users approve each transaction. The limited rollout targets U.S. ChatGPT Pro users; the wallet does not hold crypto or a cash balance. Coinbase and Circle offer a different route, using stablecoins to let agents pay for services with less human involvement.

OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on Friday, giving its AI agents a way to purchase products using American Express, Mastercard, and Visa cards. The new system lets an agent finish online checkout without accessing the customer's actual card number, and it doesn't involve cryptocurrency.

The wallet works through dots, OpenAI's always-on AI assistants, which can browse websites and carry out tasks for users. A customer saves an eligible card, reviews the order and approves the payment using a security check such as a fingerprint or Face ID.

After approval, the card network creates a payment token containing substitute card details. The agent submits the token through the merchant’s existing checkout system, while the customer keeps applicable card rewards and dispute protections, according to OpenAI’s announcement.

“An agent making a purchase should strengthen, not bypass, the trust built into payments,” Sherri Haymond, Mastercard's global head of digital commercialization, said in the announcement.

OpenAI previously introduced Instant Checkout with Stripe in September 2025, allowing people to buy from participating merchants inside ChatGPT. Wallet takes a different approach: agents can navigate ordinary online stores and use existing checkout forms, without requiring each business to build a special integration.

OpenAI is also courting merchants. Just three days before the Wallet launch, it introduced business profiles that let companies update product information and connect with potential customers through ChatGPT.

Google is working on a competing approach. Its Universal Commerce Protocol, introduced in January, aims to connect shopping agents with retailers, payment providers and post-purchase services across Google products.

Coinbase launched Agentic Wallets in February, giving software the ability to spend USDC, trade tokens, and pay for online services within preset limits. Unlike ChatGPT Wallet, the Coinbase product is primarily developer infrastructure, not a consumer checkout feature.

“It's not an SDK, it's not a library—it's a purpose-built wallet to work with an agent as quickly as possible,” Coinbase engineering executive Erik Reppel told Decrypt at the launch.

Coinbase's x402 protocol lets software pay for data or computing services as part of a web request, often using the USDC stablecoin. That makes tiny transactions possible without requiring an agent to enter card details or obtain human approval each time.

Stablecoin issuer Circle is pushing in the same direction. Its Agent Stack, launched in May, includes stablecoin wallets and tools for payments as small as $0.000001.

“USDC is uniquely well-suited for the agentic economy because it is internet-native, programmable, and always available,” Circle product chief Nikhil Chandhok said in a company statement.

Actual agent-driven demand is harder to measure. In September, blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs estimated that agents accounted for only 0.6% to 7.5% of filtered x402 commerce by value, using models that cannot conclusively distinguish agents from scripts.

For consumers, ChatGPT Wallet offers familiar card payments rather than a digital asset balance. OpenAI's terms say merchants remain responsible for deliveries and returns, and users must generally contact their card issuers for billing disputes.

OpenAI plans to let users authorize future purchases within spending limits or specified categories, but has not announced when that feature will arrive. In the meantime, it warns that merchant websites may block shopping agents or flag otherwise legitimate Wallet purchases as fraud.
