Metzger considers it an excellent complement to her skincare routine and is a proactive way for her to address her mature skin concerns.

On the downside, the customization component overcomplicated things, said Metzger. Crunched for time? Same! In just three minutes, Solawave emits a powerful blend of four LED wavelengths—red, near-infrared, deep red, and amber—to smooth lines on my décolletage. This device is still worth using—I saw a literal glow-up within my first month of use, and it only got better with time.

Boasting a 4.5/5 star rating from nearly 350 reviews, this red light therapy device is beloved by Amazon shoppers for its ability to offer cosmetic benefits and support your at-home recovery.

That said, there is a con to keep in mind: The LED mask sits close to the face despite its more structured design. On the downside, it's a bit heavier than the Qure mask, which means it can become cumbersome after multiple wears, and the high price tag may deter some. While it’s an upfront investment, using this device for a month will still be cheaper than trekking to your dermatologist for an initial treatment and weekly upkeep.

Our testers—Earley, Wohlner, and Zitz—committed to a six-week testing window. They completed each 10-minute session three times a week and were pleased with the results. What makes this tool stand out? It combines red, acne-fighting blue, and green LED light to reduce inflammation and fade hyperpigmentation. And this palm-sized device glides effortlessly on your face and body. All you need is three minutes a day to minimize wrinkles.

#4902. Zero Motorcycles unveils $8K electric motorcycle, street-legal dirt bike, and much more

Zero Motorcycles is celebrating its 20th anniversary with a major wave of announcements at EICMA 2026, unveiling several new electric two-wheelers alongside some important technology upgrades that could make its existing motorcycles even more appealing.

The biggest news is an entirely new lightweight electric street motorcycle known as Project Ventura, designed to bridge the gap between the increasingly popular world of electric bikes plus lightweight e-motos and the full-size electric motorcycle market. But that’s far from the only news coming out of Zero’s booth in Milan.

The electric motorcycle maker is also announcing a new street-legal version of its XE electric dirt bike that was previously only street-legal in Europe, introducing its LS3 electric scooter to Europe, introducing a redesigned smartphone app, and sharing more details about its upcoming DC fast-charging system.

There’s quite a bit to unpack here, so let’s get into it.

Perhaps the most exciting announcement is Project Ventura, a new lightweight electric motorcycle that Zero hopes will attract an entirely new generation of riders.

With supermoto-inspired styling, 17-inch wheels, and a more approachable design than the company’s larger street motorcycles, Ventura appears aimed squarely at riders who want something more substantial than a typical lightweight e-moto but aren’t necessarily looking for a full-size, high-performance motorcycle.

And with a targeted price of less than US $8,000, it could be one of Zero’s most accessible street motorcycles yet.

The bike features a new electric powertrain producing over 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, delivering a sustained top speed of 65 mph (105 km/h) and a momentary maximum speed of 81 mph (130 km/h).

That’s a particularly interesting distinction, as it positions the bike as being able to briefly reach highway-capable speeds with the occasional burst of extra performance, but perhaps not for longer sustained highway stretches.

Importantly, we don’t yet know the battery capacity, though Zero is giving us a hint by publishing a range estimate. The company is quoting an estimated real-world range of 93 miles (150 km), but without a real battery capacity figure to parse, it’s hard to take that range estimate at face value.

We do know that the bike will feature onboard Level 2 charging, allowing riders to plug into public AC charging stations without carrying around a separate external charger – something more common on the smallest of electric motorcycles that attempt to cut down on weight and cost by using an off-board charger.

Other features include standard ABS, Bluetooth connectivity, integration with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app, and a chassis designed to accommodate a passenger.

The riding position is upright, and the bike’s supermoto-inspired geometry is intended to deliver agile handling and a playful riding experience.

Perhaps most interestingly, Zero isn’t hiding the fact that it sees the explosion of e-bikes and smaller electric motos as a potential gateway to motorcycle ownership.

“When we set out to build Project Ventura, we had three guiding principles: first, build a bike so good-looking you’d want its poster above your bed. Second, make it a proper electric motorcycle that feels like a natural next step for the millions of riders who’ve spent the last four or five years on e-bikes and e-motos. And third, make it ridiculously fun to ride,” explained Jim Callahan, Zero’s Chief Product and Partnerships Officer.

That’s a notable strategy for a company that has historically focused heavily on higher-performance electric motorcycles. However, the launch of Zero’s smaller Sur Ron-style electric dirt bikes last summer showed that the motorcycle maker did see the writing on the wall in terms of the success of the e-moto market compared to larger flagship bikes.

Instead of trying to convince existing gasoline motorcycle riders to make the electric switch, Zero is increasingly looking toward younger riders who may have already fallen in love with electric two-wheelers and are ready for something faster and more capable.

But for those interested in the new Ventura, they’ll have to wait just a bit longer. The motorcycle is expected to become available in summer 2027.

Another major announcement is a new street-legal version of Zero’s XE electric dirt bike.

The original XE was introduced as part of Zero’s more affordable X Line of lightweight electric off-road motorcycles, offering a more accessible entry point to the brand than its traditional street and dual-sport models. While the model was available in street-legal format in Europe, the US versions were purely off-road affairs.

Now Zero is taking that same general concept and making it legal for public roads, opening up significantly more riding possibilities.

The new XE is fully homologated and features the necessary street equipment, including a headlight, taillight, and centrally mounted dashboard. A small integrated flyscreen and black bodywork give the motorcycle a more refined appearance, while wide dual-sport tires help it transition between pavement and dirt.

Zero has also revised the gearing, using a rear sprocket designed to balance off-road performance with the higher speeds required for street riding.

The result is a claimed top speed of 60 mph (97 km/h), making the XE capable of considerably more than simply putting around the neighborhood, though with a slight torque sacrifice.

For riders who live near off-road riding areas, the appeal is obvious. Instead of loading a dirt bike into a truck or trailer to reach the trails, owners could potentially ride directly from home to the trailhead, provided local regulations allow it.

That’s a particularly useful capability for a lightweight electric dirt bike, where much of the appeal comes from its simplicity, low maintenance, and ability to explore places that larger motorcycles might struggle to reach.

The new street-legal XE is expected to launch in spring 2027, with pricing starting at US $6,295.

Zero is also expanding its electric scooter offerings with the European debut of the LS3, a faster and more capable scooter designed for urban transportation and longer commutes.

While Zero has traditionally been associated with electric motorcycles, its growing interest in scooters represents another effort to reach riders who prioritize everyday transportation over outright performance.

The LS3 offers a top speed of 75 mph (121 km/h), which puts it well beyond the typical low-speed urban electric scooter category.

Zero also quotes a range of up to 93 miles (150 km), powered by a battery system consisting of three onboard batteries with a combined capacity of 5.6 kWh.

Interestingly, one of those batteries is removable and located beneath the seat. Riders can remove it to free up additional storage space, offering some flexibility between maximum battery capacity and cargo-carrying convenience.

That could prove useful for commuters who don’t always need the scooter’s full range but would appreciate extra room for everyday items.

The LS3 also comes equipped with heated grips and a heated seat, features that should be particularly welcome to European riders commuting through colder months.

Connected technology rounds out the package, including compatibility with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app.

The LS3 is expected to become available in Europe in spring 2027.

Beyond the new vehicles, Zero is also working on a redesigned smartphone application that promises to give riders considerably more control over their motorcycles.

The new app is being developed for the LS3, 2027 Street and Dual Sport motorcycles, and Project Ventura.

One of the more interesting features is the ability to customize riding modes. In addition to preset modes that adjust power delivery and regenerative braking, riders will be able to create a custom mode and individually tune parameters including speed, power, torque, and regeneration.

The app will also include a charging-station finder, allowing riders to search for nearby chargers and filter them by charging speed, network, and availability. Apple Maps integration will provide route guidance to selected charging locations.

An optional ride-history feature can automatically record trips, including their distance, duration, and route previews.

Riders will also be able to customize their motorcycle’s dashboard layout, choosing which information appears in each quadrant of the display.

Battery management is getting some attention, too. The app will provide controls for scheduled charging, target charge levels, charging limits, and long-term battery storage settings.

Zero is also adding integrated feedback and support tools that allow owners to report problems or suggest improvements directly through the app, including photos and diagnostic logs.

The redesigned app is expected to arrive in 2027.

Perhaps the most consequential technology announcement, at least for riders who want to take their electric motorcycles beyond short commutes and weekend rides, is Zero’s continued development of DC fast charging.

Zero says it is targeting a 2027 launch for its new fast-charging system, which will support compatible Street and Dual Sport motorcycles.

The system is being designed to charge compatible batteries from 20% to 80% in less than 30 minutes.

That’s a major improvement in convenience compared to the longer AC charging stops that have traditionally been associated with Zero motorcycles.

Importantly, the company is developing the system for both North America and Europe, with different charging connectors for each market.

European motorcycles will use the CCS standard, while North American models will feature NACS connectors.

The latter is particularly interesting given the growing adoption of NACS charging infrastructure across North America, potentially making it easier for electric motorcycle riders to access a wider range of charging locations.

Zero is also developing a retrofit option for eligible existing motorcycles, meaning some current owners may eventually be able to upgrade their bikes rather than purchasing entirely new models to take advantage of the technology.

The company hasn’t yet announced pricing or a complete list of compatible motorcycles, and the retrofit option remains under development.

Still, the prospect of adding significantly faster charging to existing electric motorcycles could be an important development for the brand.

There are several exciting announcements here, but I think the biggest takeaway is that Zero seems to be increasingly focused on making electric motorcycling more accessible through smaller and more affordable options.

For much of its 20-year history, Zero has been a pioneer in the electric motorcycle industry, often offering impressive performance and technology, but at prices that made its motorcycles difficult for many riders to justify. The bikes have long won acclaim, but $20k was a big ask.

The company’s more affordable X Line bikes have already demonstrated that Zero is interested in attracting riders who might never have considered one of its larger electric motorcycles. The street-legal XE takes that concept a step further, and Project Ventura could be an even more important addition.

I’m particularly intrigued by Zero’s explicit acknowledgment that millions of people have spent the last several years riding e-bikes and smaller electric motos, and that many of those riders may be ready to graduate to something bigger.

That’s an audience I’ve been watching grow for years. These are riders who are already comfortable with electric drivetrains, who appreciate the simplicity of twist-and-go riding, and who don’t necessarily have any attachment to gasoline engines or traditional motorcycle culture.

For those riders, a lightweight, fun electric motorcycle capable of 81 mph and priced below $8,000 could be an awfully compelling next step.

The new street-legal XE is similarly exciting, especially for riders who want to combine urban transportation with off-road adventures without needing a truck to haul their bike around.

During the late 60’s to the early 70’s the in thing in motorcycles was the street legal dirt bike. I had a 1971 model Kawasaki 125 street legal dirtbike that I bought for $525 and it was great for getting around as a kid. When this street legal type of EV bike goes below $5000 it could be the next big thing.

And while the new motorcycles are likely to get most of the attention, I wouldn’t overlook the DC fast-charging announcement. Charging speed has long been one of the biggest limitations facing electric motorcycles, particularly for riders interested in longer trips. A sub-30-minute charging stop isn’t quite gasoline-level convenience, but it’s getting much closer to something that can work for real motorcycle touring.

Of course, several important details remain unknown, and we’ll have to wait until 2027 to see how these products and technologies perform in the real world.

But taken together, these announcements suggest Zero is making a serious effort to expand beyond its traditional audience and build electric motorcycles for a much broader range of riders.

And after two decades of helping pioneer the electric motorcycle industry, that’s exactly the kind of evolution I’d like to see.

In terms of safety, I found this trimmer rarely—if ever—caused cuts or irritation. However, that safety seems to come at the cost of precision. Braun built this trimmer to power through all kinds of hair, no matter the length or location. These issues tend to arise when the blades cut hair beneath the skin’s surface, creating friction and complicating regrowth.

In contrast, a single- or double-blade razor trims hair cleanly at the surface, reducing skin damage and delivering a smoother, gentler shave. But I found the BIC Flex 5 Sensitive razor to be the best of both worlds. Covering the ground of a five-blade razor with the softness of a one-blade razor.

Not only did it speed up the admittedly long process of pubic shaving, but it did so without destroying my most delicate skin. The only trade-off here is that this razor doesn’t get quite as close as other, less-gentle blades. Still, it gets much closer than the trimmers on this list, and nearly as close as the Gillette Intimate Razor. Besides, going entirely bald down here is rarely a goal of mine, so I saw this as a positive.

If you’re looking to go as close to bald as possible, this is your best option. Designed specifically for body grooming, this razor features a compact, ultra-grippy handle that minimizes the risk of dropping and helps you maintain control while in the shower (or contorting yourself to reach every part of your groin). The blades are about as spaced out from each other as I’ve seen on any razor, which helps prevent clogging—something that is even more common when dealing with thick body hair.

Surrounding the two blades are a lubricating strip, an anti-ingrown bar, and an anti-irritation bar that work to reduce friction and help prevent trapped hairs. Plus, the blade head sits on a flexible pivoting disc, which helps the razor follow the contours of your body for smoother, more consistent contact with the skin.

Testing Notes: I’m not usually one to go completely bald below the waist, but this razor makes a strong case for it. It left my skin smooth and irritation-free without any lingering bumps in the days following, which is something I’ve found to be common when dealing with body razors. The grip is incredible and the pivoting head makes getting into the nooks and crannies of your body easy.

Before diving into the most intimate of manscaping, it’s important to consider a few key components of the device you’ll be using, given the sensitivity of the region. Not only to avoid any dreaded nicks or cuts, but also to ensure that the process is completed as seamlessly as possible.

Whenever you’re dealing with a trimmer of any kind, the battery life is one of the most prominent considerations. No one wants their device to sputter out and die when they’ve only managed to trim half their beard, and the same is true for the nether regions. Sure, it may be less noticeable than having half a beard, but it can still be uncomfortable. Look for devices that can hold a charge for at least an hour; this should guarantee you two to three sessions per charge.

Any less and you’re going to have to really be diligent with charging after every use or run the risk of it dying out before the next job’s done. The easiest way to avoid this scenario is to look for a rechargeable device, but more on that in a sec.

If you’re a committed pubic trimmer and never travel without one, look for the lighter options to ensure you can comfortably keep them in a carry-on or bag without weighing yourself down. While the TSA and airlines do not generally have a weight limit specifically for grooming devices, they do limit the weight of your bags, so we recommend sticking to trimmers that are under 10 oz to avoid too much bulk. Plus, if you’re new to this type of thing, steering away from tools that are heavier than this until you get a better idea of the process will help you avoid any painful slip-ups.

Similarly, how often do you change up your overall manscaping look? If you find yourself often changing up lengths and styles, you’re going to want to grab a device with multiple attachments and length options. The Braun Series 9 is the best-case scenario here, as it comes packed with nine attachments that create a total of 40 (!) length options. On the other hand, if you typically go full bald or keep it one consistent length, focus on the device’s head shape and blade material or close shaving ability rather than the number of attachments.

For the closest shave (outside of a cartridge razor), look to stainless steel or metal blades, as these can handle the most motor power and are more adept at plowing through thicker hair. While most of the trimmers on this list (and pubic trimmers in general) do not list their official motor power, having stainless steel blades is often the best indicator of a powerful tool, as it shows the brand looks towards the highest quality materials and performance available.

Not to mention, stainless steel blades are typically easier to clean. That being said, the risk of nicks and cuts is higher, so if you’re new to pubic trimming, opt for ceramic or plastic blades. These are gentler on skin, though they won’t get you as close to bare skin.

Use a rechargeable pubic trimmer to avoid mid-trim shutdowns and eliminate the need for spare batteries. Keep it charged between 30 percent and 80 percent to maintain performance and prevent it from dying when you need it most.

Do you prefer to do your manscaping in or outside of the shower? There is no wrong answer, but whichever you prefer is worth keeping in mind when choosing a trimmer. Some are made to be used wet, like the Philips Norelco OneBlade, while others not so much. If you’re a dedicated shower groomer, focus on the fully waterproof options.

As Men’s Health’s grooming editor, I test electric razors and similar devices for a living. When it comes to pubic trimmers, we’ve been testing these devices for nearly three years since this story was first published in 2023. For this update, I tested or retested over 15 pubic trimmers and razors, while consulting with skin and haircare experts on which tools they recommend in 2026.

I also considered top-reviewed trimmers that had high customer ratings on trusted e-commerce websites. After putting each device to the test, I evaluated its effectiveness, safety, and value. Following 12 months of testing, these seven tools proved to be the best for the job.

1. First and foremost, make sure you have ample time and are not rushed. This is not something you want to speed through.

2. Position yourself in front of a mirror with good lighting to make sure you have good visibility for all the crevices.

3. Grab your trimmer and pick your desired length. If you plan to fully shave your pubic hair, set the length long enough to shave easily but not too long—about a couple of days’ worth of stubble. If you’re trimming, start with a longer setting than you want at first; you can always trim it shorter later.

4. Apply baby powder on your pubic area while it’s dry to help soak up extra moisture and plump up the hair.

5. With short, gentle strokes, use the trimmer to cut the hair. Pubic hair grows in a variety of directions, so you’ll want to go slow and possibly go over the same areas a few times. For your scrotum and shaft, go extra slow and stretch the skin to flatten it and make it easier to trim. If you’re trimming your buttcheeks, crack, or perineum, you may want to place a hand mirror on the floor to help see where you’re trimming. You can also place one leg on a tub or toilet to make the area easier to see.

6. If you’re happy with the trim job, then you’re done! Hop in the shower to wash off.

7. If you’re going to shave completely, once you’re out of the shower, apply a pre-shave oil and shaving cream to the areas you’re going to shave. The key here is not to be stingy with the cream.

8. When you’re taking a razor to your nether regions, you’ll want to be extra careful. Shave with the grain of the hair in short, slow strokes. Do not—I repeat—do not rush. You’ll want to use the same stretching technique on your scrotum and shaft as you did while trimming, and the mirror is ideal if you’re taking the razor around back.

9. Make sure to rinse the razor frequently to avoid clogs and reapply shaving cream as needed.

10. Once you’re done, hop back in the shower to rinse everything away.

11. Apply a moisturizer or body oil to the area to help keep it protected. You may also want to apply a moisturizer or anti-chafe product regularly (like at least once a day) to help reduce friction, which can cause irritation on shaved skin, especially below the belt.

Maybe you’re a regular manscaper, or perhaps you just took the plunge into trimming out your nether regions. Regardless, one truth holds true: As soon as you take off the hair, it blooms right back again.

Sure, it might seem that your pubic hair is on a steroid-fueled regrowth. But that’s actually something of an optic illusion, says Dr. Alexes Hazen, MD, a reconstructive and cosmetic plastic surgeon at NYU Langone Health.

People who trim or shave their pubic hair often believe it grows faster than the hair on their head, but that’s a misconception, she says. We merely notice hair growth more and its speed when it’s shorter.

With pubic hair—and other body hair—the entire process takes about 30 to 44 days, Dr. Hazen says. That means the same pubes that started to grow will shed in about a month to a month and a half.

#4900. Is Pilates Effective For Weight Loss? Instructors Share How To Incorporate It Into Your Routine

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It’s nearly impossible to scroll through social media right now without seeing some celebrity or influencer rave about the perks of Pilates. But even with all the buzz surrounding this popular practice, details are a little fuzzy on whether Pilates is an effective workout for weight loss.

First off, know that the health and fitness benefits of having a Pilates practice are so much more than that. This form of exercise is known for improving your posture, breathing, flexibility, and core strength. As Claudette Sariya, CPT, a personal trainer and fitness educator based in New York City, notes, “any movement that you can enjoy regularly and consistently can help you lose weight.”

So, doing Pilates (or any workout for that matter) to stay active paired with a nutrition plan is likely to help you with weight loss. But it probably won't help expedite your weight loss in the same way that, say, lifting heavy weights would. (We'll get into why!)

The focus of Pilates is not weight loss, experts point out. "Pilates should be considered part of your self-care routine," says Jacquelyn Brennan, CSCS, pilates instructor and co-founder of Chicago-based Pilates and Coffee. "We all need to move our spines more, move our joints through every range of motion, and everyone needs to be breathing better."

All of those healthy practices together can aid weight loss, though. Here's everything to know about doing Pilates when you're trying to lose weight.

Meet the experts: Gabbi Berkow, RD, CPT, is a nutritionist and Pilates instructor. Jacquelyn Brennan, CSCS, is a Pilates instructor and co-founder of Chicago-based Pilates and Coffee. Claudette Sariya, CPT, is a personal trainer and fitness educator based in New York City. Sonja R. Price Herbert is a certified Pilates instructor and founder of Black Girl Pilates. Nofar Hagag is a Pilates instructor and creator of the Nofar Method.

One form of Pilates isn't superior to another to drop pounds, experts agree. "For weight loss, I don’t think one type of Pilates is necessarily best,” says Berkow. Yet, there are different flavors—and finding one that you enjoy and will keep coming back to can, in turn, help you commit to a fitness routine and lose weight.

When someone mentions Pilates, they're often referring to Romana’s Pilates, which features exercises that Joseph Pilates (the founder) developed, explains Gabbi Berkow, RD, CPT, a nutritionist and Pilates instructor. Some studios are dedicated to classical or Romana’s Pilates (which is what Berkow is trained in) but there are studios that feature different Pilates-based workouts, which means they use Pilates-inspired moves but don't follow the classical version to a T. Some Pilates classes take place on a mat (a.k.a. mat Pilates), while others occur on a reformer, which is basically a sliding, spring-loaded platform.

You also might hear the term "athletic Pilates," but that is usually a description of the pace, says Sonja R. Price Herbert, a certified Pilates instructor and founder of Black Girl Pilates. These classes are designed to be fast-paced and high-intensity, and may even have some high-intensity interval training (HIIT) exercises and elements in the mix, which would make them better for weight loss due to the way HIIT training can help you burn more calories during and after the workout.

But if you really want to maximize your Pilates practice for weight loss and strength, it’s a good idea to use both the reformer and Cadillac machines, says Nofar Hagag, a Pilates instructor and creator of the Nofar Method. “By incorporating cardio-focused movements—such as squats, planks, and Pilates burpees, your heart rate increases, boosting calorie burn and metabolism,” she says. “These high-energy moves are paired with strength-training exercises, like side leg lifts and abs teasers, to build lean muscle and improve body composition.” (Reminder: Loading your muscles with resistance is key for muscle growth—and more muscle mass helps you burn more calories at rest and, in turn, lose weight.)

What you also want when it comes to Pilates and weight loss: an instructor who knows what they’re doing, is committed to safe movements, and who will challenge you, says Berkow. “You want to make sure your Pilates class is a workout. It shouldn’t be just a series of slow, easy stretches. Pilates has to contribute to your total daily calorie burn for it to make a difference in weight loss,” she says.

If you’ve ever gone to a class, you know how insane the core work is (seriously, the famed Hundreds exercise is not for the faint of heart...or abs).

While you cannot spot-reduce fat, Pilates can help you learn how to properly engage your pelvic floor and deep core muscles, says Brennan. "Pilates will teach you how to engage your muscles correctly, which will lend to increased activation during core exercises and lead to [the appearance of a] 'tighter tummy,' " she says.

However, to see abs definition, you do have to lose the fat that sits on top of your muscles, which requires proper nutrition, says Berkow. Think: a diet rich in whole, fresh foods and a limit on overly-processed foods and snacks.

There is some research to suggest that you can lose weight doing Pilates—but it's tough to give an exact number of pounds considering so many individual factors play into weight loss, such as genetics, sleep and stress, lifestyle habits, and more.

A meta-analysis of 11 randomized controlled trials published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2021 found that pilates “dramatically” reduced body weight and body fat percentage in adults with overweight or obesity. And the longer the person practiced Pilates, the bigger the weight loss. Older research has had mixed results, though, with one small study concluding Pilates was indeed helpful for weight loss, while another found it had no impact on weight loss in post-menopausal women.

You want a mat that offers a little extra cushion than the standard yoga mat to protect your vertebrae when rolling onto your back.

ProBody Pilates Ring And Mini Exercise Ball

Pilates teachers love a good prop. You may want to have a few options—like this Pilates ring (a.k.a. magic circle) and ball set—handy for online classes.

Many studios require sticky socks for both safety and sanitary reasons, so stashing a pair in your gym bag is always a good idea. These Pointe Studio socks offer a non-slip bottom in tons of cute colors and patterns.

Looking for a mat that's a bit more aesthetic? The 8mm-sized Bala Play Mat is another cushy option (and it’s antimicrobial, to boot!).

If you want to invest in your Pilates practice, this home reformer is a cult favorite that often shows up in professional studios. During testing, we found this machine to have a sleek, low profile, sturdy frame, and impressive footbar adjustability.

Again, traditional Pilates isn’t a modality designed for weight loss. Generally, traditional classes do not pack enough of a cardio or strength training component, Herbert says: “It is not a steady-state [cardio modality] like running, jumping, or walking. There is also not enough weight [or resistance] to aid in a decrease in body fat.” Instead, Herbert says that “Pilates focuses on awareness of the body, efficiency of movement, and breath.”

Pilates will, however, deliver far more benefits than just a lower number on a scale that may indirectly help with weight loss. For instance, Pilates involves breath work, encouraging deeper belly breaths that are in direct contrast to the shallow breathing many of us do on the regular. “Shallow breathing leads to increased cortisol levels, which contributes to weight gain. One could say that through pilates and learning to breathe better, you’d have lower cortisol—and thus, stress—levels, something that can help you lose weight,” Brennan says.

Feeling better, both mentally and physically, will also encourage you to take care of your body, says Berkow—and Pilates can definitely be a key part of achieving an overall weight-loss goal.

#4899. Bitcoin ETFs Lose $2.1 Billion in November as Outflow Streak Hits Seven Days

Bitcoin ETFs Lose $2.1 Billion in November as Outflow Streak Hits Seven Days

Bitcoin ETF investors are still heading for the exits, and the price slide is speeding up.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $185.4 million on Friday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, extending their outflow streak to seven straight trading days.

The funds lost about $829 million this week after shedding nearly $1.3 billion the week before, bringing November’s outflows to roughly $2.1 billion.

The selling so far this month has been relentless. The funds bled $1.4 billion over five sessions earlier in the streak as investors cut risk. Cumulative net inflows since launch have slipped to $55.3 billion, and total net assets fell to $94.9 billion, below the $100 billion mark they held through much of October.

Other crypto funds haven’t escaped the rout. Ethereum ETFs took in a modest $2.3 million on Friday, snapping a six-day outflow streak, but still lost about $336 million on the week and roughly $702 million so far in November. Solana ETFs shed about $28 million this week, though they retain $1.6 billion in cumulative net inflows.

Spot crypto ETFs hold the underlying asset, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum, and trade on stock exchanges like ordinary shares, giving investors exposure through a regular brokerage account. Bitcoin funds have drawn $55.3 billion in net inflows since debuting in January 2024. Because issuers report flows daily and much of the money comes from institutions and financial advisers, the figures have become a closely watched gauge of investor sentiment.

The outflows have tracked a sharp sell-off. Bitcoin traded near $64,500 over the weekend, down 6% over 24 hours and about 15% on the week, according to CoinGecko, and it has lost more than 22% over the past month.

Ethereum fell 8.4% to about $1,790, and Solana dropped 12% to roughly $70. Total crypto market value slid 4.5% to about $2.3 trillion.

Bitcoin hit a 12-week low this week as fears of further Federal Reserve rate hikes erased its summer rally, and concentrated liquidations pushed the price below $69,000 earlier in the week.

Not every institution is retreating. JPMorgan’s holdings of Bitcoin and crypto-linked securities are approaching $1 billion, according to its most recent SEC filing. However, those purchases predate the more recent market downturn.

#4898. BYD’s 3,000-hp EV crashes at about 280 mph — Watch the driver escape unharmed

BYD’s electric supercar delivers an insane nearly 3,000 hp from four electric motors. During a high-speed test, the Yangwang U9 Extreme crashed at about 280 mph, but the driver walked away unharmed.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme is a “dream car,” as BYD calls it, a souped-up, track-focused version of its electric hypercar.

After it became the world’s fastest production car last year, reaching a top speed of 496.22 km/h, or about 308 mph, BYD is attempting to beat it by breaking the 500 km/h (310 mph) mark.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme features the world’s first mass-produced 1,200V ultra-high-voltage platform and BYD’s e4 platform.

The quad-motor setup is the first in the world rated at 30,000 rpm, BYD said, delivering nearly 3,000 hp (3,000 PS) combined.

While BYD is preparing to attempt a run this month, the company shared a video of the Yangwang U9 Xtreme crashing in a violent high-speed test.

During the first run, it clocked over 350 km/h (217 mph), no problem. On the second run, it hit over 420 km/h (261 mph).

However, during the third run, BYD was attempting to reach over 450 km/h (280 mph) when the vehicle violently crashed into the guardrail and continued spinning out of control. You can see some of the footage from inside the vehicle.

BYD said that after a comprehensive medical exam, the hospital found the driver in good health with no serious injuries.

When I was still in law enforcement, we did some pursuit driving training and you learn a lot about the dynamics of a vehicle. It's amazing just how quickly and badly something can go wrong at just 100 mph let alone nearly triple that speed. The fact is that the average person can't drive to the max limits of a basic car like a Corolla let alone super cars.

Is it time to reign in the HP and speed wars? Do we need vehicles that can do 0-60 in less than 3 seconds? Unless these companies begin to require 40+ hour specialized training courses in order to buy/operate these high HP vehicles today, then maybe it's time to stop the silly push for more.

And BTW. No matter what the performance levels are of any cars today, I still feel that it would be smart to push legal driving age to at least 17 or 18 instead of 16 and make getting a DL harder to do with way more emphasis on driver's education training.

The vehicle’s high-strength carbon-fiber cabin also held up impressively despite the front and rear damage.

It didn’t take long for BYD to try again, reaching a top speed of 457.89 km/h (284.5 mph) on the next run. Jiang Gong, one of Yangwang’s riders, said he sees some leeway and believes it can break 500 km/h (310 mph).

At the end of the video, BYD said (translated into English), “The ultimate pursuit has no end; the summit will eventually be reached.”

If you need extra support, we recommend underwear with a pouch or a snugger fit around the waistband. For some men with testicular pain or discomfort, they may want to find a style that fits well and doesn't ride up or bunch, as this could aggravate their symptoms.

Your underwear is the first thing you put on and the last thing you take off, so it has to work with you, not against you, all day long. If it doesn't do its job, you'll feel it, whether it's discomfort, chafing, or overheating.

Think about it: excellent underwear isn't just about looking cool (though that's like icing on the cake). It's about how it performs in real life. Are you lounging at home? Going for a long run? Stuck on a flight for hours? Each of these scenarios demands something different. You need underwear that supports your lifestyle, whether that's stretch for flexibility, moisture-wicking for sweat, or breathability to keep things fresh down yonder.

The best breathable underwear manages heat and moisture so sweat can escape instead of getting trapped against your skin. Many use micro-knit or mesh-like weaves that create tiny air channels within the fabric, allowing heat to dissipate and air to circulate as you move. Others incorporate moisture-wicking fibers to pull sweat away from the body and spread it across the surface of the fabric so it evaporates faster. Some brands even add targeted “cool zones” or thinner panels in high-sweat areas to boost airflow where you need it most.

When underwear can’t breathe, moisture builds up, leading to overheating, chafing, irritation, and odor. Breathable underwear works with your body by keeping things cooler, drier, and more comfortable throughout the day. For Men’s Health guys, breathability makes a difference for everyday wear, long commutes, desk jobs, workouts, travel days, and humid conditions. It’s especially clutch for guys who sweat easily, live in hot climates, train hard, or spend long stretches in the same pair from morning to night.

As part of the Men’s Health style team, led by our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, I’ve tested some of the best—and worst—underwear on the market firsthand. Since 2015, our team has worn, washed, and stressed-tested more than 100 pairs across every major style, brand, and fabric imaginable, from classic cotton briefs to high-tech performance boxer briefs and luxe everyday upgrades.

Testing wasn't limited to just one body type or fit preference. In addition to my own wear tests, multiple Men's Health editors with different builds pitched in, spanning sizes from small through XXL. This allowed us to see how each pair fit and performed across a wide range of body types, rises, thigh sizes, and proportions—and to flag issues like inconsistent sizing, rolling waistbands, or fabric that only works on one kind of frame.

I wore each pair repeatedly in real-life situations, including workdays, workouts, commutes, travel, and weekend outings. I looked at how each pair performed over time, paying close attention to whether fabrics remained soft without pilling, waistbands held their shape, seams avoided chafing, and support held up after hours of movement. I judged each pair on fabric quality, fit, breathability, odor control, stretch and recovery, durability after repeated washes, and comfort levels ranging from morning to night. Only the pairs that consistently delivered comfort, support, and long-term performance earned a spot on this list. What you’ll find here are the top 12 best men’s underwear options that rose to the top after years of hands-on testing by the Men’s Health team.

Boxers: They’re classic, loose-fitting shorts that are lightweight, with lots of breathing room, and zero restriction. They’re great for lounging or sleeping because they feel airy and relaxed, but that same looseness makes them less practical under slim pants. Fabric can bunch, ride up, and offer little to no support if you’re moving around a lot. Boxer briefs: They’re cut like boxers but fit snugly like briefs. That means they hug your thighs, hold everything in place, and layer smoothly under jeans, trousers, or even gym shorts. They also prevent chafing since the fabric creates a barrier between your thighs—a lifesaver if you walk a lot or hit the gym. The tradeoff? They’re less airy than boxers, but most guys prefer the balance of comfort, coverage, and support.

That really depends on your laundry schedule. If you’re someone who does laundry once a week, aim for at least 10 to 12 pairs so you’ve got a little cushion. If laundry happens less often—say every two weeks—you’ll probably want 15 to 20 pairs. If you’re very active, then consider stocking your drawer with 25 to 30 pairs. Basically, you want enough to last until wash day plus a couple extra for workouts, surprise trips, or the occasional lazy Sunday when you just don’t feel like doing laundry.

A good rule of thumb: it’s reasonable to refresh your stash every six to 12 months, but quality underwear can last longer depending on fabric, frequency of wear, washing, and condition. If the elastic’s shot, they’re sagging, developing holes, or the fabric’s thinning, that’s your cue to toss them. Think of it as a rotation—you don’t need to replace everything at once, but gradually swap in new pairs so you’re always stocked with comfortable, supportive ones.

Every man has worn them at some point; boxers are light and loose and so freeing. They're the classic underwear style for men that feels very relaxed with short legs. This type of underwear is perfect for lounging around the house, sleeping, or wearing under relaxed-fit pants. Also comes in a variety of prints and patterns (hello, personality).

Think speedo. Think upside-down triangle. Briefs provide the required coverage and optimal support while exposing more skin for ease of mobility. Here, there's no risk of leg fabric riding up (because there's none).

Perhaps the most popular one, it's a hybrid of loose-fit boxers and tight briefs, offering a solid balance of support and comfort. If you’re not a fan of underwear that rides up too high, go for boxer briefs that have a longer leg and a snug fit, like compression underwear that’s perfect for the gym. They should skim the leg versus squeezing you too tight.

Like the title says, a trunk is similar to boxer briefs but with a shorter cut—halfway up the thigh. It's best for guys who want something fitted but less fabric around the leg. For some visual assistance, think of trunks as the underwear style that most CK models wear on big billboards.

It depends on personal preference, comfort, and the activity. Here's a quick breakdown to help guide your choice, weighing the pros and cons of both.

Tight underwear (e.g., briefs, boxer briefs) provides better support, which is especially useful for physical activities like running or working out. This type reduces chafing and prevents excessive movement, which can help with comfort throughout the day. Works well under slim-fit pants, as it avoids bunching and creates a cleaner silhouette. If it's too tight, it can restrict airflow and potentially cause discomfort or sweating, especially in warmer weather. Overly tight fits might not be ideal for guys concerned about reproductive health, though the effect is typically negligible with properly sized underwear.

On the other hand, loose underwear is better suited for lounging or casual, low-impact activities since it allows more airflow and freedom of movement. It feels more breathable, making it ideal for hotter climates or relaxed settings. Also, loose underwear can be paired with loose-fit pants for added comfort. This option lacks support, which feel uncomfortable during workouts or physical activity. Plus, it can cramp your style—bunching up under tighter pants and offering a restrictive feel.

If you want to protect the structural integrity of your underwear's waistband, the best way to keep them from stretching is to hand wash them and hang them dry. But given how impractical that is, the second best option is to put them in the washing machine on cold water and use a low dryer setting so the elastic doesn't warp. However, our testers say that most of the pairs they've tried have kept their waistbands' shapes even after several trips to the laundromat. If your underwear's waistband has lost its shape, you're probably overdue to replace it.

Even the best underwear won’t last if you don’t take care of it properly. Washing underwear inside out helps remove sweat and bacteria more effectively while protecting the fabric’s surface. Cold or warm water is usually best, as hot water can break down elastic fibers and cause shrinkage over time. Skip harsh detergents and fabric softeners, especially for performance or moisture-wicking underwear. Softeners can coat fibers and reduce breathability and odor control. When possible, air-drying is ideal, as high heat from dryers is the fastest way to kill stretch and warp waistbands. If you do use a dryer, stick to low heat.

#4896. Arthur Hayes ‘flattered’ as Coinbase backs US stock perps

Arthur Hayes said he was “flattered” by Coinbase’s defense of US stock perpetual futures, a decade after BitMEX launched perpetual swaps.

Arthur Hayes, co-founder of BitMEX, said he was “flattered” by Coinbase’s support for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) in a US legal dispute over stock perpetual futures.

“When we launched the perpetual swap at BitMEX in 2016, Washington’s reaction was less than warm,” Hayes told Cointelegraph. “Ten years later, Coinbase is in federal court defending the right to offer them on US stocks. I’m flattered. Imitation is the sincerest form of regulation.”

Coinbase and five other companies submitted a brief on Monday opposing the alliance’s request to block trading in perpetual futures tied to individual stocks. The court accepted the brief on Tuesday.

The Capital Markets Alliance Association (CMAA), which brought the lawsuit, says the contracts should be treated as security-based swaps, which face tighter restrictions on retail trading.

Hayes was CEO of BitMEX when the crypto derivatives exchange launched its Bitcoin perpetual swap, which let traders take leveraged positions on Bitcoin without a fixed expiration date. The product helped make perpetual swaps a staple of crypto trading.

The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reportedly submitted a proposed court brief on Monday, opposing the alliance’s request to temporarily halt trading in the contracts.

The agency said it was reviewing the exchanges’ rules for listing the contracts. The brief left open whether the SEC would set those rules aside and whether the contracts qualify as security futures or security-based swaps.

Related: EU DeFi proposals could push users to riskier platforms, says Coinbase exec

In a Tuesday court filing, CMAA said that the CFTC had approved the contracts without adequately explaining its decision or addressing unresolved regulatory questions.

The group also cited about $375 million in reported 24-hour notional trading volume for Kalshi’s stock perpetuals shortly after launch, claiming the products were already diverting business from traditional stock markets.

Stock perpetuals let traders speculate on individual share prices without owning the underlying stocks. Unlike traditional futures, the contracts have no fixed expiration date.

On Nov. 3, US District Judge Valerie Caproni denied the group’s request for a temporary restraining order because it had yet to show likely irreparable harm. She found the alliance was likely to succeed on its claim that the CFTC exceeded its authority.

Wojciech Kaszycki, strategy adviser to BTCS SA, said the lack of a fixed expiration or delivery date could complicate the case for treating perpetual contracts as futures.

Kaszycki told Cointelegraph that the case “sale for future delivery.”

However, he warned that a ruling against the CFTC could push trading activity toward offshore and decentralized platforms.

“The product doesn’t die; it just changes address,” he said.

LED face masks are hands-free, so you can wear one while on your phone, reading, or watching TV. Here’s what to know when purchasing the best LED face mask.

Most at-home red light therapy devices use a mix of red and blue wavelengths. However, each LED shade offers different benefits, so you’ll need to find the right color for the skin concerns you want to treat, says dermatologist Leah Ansell, MD. Here’s a quick guide:

Standardized wavelengths are helpful, but the number of lights is also important, says dermatologist Azadeh Shirazi, MD. A higher concentration of LED bulbs provides more even coverage.

Not all LED face masks are built the same.

Carving out time for self-care in your busy schedule can sometimes feel like a stretch. Thankfully, these LED face masks require a relatively low time commitment. The popular Dr. Dennis Gross face mask requires only a quick 3-minute daily session for the best results. Others range from 10- to 15-minute sessions for three to five days a week. With such speedy treatment, it’s no wonder the makeup artists for Halle Berry and Carey Mulligan have primped their clients using CurrentBody Skin.

LED face masks are usually class II devices. They’re either FDA-listed or FDA-registered, meaning the brand notified the agency about the device. However, this listing doesn’t indicate the products are approved, cleared, or authorized by the agency.

They could also be FDA-cleared, meaning they are similar to other devices that are legally marketed for the same use. Our editors prioritized testing face masks that are either FDA-listed, -registered, or -cleared. And I referenced the FDA database to verify the status of our recommendations.

After all, you're going to have to put in the time to see the results, so it might as well be an enjoyable experience. If you're fidgety and can't commit to sitting still or lying down for 15 minutes straight, look for a cordless option. Now if comfort is king, look for adjustable straps, a padded interior, or a flexible outer shell. TheraFace boasts all of these features and even vibrates for extra relaxation.

Yes, it’s generally low-risk for most users, says dermatologist Dendy Engelman, MD. "LED light therapy is not an invasive treatment, and when done properly, the risks are minimal," she says. A 2018 study in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology points out that this treatment has an "excellent" safety profile, Dr. Ansell says. While they're safe to use on the skin, there's concern about eye damage from these lights. So, it's a good idea to wear the eye inserts to help protect them.

If you’re photosensitive or have connective tissue conditions, you should either skip LED light therapy or approach it with caution, advises Dr. Ansell. If neither issue is a problem for you, Dr. Engelman suggests wearing it a few times a week, but it's crucial to refer to your specific mask's instructions for the recommended time.

Start with clean skin, says Dr. Engelman. After washing your face in the morning or at night, set your mask to the proper wavelength, then put on goggles. Comfort is key, so feel free to adjust any straps and align yourself with the cushioning (if your mask has any) before using it. Post-use, finish the rest of your skincare routine, and definitely use it before applying retinol, says Dr. Shirazi.

#4894. Tesla cuts FSD’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe

Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

The RDW’s notice is the clearest official confirmation of how the system was configured when the Dutch regulator approved FSD Supervised on April 10. The “speed margin,” which lets the system deviate from the detected limit for “safety and traffic flow,” could go up to +50%. On a 100 km/h highway, that’s 150 km/h. In a 30 km/h city zone, it’s 45 km/h.

Now the margin tops out at +10%. It also resets to 0% every time the car starts, and the RDW says other speed-related functions are now disabled by default. It didn’t say which ones.

The new name shows up on the in-car display, in the owner’s manual, and in other driver information on HW4 vehicles. Tesla pushes all of it over the air.

The RDW describes the update as “several minor changes” that Tesla asked it to assess. The regulator says it checked the implementation, found no adverse or unintended effects, and folded the changes into the existing type approval without amending or extending it. It also stresses that the rename doesn’t change what the system does. It’s still driver assistance, and the driver is still responsible.

The RDW notified the nine member states that recognize its approval: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. That’s 10 countries counting the Netherlands, up from eight at the start of October.

The EU-wide decision still sits with the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV). The RDW says those talks are confidential and won’t comment on them. As we reported, the EU pushed the vote to December at the earliest, and passing it takes a qualified majority: 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Speed has been the biggest problem for Tesla’s file in Brussels. In June, Sweden asked the EU to reject FSD unless Tesla removed the ability to set speeds above the posted limit. In September, a Brussels pedestrian safety group found the system speeding in 55% of the 30 km/h segments it tested, in a country that had already approved it. France has cited urban speeding as one of its reasons for refusing to recognize the Dutch approval.

Then, on October 6, Germany’s Transport Ministry said it would back EU approval after Tesla agreed to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name, which the ministry called misleading, and to cap speed tolerance at 10%. Today’s RDW update delivers both.

But 10% isn’t what Sweden asked for. Sweden wanted no setting above the limit at all. Several European countries are known for enforcing speed limits strictly.

Good, but that’s only part of the problem. Tesla’s biggest issue with FSD right now is that it doesn’t properly detect the speed limits.

Doing 10% over the limit in North America is almost expected. However, in Europe you can get a speeding ticket for 5 kms over the limit by an automated camera/radar system. When I rent a car over there I drive the posted limit.

Being locked at 10% over the limit doesn’t mean much if you don’t know the actual limit.

The name change is needed globally and it is past due. “Tesla Assisted Driving” describes what the system does. Meanwhile, Tesla still sells the exact same kind of software in the US as “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for $99 a month. If it’s misleading in Berlin, it’s misleading in California.

Practically, this update gets Tesla Germany’s vote. The question for December is whether a 10% cap is enough for France, Italy, and Spain, or whether Sweden’s zero-tolerance line wins out.

#4893. How Wall Street Is Racing to Claim the Onchain Dollar

How Wall Street Is Racing to Claim the Onchain Dollar

For years, stablecoins were crypto’s business, dominated by Tether and Circle and used mostly to trade digital assets. That era is ending.

Over the past few months, and especially the past few weeks, the biggest names in traditional finance have moved en masse to claim a piece of the onchain dollar. Here’s the map of a land grab that’s accelerating fast.

The clearest signal came this week, when Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Santander, and Deutsche Bank were reported to be among banks committing roughly $270 million to a joint dollar-stablecoin venture codenamed “Project Faro.”

The capital funds five years of operations for a U.S.-incorporated issuer targeting a 2027 launch, part of a 21-institution coalition that has swelled from an initial group of 10. The goal is explicit: challenge Tether and Circle, which together still control about 85% of a roughly $290 billion market.

While the consortium plans, SoFi has shipped. Earlier this week, its SoFiUSD, billed as the first stablecoin from a U.S. national bank, expanded onto Polygon this month alongside Ethereum and Solana, reaching the bank’s 17 million-plus members.

SoFi also launched SoFi Earn, a tokenized deposit paying 4.40% yield that converts into SoFiUSD, and already settles its entire card program over Mastercard’s network.

Meanwhile, the federally chartered crypto bank Anchorage Digital has positioned itself as a settlement backbone.

Anchorage’s tokens can now settle transactions on Visa’s network, starting with Western Union’s USDPT, and it recently anchored both sides of the U.S.-Mexico stablecoin corridor, custodying tokens across one of the world’s largest remittance routes.

Mastercard has been the most aggressive incumbent among payment giants.

It launched a Global Money Platform with acquired stablecoin firm BVNK, rolled out a Stablecoin Security tool to screen payments for fraud, and unveiled Agent Pay for Machines, letting AI agents transact in stablecoins.

Visa, meanwhile, has expanded its own stablecoin settlement program across multiple blockchains.

The crypto-native incumbents, not to be left out, are also racing to entrench.

Circle struck a deal to bring USDC settlement to banking rails in Latin America, starting with a Colombia pilot, part of a broader expansion into dozens of emerging markets.

The catalyst is regulation. The GENIUS Act, signed in 2025, created the first U.S. framework for dollar-pegged tokens, giving regulated institutions a clear path into a business they had largely watched from the sidelines.

The Donald Trump administration has framed dollar stablecoins as a tool to extend the dollar’s reach and global hegemony, and banks that once dismissed crypto now see a settlement business they can’t afford to cede.

Much of this remains early. Project Faro has no token, no CEO, and no final name. Tether and Circle still dominate, and bank-issued tokens face a steep climb to win share.

But the direction is unmistakable: the onchain dollar, once crypto’s turf, is now contested ground, with Wall Street, the card networks and the stablecoin incumbents all racing to own the rails money moves on.

#4892. Every Lululemon Shoe Ranked: I Tested Them All, and I Have Thoughts

After putting Lululemon’s full shoe lineup to the test, here’s how each pair ranked.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Lululemon set the bar high for athleisure with its buttery-soft leggings, and continues to deliver on that front. However, since it had always been primarily an athletic wear brand, it wasn’t part of the running shoe or walking shoe conversation. But that changed in 2022 when Lululemon expanded into footwear. Since then, the brand has slowly built a following in that category, too.

I originally tried a pair of Lululemon sneakers a few months ago after reading rave reviews, but quickly stopped wearing them because they felt too snug at my usual size. But I kept seeing positive feedback from other people, making me wonder if I wrote them off too soon. After all, Lululemon is known for careful construction, thoughtful tailoring, and high-quality products.

Like many other shoe brands, each of Lululemon’s sneakers is designed with a specific purpose in mind. The brand’s shoes match Lululemon's overall understated aesthetic. While there are a few bright colors here and there, you also have plenty of neutrals and muted shades to choose from. That alone makes them stand out in a sea of eyeball-searing sneakers.

To see what I was missing beyond looks, I tried each of Lululemon’s athletic shoes—BeyondFeel, Split Shift, Wildfeel, and Chargefeel 3—to see which is the best. And since it’s best to know what you’re getting into before you grab a pair just because it matches your favorite gym outfit, I get into the details about each shoe model below. I was surprised at how wide of a range the brand offers: There’s a Lululemon sneaker for just about anything. Still, one had to come out on top. These are the best Lululemon shoes, ranked, based on months of testing.

The BeyondFeel is the shoe I originally passed on before because it ran snug. So, PSA: Consider sizing up if you prefer a roomy fit or have wide feet. While Lululemon says online that these fit true to size, that wasn't the case for me. Once I went up half a size, I was hooked.

The BeyondFeel is Lululemon's max cushioned shoe, so you can think of it like a Hoka Bondi 9 or On Cloudmonster 3. It's designed for everyday use. Think: running errands, power walking, actual running—it's all comfortable in the BeyondFeel.

I noticed a difference from my daily trainers the second I slipped my feet inside. The best way to describe the feeling is like the first time I put on a pair of Align leggings. I was immediately comfortable, with no chafing, pinching, or any other issues.

This shoe has a nice, roomy toe box, giving your feet plenty of room to swell naturally as you go about your day or rack up the mileage. It also has a stable heel and good grip although, heads up: The shoes may squeak a little when you first wear them inside.

Lululemon designed the BeyondFeel differently for women vs. men, adding an extra 2 millimeters of foam at the forefoot to take some pressure off the knees and hips. I wouldn't wear the BeyondFeel for long runs, though—it doesn't have much energy return, which is that slight bouncy feeling you may get in a shoe. But I was happy to log a few miles in them here and there, along with wearing them for weight training and just running errands. Their stylish look and comfortable feel make them a good choice for nearly everyone.

The Split Shift is Lululemon's neutral everyday running shoe, which is another way of saying it's a good shoe for most runners. The first thing you'll notice is how lightweight the shoe is. At 7.8 ounces, it's not the lightest shoe ever made, but it definitely won't feel like your feet are dragging you down when you're logging higher mileage. This sneaker has an equally breezy upper, giving it an overall airy feel.

I really appreciate the springiness of these shoes. It's not so much that it feels like you're running on mini trampolines, but there's a good energy return here to help propel you forward with each step. That's definitely a noticeable change from the BeyondFeel, which has pretty much no energy return by comparison. There's a gusseted tongue that gently hugs your ankle, along with some extra padding around the ankle that prevents rubbing. The outsole doesn't feel as grippy as the BeyondFeel, but it's a good choice for everyday road running.

My only complaint with the Split Shift is that the toe box runs a little narrow. I'm used to running in shoes with a wide toe box, and the Split Shift's smaller width across the toes means they probably won't be my go-to for everyday miles. Like the BeyondFeel, I'd suggest going up a half size if you like a roomy toe box or have wide feet.

Lululemon's Chargefeel 3 looks different from the brand's other shoes out of the box. It has an hourglass shape, with a narrow middle, more room at the toes, and an exaggerated base at the heel for stability. That shape is intentional, since this shoe is made for cross-training, hybrid, and HIIT workouts. The Chargefeel 3 is on the lighter end of weight for a gym shoe at 8 ounces, and it feels light on your feet. Still, it has everything you want in a shoe you'll be doing cross-training in, like a locked-in feeling in the heel, snug laces, and ability to handle lateral movements.

The grip on this shoe is impressive. I was able to stop cleanly while doing direction-changing indoor sprints at the gym, with no squeaking. The shoe also features a ShiftFoam midsole for a little energy return. Its not nearly as bouncy as the Split Shift, though—but you don't want that in a shoe you'll be doing hybrid workouts in anyway.

The Chargefeel 3 has a 6mm heel-to-toe drop, which may be high for those looking for a neutral strength training shoe, so it might not be ideal for lifting. It’s laser-cut mesh helps tamp down on foot sweat, along with Nulu fabric heel lining to mimic the feel of your favorite leggings.

And if you're looking for a running shoe, scroll up. This is really a gym shoe that you can do a little running in in a pinch—not something you want to do any significant mileage in. And while the Chargefeel 3 made me feel locked-in and secure during gym workouts, it's not so comfortable that I'd wear this shoe outside of exercise. If you're looking for a dedicated hybrid shoe, though, it's worth a look.

Some athletic shoe brands will slap deep lugs on a sneaker and call it a trail shoe without addressing other needs. But it's clear that Lululemon's Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

There's a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you're going down. Like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. That wasn't a huge deal on shorter runs, but it started to annoy me on longer runs. Like many others on this list, I'd consider going up a half size.

My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that's pretty common in a trail shoe. (It got better with time and more wear.) It's also worth noting that the Wildfeel isn't the most breathable shoe you'll find, and my socks were a little sweatier than usual because of it. None of these are dealbreakers. But it also meant the Wildfeel was my least favorite shoe in Lululemon's lineup.

To choose the best Lululemon shoes, I put each through regular testing over several months. I used each shoe on a near-daily basis for weeks, making sure to test it for the way it was designed. So, I wore the Wildfeel on trails and the Split Shift on daily training runs. During each testing session, I took notes on the shoe's fit, traction, stability, and overall comfort. From there, I ranked each shoe based on its testing results, along with how well it matched up to their intended use.

The best Lululemon shoe for running depends on the type of running you plan to do. If you’re in search of a neutral everyday trainer, the Split Shift is a good choice. It’s lightweight and slightly bouncy, giving you plenty of support and cushioning over daily miles. The BeyondFeel is another solid option. It’s highly cushioned for maximum comfort, making it a better choice for shorter runs.

The best Lululemon shoe for HIIT workouts is the Chargefeel 3. This sneaker has a unique hourglass shape to create a locked-in feel you’ll appreciate during HIIT workouts, along with a wide base for stability. The shoe’s grip is impressive, allowing you to stop quickly and change directions during indoor workouts.

Lululemon used to offer the Strongfeel shoe for strength training, but it’s been discontinued. Now, the Chargefeel 3 is the best option for many strength training workouts due to its wide base and stable platform. But as noted above, the shoe has a higher heel-to-toe drop of 6mm, so it’s not ideal for moves like deadlifts. So if lifting is your priority, you might want to consider a more neutral shoe for optimal biomechanics.

Lululemon often says online that its shoes fit true to size, but that wasn't my experience. I don't have wide feet, but I do appreciate a roomy toe box to accommodate the natural foot swelling that happens on workouts and runs. Most Lululemon shoes tend to run narrow across the toe box. If you have wide feet or just prefer more room to spread your toes, consider going up a size.

#4891. Volkswagen’s affordable ID. Polo wins German Car of the Year 2027 as EVs dominate

Volkswagen’s new ID. Polo took the overall title of “German Car of the Year 2027,” starting at just €24,995 ($28,000).

After winning in its class among entry-level models (up to €25,000), the VW ID. Polo beat out strong international competition to take the top spot as German Car of the Year for 2027 among all vehicles.

The Volkswagen Group has won two years in a row with a compact EV. Last year, it was the Skoda Elroq.

Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Polo with the 52 kWh battery at the end of April. In July, it added the entry-level model with the 37 kWh battery, starting at just €24,995 ($28,000) with a WLTP range of up to 207 miles (334 km).

The Life and Style variants are also available with the 37 kWh battery, starting from €29,195 ($32,500).

With DC fast charging speeds of up to 90 kW, the ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 23 minutes.

The prestigious award “confirms what the ID. Polo stands for,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said. He added the entry-level EV “brings electric mobility to where it can make the greatest impact: right into people’s everyday lives.”

Since orders opened at the end of April, Schäfer said “well over 50,000 people have ordered their ID. Polo.”

As the first of what the company calls “a true Volkswagen again,” the ID. Polo is the first to bear an established name and the brand’s new Pure Positive design language.

The jury includes nearly 50 German and international auto journalists, and the award is considered one of the most prestigious in the industry.

The reason this class of vehicles is winning awards is that Europe buys a lot of B-segment vehicles (small hatchbacks) that aren't intended as city-only transport. Many families use them as their only vehicle.

And, up till now, there haven't been many BEVs available in that category.

It is compact, reasonably powerful, reasonably fast charging, acceptable charging rate, has good luggage capacity and feels nice to drive.

In other segments, electric cars swept the awards, with the Kia PV5 van winning in the compact class (€25,000 and €40,000), and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric taking the top spot in the premium segment (€40,000 to €70,000). Hyundai’s electric sports car, the IONIQ 6 N, won German Performance Car 2027.

Martin Sander, the Group’s sales boss, said earlier this month the company is “seeing a significantly accelerated trend towards all-electric vehicles” in its home market.

VW Group’s Electric Urban Car Family has received nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June. The lineup currently includes the VW ID. Polo and ID. Cross, plus the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all based on the MEB+ platform.

While those in the US won’t see the entry-level ID. Polo, Volkswagen is set to launch the ID. Tiguan in early 2027 as a replacement for the ID.4.

But, over the past year, this one has outperformed all the rest and become my go-to top for all kinds of workouts. Whether I’m heading to barre, getting ready to lift, or lacing up my sneakers for a run, I know this top will do exactly what I need it to.

I’ve worn the Super Sleek Bra Tank in quite a few contexts: to the gym, to different types of workout classes, to physical therapy, and even while running. It’s also cute enough and offers enough coverage to wear around town running errands, but I tend to reserve it for working out.

While I wouldn’t usually trust something with a built-in bra on its own for higher-impact workouts, the Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank can handle it. Trust me, I’ve worn it for a 10K race. It’s got enough compression and support to get me through the miles. To be fair, I don’t have the highest demand when it comes to sports bras (if you know what I mean), but thanks to the support features, I think quite a few chest sizes could wear this as a standalone bra-tank combo.

When it comes to other kinds of workouts (like a high-energy class or lifting on my own), the high-compression fabric moves with me through every twist and bend, offering the right balance of stretch and support. It also stays put and requires minimal adjusting after big movements, if at all.

This top is made with Alo’s signature Airlift material, which is made from a sleek blend of durable polyester and stretchy elastane—aka it offers high compression with just enough stretch. Compared to that super soft material you might get in a comfy yoga pant, this top feels more like what you’d get in a classic athletic compression short. It’s a bit thicker, slicker—and it is opaque, so you can feel comfortable wearing it around in public.

The compressive material is also why the top is so supportive. It fits snugly to the body, keeping everything locked in place, while also managing to not feel restrictive or too tight. It also has removable pads (which I lost in the washing machine months ago!), but I’ve found that I don’t need them because the material is so snug. To note: Because it has a tighter fit, the brand recommends that you size up if you have a bigger cup size. (My usual size worked just fine for me.)

Part of the reason I wore this for my 10K race was simply that it looks better on me than just about every other workout tank I own. I think that’s mostly thanks to the compression of the garment, which gives it a smoothing effect and helps make me look snatched.

It has a low scoop neck cut with a racerback silhouette. The longline fit hits a bit lower on your torso than a regular bra would, giving it the look of a cropped tank with the fit of a supportive bra. I love that I can throw this on without worrying about an extra layer and feel a little more covered up than when I head to the gym in a regular sports bra. That said, sometimes I wish it were a bit longer, but most of my workout bottoms are high-waisted, so it ends up feeling long enough.

If you are looking for a bra-tank combo, the Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank is just about the top of the line. The garment’s high-compression, stretchy fit is perfect for a wide range of activities, while still staying comfortable and looking cute. My next move? Buying this top in every color.
